div.head: CREATION OF THE WORLD.
div.p: THE CREATION OF THE WORLD.

Sir,—l read in your last Saturday's report of a lecture given under the auspices of the Inter- national Bible Students' Association that the speaker committed himself to the belief that "there are three great worlds in the plan of God. The first, beginning at the creation of man, ended at the flood. It lasted for a period of 1,656 years," and so on. As the date of the flood is, by orthodox believers in the Mosaic cosmogony, variously assigned to from 3000 to 4000 8.C., one places the approximate date of the " Creation" as an event which happened some 7,000 years ago. Is it not amazing that, in these days when the schoolmaster is, as we know to our cost, very much abroad, utterance should be given in so serious a manner to ideas which I submit are directly at variance with ascertained facts? The different sciences are nothing more than the accumulated and classified knowledge of the cosmos gained by hard experience and the exer- cise of man's reasoning faculties. I would ask Mr. Alexander Kirkwood then, whether geology has not for him, and all others who take upon themselves the responsibility of guiding and in- structing others, any teaching and any signifi- cance? If Mr. Kirkwood's science is not science at all, but a parrot-like repetition of discredited teaching, how can he rightly "stimulate faith and increase (in any advantageous way) the, systematic study of the Bible"? I suggest that the 1.8.5. A. lecturer can well• afford to take pains in regard to ascertainable data, consider- ing the vast stores of exact knowledge now ac- cessible to the humblest student of nature.

During the same week as the 1.8.5. A. lec- turer was holding forth at Warrington upon a version of the origin of things now long aban- doned in its literal sense, an eminent scientist, Professor Arthur Keith, was, in another part of the kingdom, calling the attention of his audi- ence to the mute but eloquent teaching of the ancient human skull recently discovered at Pilt- down in Surrey. The discovery, he said, accen- tuated the differences regarding the origin of modern man. In the Early Pleistocene man- dible found at Heidelberg, the region of the chin was purely simian. It was possible that a race in England might have retained those very primitiVe features of chin and mouth when a contemporary race in Germany had reached a more human stage. . The characters of the human chin region showed modifications which appeared to be connected with the acquisition of the faculty of speech. The Piltdown skull indicated a large human brain and a lower jaw furnished with the projecting canine teeth of an ape. Professor Keith expressed the opinion that if Eoanthropus was placed in the right position in the Primate scale, it was the brain and not the jaw that was the guide. If Profes- sor Keith is right in fixing the date of Bonn- thropus as Pliocene, and Professor Elliot Smith, who has also examined the discovery, is right in interpreting the features of the brain as indi- cative of speech, there is then the remarkable revelation that mankind in the Pliocene period —a million years ago or even more—had the power of forming and communicating ideas by means of speech. Professor Keith believed that the Piltdown discovery reveals a past history for man "beyond the wildest guess or dream of the most speculative philosophers." Coming back to Bible teaching, I recall that St. Paul said: "Prove all things: hold fast to that which is good," meaning also, and indeed necessarily, that which is true. Verbum sat sapienti. • SCRITTATOIZ.

THE FUTILITY OF WAR. Sir,--Thanks are due to Mr. Parker for his timely review of Mr. Norman Angell's latest work, "The Foundations of International Polity." The reView contains a reference to the "peace party" which may lead some of your readers to imagine that Norman Angell's thesis is in some way superior to, and different from, the earlier work of the moral and Christian movement of the "pacifists." In reality there . is no "cleavage" between the two. There has been a tendency to run the International Polity movement as a sort of anti-pacifist pacifism under the quite mistaken impression that Nor- man Angellism stands by a merely economic thesis, while the "old" pacifism is merely an idealist, ethical movement. It is well to re- member that Mr. Angell makes no objection to the use of moral argument, but to the non-use of the material argument. There has been im- ported into this " new " movement a certain antipathy for the "old," for which Mr. Angell is not responsible. I have good reason to know that Mr. Angell is anxious to remove this wrong impression, and in fairness to his own position, it would be well to cite a few quotations from his writings. In "Modern Wars and the Peace Ideal" he says: "The proposition that war does not pay is in reality a gross distortion of the spirit of The Great Illusion.' (" The Founda- tions of International Polity" follows the same lines of argument, says Mr. Parker.) What is the thesis? It is not merely, or mainly, a mone- tary question at all. Although the public seem to have centred their attention on that section of the book which deals with the financial and economic aspect, that aspect even in sheer bulk does not represent more than one-third of the book. It does indeed take the ground that more and more must the ideals of men be centred on the tangible well-being of the race, and that more and more is it impossible to separate the moral and material in the sense that a moral aim must finally include both." Again: "By economics,' of course, I mean not a merchant's profit, or a moneylender's in- terest, but the methods by which men earn their bread, which must also mean the kind of life they lead." "It (i.e., economics) teaches us, as only some such simple and mechanical means can teach, the lesson of human fellowship." Many similar quotations could be given which breathe the same spirit and possess the same width of outlook. In the )great and good cause of peace, every school of thought and actin should have its right place in the general body of the move- ment. The relation of the " old "to the " new" pacifism has been well expressed as "the rela- tion of an intellectual argument to a moral en- thusiasm." Each is now ineffective without the other. There' is no antagonism, for they are parts of a great whole. Many people have ac- repted the " new" pacifism without realising that the " new " justifies the "old.' H. GRAY. 30, Wellfield-street.

div.head: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING IN
div.p: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING IN
AUSTRALIA.

f Ss iior g, S,—Captain ta issuei n C or fo s ofioe accuseslnadpuls ory lei t(o1r)y o ft train- con on in g with amendment of the Defence Act. In rsetvooi odu as tlteht toe rl sit electioninted orue sto ltuhtaetly3ool7onsdoid- dtmoa yt oe ops bourne, and Mr. Hugh Conroy, member for Mr. Matthews, the member for Port Mel- mpulsory military training. werriva, were returned as opposed to compul- sory military training; they wanted the Act amended in the shape of the compulsory clauses being deleted. Is that clear to Captain Cros- field? 2, Regarding the by-election at Adelaide, may I point out that the candidate who opposed com- pulsory military training stood as a single taxer first and foremost, and was not run by the Freedom League? The Freedom League does not run political candidates, but seeks to edu- cate all shades of political thought. I think Captain Crosfield should be careful of his facts. 3. Captain Crosfield infers that I said the Labour Party is not responsible for the Defence Act. The Labour party is certainly responsible inasmuch as it passed the measure, but my point is that the Labour party did not frame it. The Liberal party framed the Bill, based on Lord Kitchenees recommendation. It is no use, your correspondent talking about Mr. Hughes' (M.H.R.) support. Mr. Hughes did not create the Defence Act.

4. The Labour party and the Defence Act. Does Captain Crosfield deny that there is a strong feeling in the Labour party against the Defence Act? Your correspondent has not dealt with my statement that a large number of the trade unions are absolutelyopposed to compulsory military training. Last week's mail brought me a ieport of a powerful Labour branch (Foot: seray, Viet.) having "turned down" conscrip- tion, supported by two Labour M.P.'s, who were present, Messrs. Matthews and Fenton, M.H.R.
The delegates were instructed to vote against the compulsory clauses at the next annual con- ference.

This week's mail brings a report of the Port Melbourne Labour party's decision in this matter. A resolution against the compulsory clauses of the Defence Act was proposed by the Mayor of Port Melbourne and carried (Argus, February 3rd, 1914). Some six months ago I addressed the Mel- bourne Trades Council (the most powerful in- dividual Labour organisation in the Common:. wealth), and 95 per cent. of the delegates pres- ent opposed the compulsory military training. , I have stated on several occasions that when the Defence Act was placed on the Statute Book there was no opposition worth si)eaking about, but the people have now had practical experi- ence, and every month the opposition increases. Labour now knows that the defence forces can be used against it during strikes. Labour also knows that the regulations provide for the undermining of freedom of speech and freedom of the Press in the citizens' relations to mili- tarism, and that the authorities can when they like try any offender against the Defence Act by court martial. 5. The Churches and the Defence Act.

_ Captain Crosfield has made a great deal of the fact that the majority of the churches in Australia support compulsory military train- ing. What he ignores is that in nearly all the churches that support the Act resolute and i strong minorities are n opposition. Why I did not quote the churches in my address wasl simply because the churches do not represent the thought of the mass of the people of Australia. It is all very well to quote the nominal adherence of people to various de- nominations, but the actual membership is quite another matter. The decline of church membership is almost annually a subject for discussion at the church conferences. This is deplorable, but we must face facts. 7. In my address at Warrington I said that the Defence Act is becoming more and more un- popular. Capt. Crosfield said in his first letter that the number of 'prosecutions under the Defence Act for the whole of Australia is less than under the Education Act for a single State. Will Captain Crosfield kindly give us the facts? What is wanted is a fair analysis. Either the girls must be deducted from the education prosecutions, or the percentage of those prosecuted to the number liable. It is difficult to obtain figures for prosecutions under the Education Act for all the States and the number of school at- tendances varies in each. In Victoria the law is far stricter than in New South Wales, for instance. So, if we take the figures for Victoria the percentage will be higher than the rest of the Commonwealth. The number of children who attended State Schools in Victoria during 'l9ll-12 was 205,253; the total number of prosecutions was 7,212, which is 3.51 per cent. In the citizen forces and the senior cadets the I number of prosecutions for the nine months from January let to September 30th, 1913, was B=6. Assuming the same proportions for the remaining three months of the year. we get a total of 10,981 prosecutions for the twelve months

cadets and citizen forces was 124,619 (actually The number liable for training in the senior training 122,000 f, the percentage of prosecutions is, therefore, 8.79 per cent., as against 3.51 per pent. under the Victorian Education Act. And now I have some very interesting figures for Capt. Crosfield. I received them by cable from Melbourne, March 16th. These figures are official and issued by the Defence Department. Number of lads in training 122,000. Prosecutions to date 21,300. The prosecutions are 17 per cent. of those training. No less than 1,400 have been sent to military places of detention (fortresses, &c.) Comment needless!
JOHN W. BARRY. 21, Beech-road, Horfield, Bristol. March 21, 1914.

"Phil Squod," through his obscure vision, has charged me with uttering a slanderous statement regarding the reading of the Bible by Reformers and Free Churchmen. It is quite evident that "P.hil Squod" is very sensitive, so much so that my simple criticism has exploded in no uncertain manner his own stock of abuse. I regret hurting the feelings of "Phil Squod." As I have said, to continue the controversy on the lines adopted by him would be absolutely ridiculous, and would, in the end, leave those seekers after the truth with opinions more con- flicting than formerly. • J.D. [Our correspondent adds a passage which we have taken the liberty to delete. He says the Rev. H. Ogden has "thrown up the sponge?' As will be seen, Mr. Ogden's letter, held over by us from last week, appears to-day. "J.D." says he is at a further disadvantage, because we mutilated his letter, and so obscured some of his points. We invite our correspondent to prove or - withdraw his charge. We have re-read his original letter, and find that the only "mutilations" made were to delete an insulting reference to Mr. Ogden, and a sentence which, wee uagram- matical and could not be understood. • We have similarly removdod from his letter .this week a suggestion that our correspondent "Phil Squod" is the Editor himself and ri remark that certain characters would not bear investigation. We should not have troubled to note these matters, but we wish to /make it known generally that correspondents who desire to throw mud at other people while they take care to shelter themselves behind a nom de plume must find another outlet than "The Examiner" for their activities.—THE EDITOR.]
EDUCATIONAL POINTS.
Mr. E. Plinston and the Raising of the School Age.
FEATURES AT ADULT SCHOOLS.

Speaking at the Academy-street Men's School on Sunday morning, Mr. Edwin Plinston took for his subject "Educational Points," and re- viewed the alterations in management and other conditions consequent upon the passing of the 1902 Act. He explained the position of co-opted members on the Education Committee and the difficulties which that committee had to en- counter. _ _ _

As a result of the Balfour Act there had been a great increase in salaries to many teachers, the reduction in the size of class per teacher, and the cubic space per child fixed/upon a more healthy basis, necessitating the building of new schools.

• He approved of the medical inspection of the child, and also the dental clinic, and thought parents we're realising that the health of thc child was of more concern than ignorant resent- ment.of some parents.
Religious instruction, which aroused most dis- cussion (and some objection), he argued, should be plain teaching of the Bible as "the Book ol Books."

. In the matter of school exemption—a most contentious question—he contended that chil- dren with normal faculties should be drafted at 12 or 13 years to a higher grade school, but duc consideration to be paid to the conditions affect- ing the case as to whether 14 should be the minimum age at which a child may leave the elementary school, and he considered the by- law that "no child, even if attendances have been made, should be allowed to leave school unless going to be necessarily and beneficially employed," should be rigidly adhered to. STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S. Mr. James Fergusson, the secretary of the school, gave a lecturette on "Ideas" on Sunday morning. The speaker gave many illustrations ' mostly based on inventions, , which had theii genesis in a single idea. The steam engine, lighthouse, electricity and its many appliances, ,gas, the penny post, death duties, telegraph, telephone, motor cars, many men in the lowei ' stations of life, said the lecturer, have valuable ideas, but for want of opportunity and capital are unable to put them into practice. Thanks were accorded to the lecturer, after many corn- nients had been passed on the value of ideas.

BEWSEY MEN'S. A most interesting event took place last Sat- urday in the form of a bulb show. As this was the first effort of its kind, considerable 'interest was aroused among the members,,and the results were startling enough, as can be readily imag- ined. Most members are now much wiser and the knowledge gained will doubtless prove valu- able in future. Few events have added more zest and amusement than the first Bewsey Bulb Show. The prize-winners were: 1, Abraham Smart; 2, Richard Healey; 3, H. Gray. In the evening a tea and informal social gath- ering were held, at which a contingent of Adult School friends from " Top " Gorton, Manchester, joined. Mrs. J. A. Ransoine kindly presented the prizes. She expressed her pleasure in attending the first annual bulb show and encour- aged those who had failed to secure a prize to make another attempt next year. She urged the members to take a keen interest in things of beauty, in flowers, in plant life, and in Nature generally. Nature was prolific in beau- tiful things and well repaid us to cultivate the habit of observation. The memory would thus store up many treasures and add much joy to life. The Adult School movement stood for many things, and certainly one of them was to stimulate the cult of the beautiful. She trusted the show would be the first of many yet to come, and added that the other Warrington schools might be induced to join together in holding a sub-union show next year. Later in the evening matches at billiards and draughts were played by the Gorton and Bewsey Schools, the latter winning in both games.

'SANKEY BRIDGES MEN'S. On Sunday morning Dr. J. S. Manson gave an interesting lecture on "Eugenics." Dr. Manson said eugenics was derived from two Greek words meaning " well born." Sir Francis Galton, in 1883, coined the word to give precision to an idea vaguely present in all races. National eugenics was a study of the agencies under social control that might improve or impair the racial quali- ties of future generations„ either physically ox mentally. Eugenics considered environment in so far as its agency expressed or brought to light hereditary qualities. The idea of the struggle for existence and the operation of nat-ural selection was derived by Darwin and Wallace, not from their observa- tions of plants and animals, but from Malthus's "Essay on Population." Malthus was at one time a student of the Warrington Academy. Man's control of environment interferes with natural selection, and the interference, unless guided by accurate knowledge, may lead to decadence rather than to progress. Progress is not necessarily an outcome of organic evolution. There may be deterioration and complete extinction, as in the examples of many extinct species, such as the Mammoth and other organic Dreadnoughts of early ages. The environment may be so altered that the least fit may survive and multiply, and so lead to a retrogressive and decadent race.

There are pessimists who believe. civilisation is a failure, and optimists who believe that all things must come right. These are largely temperamental divisions. It is not safe to dog- matise either way, but to remember that the multiplication of. good stock is an important matter in all social questions, and that 'heredity is the key to the solution of many of these pro- blems. Our knowledge of heredity is yet imper- fect. Environment should be such as to give equality of opportunity,so that the noblest,innate qualities are brought to light. The Doctor then spoke Of the eugenic problem in relation to alcohol and showed that while it might be pos- sible to raise an alcohol-proof race, yet in ep doing, owing to the complexity of human char- acter, some of. its finest qualities might be eliminated in ,the process. Man will rise to the height of superhuman when he can determine the composition of his race by the efforts of his will and knowledge.

div.head: SMOKE ABATEMENT.
div.p: SMOKE ABATEMENT.

Sir,—Your readers may possibly be interested in the following resolution, which, after being passed by the Engineering Section, was ap- proved and adopted by the Directors of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce at a recent meeting:

"That this Executive, believing that existing legislation with regard to Smoke Abatement is not being effectively carried out by some local authorities, urges his Majesty's Government to afford facilities for the full discussion of a Smoke Abatement Bill, with a view to more uniform action by authorities administering larger areas." 20th March, 1914.
ARTHUR BENNETT.

CATHOLIC LECTURES: REPLY TO "J.D." Sir,—One of your brave contributors deems his letter of such value that he hides behind his initials. One's curiosity concerning him hence remains unsatisfied. It would have been interesting to meet an individual so genuinely ignorant. Then I Would commend your corre- spondent to one of your choice suggestions at the head of correspondence: Contributors are expected to impart or seek information, not to abuse. To the readers of your valuable paper I would commend the following exhibition of Catholicity. I quote from your correspondent's letter: "As to the invitation to attend his church to receive Communion, I am sure there are not many who will take advantage of this generous offer." May I remind your correspon- dent that an insult is no argument? I venture to believe that none of the ordained clergy of the Roman Church will gush over their cham- pion. I endeavoured to prove that the Roman Church is not Catholic. I declared that Catho- lic means cosmopolitan, universal, liberal. I inquired if the Roman Church would admit me to their Communion, and I ventured to say that any Romanist who came to a certain Free Church would not be denied Communion. The quotation just cited above is your correspon- dent's answer. I leave the reading public to decide whether his reply is argument or insult. He is a thorn, and an offence unto his friends. lie speaks, sir, of Martin Luther as "that arch- . .

apostate."' I had the pleasure to hear one or two of the lectures recently delivered under the aus- pices of the Roman Church Evidence Society. Martin Luther was referred to more than once, but the lecturers had sufficient knowledge of what become gentlemen to. lead them to speak Of a most worthy man and a great man in becoming language. Your correspondent sug- gests that there was a religion 1,600 years era the branch of the Church to which I have the honour to belong came into existence. I would remind your corres4ondent that one of the cardinal canons of our faith is "Where two or three are met together in My name there am I ... and that to bless." Where two or three are met together ! Surely that type of a Church is ancient enough.- And the Master is there to bless, whether a successor of Peter has the accident to be present or absent, and may I re- mind your ignorant correspondent that I believe not only in confession, but also "the forgivenese of sins." Because I refuse to relate them to any mortal man, does that make my confession .any the less real? • Vre Protestants' Confessor iS not any ecclesiasfical nominee, • but "Out Father which art in Heaven," and no human medium is needed. Perhaps now when your correspondent learns, possibly for the first time, that Protestants believe in confession of sins, lie will secure admission, if needed, to the Roman Communion, and hesitate ere he sneers at_a Catholic offer from a .Free Churchman.

I repeat what I said in the sermon mentioned. In the earry Church, and the early Church practice, there was no altar, there was no reser- vation of the ikacrament. A loaf or piece of bread was chosen from the rest of the bread used at the evening meal. A bottle or cup (not a chalice) was selected from the rest of the wine. There was a simple blessing from the presiding minister, and the elements were handed round by one of the deacons. All present partook in both kinds. And who better than the members of the early Church would know the interpre- tation placed upon our Lord's words, "This is My body and this is My blood," than those who were actually contemporaries of our Blessed Lord? The mystery to Free Churchmen is how any Church has managed to evolve so ornate a ritual as the Roman Communion from such a simple origin. One is quite ready to make a gift of what is in your correspondent's mind to any Church that will accept it. It is a novel suggestion that Free Churchmen react not their Bible in Case they be misled. I have always understood that the origin of Puritan Churches is traceable to the placing of an open Bible in the hands of the common people. Perhaps were your corre- spondent to read a course of history he would discover that of all the Churches Free Churches have contended for an OPEN Bible, not a muti- lated or Pontifical one. The Church of England may have various schools of thought upon the Sacrament, but better any wide divergence of opinion such even as a denial of the Virgin Birth, better that a man should have used his God-given intelligence than accept with mental meekness the conclusions that have been settled for him in cloistered walls or Vatican Library. H. 'OGDEN. Golborne-street Baptist Church.
Sir,—The old story of the ba4 penny, continu- ally making its appearance, is coincident with the resurrection of the ineffective, yet indelible, "Phil Squad."
The first part of his letter I will pass over, his objections being entirely. bigoted: "As they hated Me, so shall they bate you," said our Divine Lord.

" Phil Sq-Uod's" assertion that the Roman Church is not the Apostolic Church shows that lie is lamentably lacking in historical facts. History tells us that in the year 597 Augustine (the evangeliser of this land) was commanded by Pope Gregor to go forth and implant in heathen England the Christian Faith. I pre- sume "Phil Squod" favours the continuity theory, proposed by the Reformed Church. How inconsistent the doctrines and practices (gener- ally) of the Reformers are with those of the 11th century can- be seen when we take a sad, though marked, example, viz., the martyrdom of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, during the celebration of the Mass, and his veneration as a Saint of God. Protestants need not fear that the present Archbishop of Canterbury will share the same fate, under the same cenditiors, although it is quite evident that the recent Kikuyu heresy is likely to cause him mental derangement.

" Phil Squod " goes on to say that no credit attaches to Roraanism for the preservation of the Bible. History again tells us that in 1536 Henry VIII. now thought it wise—although pre- viously he had professed such Catholic belief that the Pope bestowed upon him the coveted title " Defender of the Faith "—to translate and considerably alter the Bible, to corabat the teaching and authority of the Pope of Rome. Protestants claimed, and still lay claim to, what they call the alienable right of each indi- vidual to interpret the Bible as that individual pleases, or, rather, as the spirit moves them to interpret it. Whither has that principle of private judgment led its adherents at the pre- sent day? To ajiypercriticism of the sacred Scriptures, and to a rejection on the part of the liberal school' of exegesis of the Bible as a divinely inspired book. There is no authority in Protestantism. Destroy authority, mutilate it, and what have we? Chaos and disruption two characteristic of Protestantism to-day. *Take an example. 'Three members of the Church of England— High, Broad and Low—after studying their Bibles may, and do, arrive at three different dia- metrically opposed interpretations. All cannot he right, yet each claims to be right, because each claims that the spirit moved him to inter- pret in this particular manner. And who shall correct them? Who shall say any one of them is wrong? Who dare say any one of them is wrong? mutilation Hence we find tchha turt el of tProtestanthe Bible,.a and religion the pre- secontinUal rvation servation'of the Good Book undoubtedly belongs to the Catholic Again, "Phil Squod " says that Martin Luther received his first impressions as a Roman Monk. Yes; and we all know quite well that Judas (the betrayer) received his first impres- sions as an Apostle of Christ. The concluding chapters of "Phil Squod's" epistle I neetioot discuss. Such correst>ondence must surely be detestable to those who are seeking enlightenment on doctrinal or dogmatic teaching. "Phil Squod " has treated with con-

div.head: TO HELP THE BLIND
div.p: TO HELP THE BLIND
Sir,---I wonder if you will allow me a little. Space in which to talk of a rather important point with regard to the production of Braille books? .

There are many kindly sighted people in this country who make these books by hand, and this is also done at various institutions by blind people, particularly at the National Lending Library, so ably/managed by Miss Austin. But the work is necessarily extremely slow, and the entire production of such books does not supply a fraction of the demand for Braille reading matter. I should like by your courtesy to suggest that in future Braille books thus pro- duced should be of a special nature, and not, as is usually the case at present, books of general interest, which can so much better be made in large quantities by machinery. There are many people who cannot see to read, but have some special pursuit or some special hobby with regard to which they require books that, though of great interest to them, are not of sufficient general interest to warrant their production in quantities. I want to establish a department here, the object of which will be the carrying out of this idea, provided that a sufficient demand and means of supply exist. I shalrbe very glad if people who are dependent upon Braille for reading will communicate with me, mentioning any particular book of a really special nature which they would like; and if kindly folk who are prepared to make such books will also let me hear from them. The rest will be easy, and I feel sure that great advantages will result. I was led to this idea by being told by our Chairman, Dr. Ranger (who possesses, I believe a unique Braille library), that for many years. past two ladies have devoted much of their leisure time to making hini Braille books on special subjects. 'hope this letter may perhaps have the result of increasing the number of people who engage in the kindly task of making Braille books by hand. The work is quite simple and quite easily learnt, and I am sure that much time which is now spent on comparatively useless occupations could be, with great advantage, employed foi this. _
C. ARTHUR PEARSON, Hon. Treasurer.

div.p: National Institute for the Blind, 206, Great Portland-street. March 24th, 1914.

[The Lord Mayor of London has opened a fund to assist the National Institute for the Blind in its endeavour to increase and cheapen the supply of Braille literature. This week "Punch" has a touching cartoon dealing with the appeal, entitled "Lightening the Darkness."—ED.]

div.head: BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN SPECIAL SERMONS.
div.p: BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN SPECIAL SERMONS.

The sePvices held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday last were of a special nature, an effort having been :made to liquidate a debt on the Society Funds. The musical side of the service was distinctly special, the choir rendering several anthems in capable style. The afternoon service was presided over by Mr. J. G. Withinshaw, of Penketh, and in addi- tion to items rendered by members of the choir, the services of Miss Hilda Cragg-James and Mr. T. Bradford Barton were requisitioned. Miss Cragg-James quite maintained the very pleasing impression which was formed on her previous visit, each of the several items being really very good. Mr. Bradford Barton's playing was de- lightful; each piece was interpreted in a charming manner, and caused the listener to long for more.

! The Rev, H. Williamson suited the important ! nature of the services by preaching two able sermons. In the morning his subject was "A study in disappointment," the text being taken from Jeremiah xviii. 3,4: "Marred, . . . so he made it again." In the evening the text was taken from St. Luke vii. 22: "The poor have the Gospel preached unto them?" • The words of the text, he said, seemed to be an anti-climax to the list of happenings which pre- , ceded them. It was quite in order that the afflicted ones should be healed of their various ailments; but merely to preach the Gospel to the poor appeared quite beside the mark. Had they received a living wage, or been provided with a sufficiency of this life's goods, justice would have been done. But the central inter- est of the New Testament was not the interest of the larger section of the community to-day. Modern interests centred themselves in economic and political freedom, but the New Testament aim was spiritual freedom. .. • The modern interest in economic freedom evi- denced itself in strikes and the attention dis- played to questions of unemployment. These interests, moreover, were legitimate ones. Men should have adequate remuneration and live decently. The Church was anxious that a man's position of independence should be assured and secured, despite sickness atrid un- employmerd. There must be no dependence on charity. ,The demand was most Christian, and , it was a stain on any country's honour that a man of characteF could not earn enough to keep body and soul together. Political freedom was also a most desirable boon. Christianity was anxious that everybody should be free to express his political views, and do something to carry those views into effect.

_ This magnificent gift was the child of Chris- tian teaching, and it was the disgrace of some lives that they voted according to what paid best personally. The right to vote was bought with blood, and to treat this boon carelessly, or to sell it for a mess of pottage, was unfair to their fellow-men and to those who ,died to win these privileges. But the New Testament left those interests on one side and concentrated on spiritual freedom. Jesus Christ was an example of spiritual freedom. Dependent on charity, the Saviour was, nevertheless, perfectly free econ- omically. When a man commenced with the greater freedom, he was bound to go further; for the three taken in that order hung together. Thus Christ conferred the greater blessing on the poor when He preached the gospel to them. The collections for the day realised £4O.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES WOMEN'S.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES WOMEN'S.

" Florence Nightingale" was the subject of a very interesting and educative address given by Mrs. R. Pemberton on Tuesday evening. The speaker said that Florence Nightingale received her name from the town in which she was born. For a child of her day she had a most unusual education; perhaps that was partly due to the fact that there were no sons in the family. She received the schooling usually given to a boy, which fact, no doubt, fitted her so well for her. sphere in later days. Her wonderful powers of self-reliance, initiative and administration were the result of her early training. Her school- days finished, she was not content to settle down as most young ladies of her position did in her day, and do Berlin wool work, or .wait until a husband came along. She felt she must do something and be trained as a nurse. During the Crimean War, when women were so much needed at the-front, and not one English woman was trained, Florence Nightingale went out to nurse the wounded soldiers. She had great difficulties to contend with, fed " tape placed all sorts of difficulties in her way, but she showed great resolution and opened stores for the . sake of her wounded soldiers in defiance of officers' orders, and gradually wore down official opposition. After relating many incidents of her noble work, the speaker said that Florence Nightingale was much more than a nurse and the "Lady with the Lamp," she was a greet administrator, and a pioneer in the demandi that woman should have a free choice in deciding her own career. She was also one of the earliest of Suffragists.

A charge against an alleged youthful shop- breaker was heard at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday, when Walter Tarbur- ton (16), of 2, Dolman's-yard, was charged with breaking into and entering the King's Cafe on March Bth, and breaking into and entering Messrs. F. R Pierpoint's shop at 125, Bridge- street, and stealing a large quantity of cigar- ettes, chocolates and confectionery. The pris- oner had been remanded from the previous week with a view to inquiring as to whether lie would be acceptable for a Borstal prison, and a fav- ourable report had been received. Miss Lilian Norman, the manageress of the King's Cafe, and who resided at 40, Bewsey- street, said on Saturday, 7th March, she made the premises secure at nine o'clock, and on Monday morning she found that the place had been broken into and found the drawers had been ransacked and goods thrown about. The articles mentioned in the charge were missed, and the charity collecting box was broken into and the contents missing. She informed the police. Also another charity box had been missed, which the constable showed her on the Tuesday. Later the same day P.C. Green showed her a quantity ,td cigarettes. She identified the property as that of the Cafe, and it was valued at 225.

div.head: ANOTHER WITNESS'S STORY.
div.p: ANOTHER WITNESS'S STORY.

Miss Eva Percival, manageress of Messrs. Pierpoint's, and who resides at 23, Florence- street; gave evidence. She made the premise secure at 9.45 on Saturday, 21st February. At eight o'clock on the following Monday morning she found that the shop had been entered. The drawers had been ransacked and the safe turned over. She missed the articles mentioned in the charge. The value of the property was about 9s. 6d. 1.

div.head: STRIKE INCIDENTS.
div.p: STRIKE INCIDENTS.
" Scab " Shouters Bound Over.

At the Borough Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. J. Rymer Young (in the chair) and other magistrates, John William' Sumner, 26, Robson-street, and John Hollingsworth, 78, Oldham-street, were summoned for having been guilty of disorderly behaviour. In the case of Sumner P.C. Skelton said he was in New-road with P.C. Green and othei, officers, escorting. two workmen from Fletcher. Russell's Works-to their homes. A large crowd of strikers and other people were following, and the defendant shouted "Scab" at the top of his voice.

The Chief Constable said the men who had a desire to go to work were shouted after in such a manner. The defendant had nothing to do with the works. He was drawing sick pay from Crosfield's and yet he was with a large crowd of people endeavouring as much as he could to provoke a breach of the peace. Such Conduct was causing the police to escort workmen home daily.

The Chairman said defendant might be better employed minding his own business. In the case of nollingsworth,7P.C. Skelton said that they were escorting a man in Wilderspool- causeway. There was a large number of strikers and defendant shouted "Scabby Joe." Defendant: I did not shout. P.C. Skelton: I was right beside him. lle ran .-away up Chester-road and did not come back for an hour and a 'half. The Chief Constable: It is a similar ease where a crowd might have been excited. There are a few of the workmen anxious to go to work, and I think the strikers could carry on their parts without such demonstrations. Personally, I have no sympathy with either side, but we want them to be decent in the streets.

The Chairman: They behave like Members of Parliament. Do you (defendant) work at Fletcher's? Defendant: Yes. Both defendants were bound over in the sum of X.. 5 each and ordered to pay 7s. each costs.

div.head: HINTS FOR FATTENING.
div.p: HINTS FOR FATTENING.

During the) whole process of rearing both stock ducks and those for consumption it is highly important that they be regularly sup- plied with. green food. Drinking writer should be given to those being fattened, but they must not be allowed to swim This would retard the process of preparation by several Weeks. On the other hand, those to be reared to adulthood should be allowed to swim from the commence- ment of their career. The value of this will be seen in the hardihood of the ducklings that will eventually be produced. When about nine or ten days old, ducklings require little in the way of brooding, and if put into a roomy coop or crate they will do well ,by themselves. It is, however, very necessary that their sleeping- place be thickly bedded with straw or other form of clean litter.

div.head: CURIOUS INCIDENT AT FIUNCORN.
div.p: CURIOUS INCIDENT AT FIUNCORN.

A curious story was told at an inquest held at Bancorn on Monday. The inquiry was held on Sarah Ann Bolton, of 64. Cawdor-street—The husband, who is a waterman, said she com- plained of pains under the heart on Tuesday evening. MI left the house at 5.30 on Saturday morning to go to work. From appearances ha thought she was all right, but she must have been dead then. Two hours previously she had asked him the time. She was discovered dead in bed by a neighbour about 9.15.—1 t was stated that the woman had been in failing health for Solite time, but had not been medically attended.—Dr. N orphy sald death was due to syncopb.—A .verdict was given in accordanco with the medical evidence,

Perhaps the meanest and the most common fraud of all those practised in cow dealing, says " Farm .and Home;" especially since epizootic abortion became such a scourge in dairyland is that of fitting a cow with a calf not her own, and selling the pair at a high price on account of their supposed relationship. When a cow is seen standing in a market with a young calf by her side, the pair displaying a mutual affection towards each other, is it not indubitable evi- dence as to their relationship? Not at all. They may be no more akin to each other than the poor little foundling is to the professional baby farmer who has adopted it for a consideration, except that the cow, having acquiesced in the substitution, displays some affection for her foster calf, and is prepared to do her duty by it. -It is not uncommon for a -calf to be put to a cow that has been some time calved, or, more commonly, that has given birth prema- turely to a dead calf, in order to tempt those in search of recently-calved cows to buy her. If the calf is judiciously selected as to age and colour, and time is afforded to permit them to become attached, the fraud often works. The town cowkeeper and those who " milk and feed," and who do not care to undertake calving risks, including "milk fever,"k are buyers now a newly-calved cows where they used to he on I the lookout for " springers." If they get ti. cosy palmed on to them that has been calved several weeks they lose some of the best of the milking period. In the case of the cow that has! "picked" her calf, and that has been fitted out with a- calf to be sold with her as evidence of her having calved at her full time, the trouble- some infectious abortion is often introduced into herds hitherto free from it.

SPREADING DISEASE. When fining Ernald Emery, Talbot Villas, Brereton, 10s.. and costs for failing to comply with an Order of the Board of Agriculture for the prevention of wart disease in potatoes, tin Chairman of ,the Bench said defendant had evi- dently been wilfully negligent. It was stated that the defendant had carted away diseased haulms and heaped them upon a neighbouring allotment—" an almost certain method of spreading the disease."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914.
FARM AND GARDEN.
PIG BREEDING AND FEEDING FOR MARKET. '

Although a small man does not at all times make the best of his pigs by sending them into the market' auction, lie had far better do this than consign them to a salesman. He has, however, a better chance of making his piggery pay if he adopts one of the following practices :—First, by feeding his pigs as porkers, and having fixed a day for killing, to obtain orders for joints among his neighbours at cur- rent prices. If he has a joint left on his hands, he should learn to pickle or cure it, either for sale later on or for his own consumption. Some men are excellent hands at curing; the time occupied is but little, the cost is a trifle, and, if well done, the meat is more agreeable and nourishing, if for no other reasdn than that it iS not preserved with a drug like boracic acid, which is practically the basis of all factory curing. I strongly advocate' the employment of sugar, which is much more wholesome than salt when the latter is used in large quantities, and especially as it is a food, although one not to be eaten with impunity. Salt, when consumed to excess, as is sometimes the case, is now known to be harmful. For these reasons the mild- curing system by the aid of sugar is the most desirable; pig meat then can be cured and sold advantageojtsly. Last of all comes the butcher, and if a small breeder can find a tradesman who will take his pigs with regularity, he will do well to please him by breeding and feeding pre- cisely what he requires, both as to quality and weight.

A pig weighing 3501 b. or 4001 b. in the carcase will cost 25 per cent. more to .produce by the pound than a pig of half the Weight, and still realise less by the stone. It is therefore a much better plan to feed two or three pigs of small weights instead of one to a large weight, and thus ensure better quality, less fat, and full market price at a smaller cost for production.— James Long, in "Farm and Home."

MILK PRODUCERS' TROUBLES. Mr. James Sadler, secretary of the Cheshire Milk Producers' Association, addressing the Shrewsbury Farmers' Union on Saturday, said the milk prcidUcei.s had never in his experience had such, a combinatiOn of circumstances to contend with as they had to-day. Labour charges were going up, farmers had to submit to a greater amount of inspection than ever, there ,was the Tuberculosis Order, and there was also the increase of railway rates. He wished 4e could persuade a good many in the milk trade to go back to some other type of farming. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Synthetic Milk.
div.p: Synthetic Milk.

Perhaps one of the greatest things that was going to affect the milk trade was the discovery of what was called synthetic milk. The Ger- man chemists had now produced artificial milk, which not only looked like milk but curdled like milk, and from, which they could make cheese and butter, and yet it had never seen a cow. • (Laughter.) That Was one of the most serious things which had happened in regard to the milk industry for many years. The meeting agreed to form a Milk Committee to co-operate with the Cheshire Milk Producers' Association for further strengthening that organisation.

div.head: SPURIOUS CALF.
div.p: THE SPURIOUS CALF.
WINTER CORN AND PASTURES.

The landscape, says " The Times," presents a healthy 'appearance. The grassland remained green throughout the winter, but the hue has deepened perceptibly in the past few weeks, while the increasing verdure of the winter -wheat and the rapid progress of the February secdings add to the expanse and prominence of green in the general survey. The early spring corn has come along with vigour, and the wish is frequently expressed that a wider area had been drilled when the conditions were favour- able last month and in January. An early sup. lily of grass is anticipated. Already the pas- tures are growing freely, herbage being suffi- ciently plentiful to reduce the demand upon the limited supply of roots. The dairy herds are turned out daily, and farmers state that the grass diet has already influenced the yield ,of milk. The approach of the grazing season is viewed with misgiving in consequence of the continuance of foot-and-mouth disease in Ire- land. British glaziers require anything from a hundred thousand to a quarter of a million of Irish store cattle to stock their pastures, but there is' no immediate prospect of the supply being provided. Flockmasters Write hopefully of the lambing season and the health of, the flocks generally.
' 'MILK CERTIFICATION.

Last Friday the President of the Local thiv- ernment Board received a deputation, composed of Lord Shaftesbury, Mr. C. S. Bathurst, M.P., Mr. W. S. Corbett, and Mr. Wilfred Buckley, from the Agricultural Organisation Society in reference to the opinion formed by that society that the principle of milk certification should be adopted in the forthcoming Government measure.

Certified milk, as the term VA understood in the United States,, is, " The Times" explains, milk of guaranteed purity, a bacteriological standard being used as regards the milk itself and a score card system as regards the farms. , •Mr. Wilfred Buckley writes, stating that the most efficacious, if not the only way of improv- ing our milk supply, " is the grading of milk based on its bacterial contents with the produc- tion of certified milk as its foundation and its source of education." Ile shows that in New York a cleaner milk supply has led to an in- crease of 40 per cent. in the consumption of uiilk, and continues: "That milk can be sup- plied with a low bacterial count is proved by, examinations that the •Lister Institute have made this week of raw milk purchased from two 1 dairies in London, produced on faruia'wllere it

Mr. C. B. Davies, a member of the Live Stock Committee for the county, described the pro- gress made under the Board ,of Agriculture's ' scheme for live stock improvement. An officer for the county had been appointed, and they had about £l,OOO available for assisting the pur- chasers of suitable breeding stock. • In reply to a complaint that the scheme had not been sufficiently advertised among farmers, Mr. Sadler explained that the position of the county had been seriously prejudiced by , the action of Lancashire (which was to have formed one " province " with (heshire) in refusing to come into the scheme. While other counties bad been able to get on with their work, and in many cases had already bought bulls, Cheshire had been without funds. Owing to their Part of the scheme being held up they had been tillable to spend anything on propaganda, though the live stock officer had attended a great many farmers' meetings. Another serious matter was that owing to the delay most of the other counties had got ahead of them.
On the motion of Mr. Goodwin, seconded by Mr C. E. Young, it was decided to ask the Board of Agriculture to allow non-pedigree bulls with a milk record and approved sires and dams to be eligible.

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
Simlaflint, Devices to llinhoise the Chances of Accident.
NEGLECTED LUBRICATION.

In a recent issue of one of the London evening papers a writer on cycling topics attributes sumo of the carelessness which nearly all riders ' exhibit in the matter of lubrication to the manufacturers, who do not always provide suit- able lubricators. Nowadays many of the best maicers use the hinged lubricators whenever possible. These are quite satisfactory, very accessible, and with apertures of correct size. Up to the present no one seems to have intro- duced a good system of pedal lubrication. The pedals are subject to very hard wear, and, being near the ground, easily catch dust and dirt, necessitating more frequent cleaning and oiling than perhaps any other part of the machine. Their function prevents the use of hinged lubri- cators of the present type, and the sliding ring with the small projection fitting into a hole is far from satisfactory. 'The continual pressure of the foot tends to move it about, and time after time the aperture is exposed to dirt of every kind at the end of a ride. Other parts of the machine present much less difficulty and retain their oil without any appreciable quantity of dirt for a fair length of time.

Brakes and Their Care. One of the commonest faults of the ordinary rim brake, particularly the one acting on the back wheel, is the uneven action on the two sides of the rim. Very often one rubber grips the rim almost a quarter of an inch further from the spokes than the other, thus causing both a loss of brake power and strain on brake , and rim. Sometimes the rim is at fault, either not running in the exact centre or slightly buckled, but more often the deficiency lies in the brake work. If the discrepancy is not too great, a washer inserted between the offending. brake shoe and the brake are. will considerably improve matters, otherwise the services of -the Professional repairer must be requisitioned. The brake is one of the most hard-worked parts of a bicycle, as well as the strongest. and requires very little attention; but, nevertheless, a careful examination will sometimes avert disaster. Many brakes have a number of small screws, whieh, after a hard season's wear, may possibly work loose, and may easily fail at a critical moment, unless attended to in time.

Tho Auto Wheel. The lath; auto wheel attached to the back wheel of the ordinary cycle is becoming quite a common sight on the road, and bids fair to attain increasing popularity. Only a few days ago I saw one attached to ft tandem; both the riders looked fairly weighty and the machine was further burdened by a child fastened to a seat on the front handle-bar, yet the Whole equipage went merrily along without any diffi- culty. The great advantage of the auto wheel is that it is easily detachable, thus enabling the machine to be used as an ordinary cycle at the convenience of the owner. We should like, however, to have some particulars of tyre ex- penses, which seem likely to be rather heavy, before returning an entirely favourable verdict. Again there is a distinct strain on the back of the cycle, which, at all events, demands that the auto wheel is only attached to a thoroughly reliable machine. The important point to bear in mind is that the neat little mechanical device is air auxiliary source of power, not a substitute for the rider's own effort.

, it looks as though it will be necessary to utter repeated warnings against starting in gear. Again and again we have reports of accidents from every quarter caused by careless starting, every one of which might have been prevented by the exercise of a little care. There is only one safe plan.: before attempting to turn the starting handle, always feel that the gear lever ,is in the neutral position. 'Do not assume that because everything was right when you left the car perhaps half an hour previously the same happy state of affairs is likely to continuo inde- finitely. There are always small boys about who want a little encouragement to amuse themselves with a waiting car, and only this week we heard of a case where the gear lever had been placed in the reverse position and the brake taken off, with rather alarming, although fortunately not serious, consequences. After all, it is a very easy matter always to make a careful scrutiny before starting results.

Light Car Trials. The light car trials projected by the Scottish Automobile Club have been definitely aban- doned, for this year at any rate. From the very first we have never been able to see why the Scotch Club should give way to the palatial establishment in Pall Mall, or, for that matter, why both trials should not have taken place as originally projected. At any rate, having due regard to the facts of the case, it seems as if the wrong party has given way, and if alternate trials are to be held every year, the Scottish Automobile Club should have had the preference for 1914, whereas, according to existing arrange- ments tile Royal Automobile Club will promote the first of such competitions, with Hereford as a centre. Next year the Scottish Club will organise a big road trial for light cars through the Highlands. Still it is satisfactory to know that the dispute, if such it could be described, has been settled in a :manner satisfactory to motorists both North and South of the Tweed.

AI a meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture on Monday in Crewe, Mr. A. M. R. Legh, president of the Chamber, was in the chair.

div.head: Swine Fever and Foot-and-Mouth Disease.
div.p: Swine Fever and Foot-and-Mouth Disease.

_ Speaking of the swine fever regulations, Mr. J. Sadler, secretary to the Chamber, said that the Government Committee appointed to inquire inlo the best means of meeting that disease had in its second interim report dealt with one point only—the experience of different parts of the world in the use of the serum treatment. He thought it was unfortunate that they had not considered what could be done, quite apart from technical matters' of that kind, to make the regulations less irksome from the point of view of the pig dealers. Mr. C. E. Young so the appointment of a committee of the Cheshire Chamber to eon- ed suggest sider in what way the existing regulations might safely be relaxed, and his suggestion was sec- onded by Mr. J. Furber on the understanding that the Committee's inquiry should extend also to the foot-and-mouth disease regulations. A committee was appointed to consider all the questions raised, and with power to approach the chief constable of the county if necessary.

Should Roads be a Local or National Charge? The Chairman moved : •' That in the opinion of this Chamber the expenditure required for the upkeep of the roads of the county, an ex- j;eilaliture which is constantly on the increase, ho charged to the existing extent l ti on ntlliewlig local rates, inasmuch as the great bulk of the traffic under modern conditions is no longer local, and that therefore the cost-of the maintenance should come largely from Im- perial sources." Emberton opposed the resolution. In any case, he said, the money for the roads would have to be found, and if it were raised by taxa- tion instead of from the rates it was difficult to say whether the burden would be more equit- ably distributed. Ile thought that if under the present system they were paying for other coun- ties' traffic, the matter was balanced by the fact that the other counties took Cheshire traffic as well. But his greatest objection to the resolu- tion was that if they relieved the County Coun- cil of the burden of maintaining the roads they would say, "We've get so much more money to s and would promptly spend it on some- thugThe Chairman spoke in favour of larger national contributions to the cost of the genera' services which were administered by the county. The resolution Was seconded by Mr. C. E. ii:d' else. • Young and carried, with the addition of a clause, suggested by Mbr. P. M. Oliver, remind- ing the Government of its promise to deal with the question in the present session.

div.head: PRUNING ROSES.
div.p: PRUNING ROSES.

The majority of roses may now be pruned. Notwithstanding the great advance made in rose-growing during the past year or two, it is surprising to see the number who still persist ill pruning their roses as one• would a hedge, all shoots being cut over, big and little alike. Ex- pert rose-growers know the peculiarities of each variety and will prune accordingly. But fin those having only a miscellaneous collection, the following rule may be followed : Cut clean away. all weak and sickly shoots, leaving only matured shoots of moderate thickness, and these may be rut back to within 4 inches to 6 filches of the • base.—`l Tho Gazdeu." . '

Motor Signals. Another motor signalling device has just been placed on the market, which promises to be of great use in crowded thoroughfares. The regu- lator comprises two switches attached to the spokes of the steering-wheel of the ear, clearly marked " right" and " left," and controlling a white arrow on a , red background, the whole enclosed in a metal box at the back of the car. A touch of the switch causes the arrow to point in the required direction, thus affording warning to pedestrians and drivers of following vehicles. Another more complicated variety also shows the words " Slow " and " Stop" in white letters in a red field. This is mechanically operated; the word " Slow " appears as soon as the clutch pedal or foot brake is applied. The wprd " Stop" appears on the regulator on the appli- cation of tlik hand-brake, which is generally used whenever the driver intends to bring the car to a sudden 'stop. Such an efficient signal- ling device will certainly tend to minimise the possibility of. accident.

A start has been made at Bury with the work -of preparing for the electrification of the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire main line from Manche- ter to Bury, the Catforms at Bolton-street sta- tion being raised several inches to better accom- modate the electric coaches.

Nowadays it is rather the fashion to minimise dangers on land or sea; and .in the time of Scoresby, the famous English whaler, it was also, more or less the fashion to do so. But he frankly says "I do not try to minimise the risks of sea life and whaling," and he gives duo thanks to his Maker for many hair-breadth escapes which we to-day might only put down to our own efforts and straight powder. "When the bear is found in the water," he continues, " crossing • from one sheet of ice to another, it may generally be attacked with advantage; but when on shore, or more especially when it is upon a large sheet of ice, covered with snow— on which the bear, supporting itself on the surface with its extended paws, can travel with twice the speed of a man, who perhaps sinks to , the knee at every step—it can seldom be assailed ith either safety or success. Most of the fatal accidents that have occurred with bears have been the result of encounters on the ice, or in. judicious attacks made at such disadvantage." 1 am inclined to think that each :person feels differently about approaching a bear on the ice, depending on temperament and age. l'ersonally, I feel. a faint chill—such as you have before diving off a rock into the sea—and after success something of the glow you have after coming out. I rather think that Younger people have a similar sensation before and after, but stronger. In fact, so strong as at first to upset their aim and afterwards to make them wildly jubilant. • The naked feeling I am sure is there, clothes feel of no account; there is the snow, the sky, and the big bear hundreds of times more power- ful than yourself—and your rifle. Before you dive into the sea you know you can swim a stroke or two; before you wander over the floe to Bruin, you know you have to trust to your aim."—W. G. Burn Murdoch, in "Country Life."

WORLD AT NO COST.

In these days of vigorous advertising, many ingenious ideas have been exploited, but surely nothing has been more striking than the lavish generosity of Messrs. Joseph Watson and Sons, of Leeds, the makers of "Watson's Matchless Cleanser." This firm is just bringing to a close a competition which must have attracted atten- tion in every part of the country. The prize. giving is based wholly upon the number of " Matchless Cleanser," " Nubolic," and " Sparkla" wrappers which are sent in, and the prizes themselves are of such extraordinary value, and so numerous as to excite wonder and admiration. No fewer than four motor cars will be given away, and some lucky person will ob- tain a first-class free tour of the world (value £200). But Messrs. Watson's generosity does not stop there. 'Other prizes include a dozen pianos and organs, 15 Chesterfield lounges, 150 vacuum cleaners, and literally hundreds of ,thousands of acceptable and valuable household requirements. A unique feature of the compe- tition is that a prize is guaranteed to every com- petitor who sends wrappers according to the rules, and every prize is guaranteed the value stated. Readers should particularly note that the last date for sending in wrappers is March 31st.

div.head: DEATH OF COLONEL P. E. WARBURTON.
div.p: DEATH OF COLONEL P. E. WARBURTON.

The death occurred on Tuesday at Arley Hall, Northwich, of Colonel Piers Egerton Warbur- ton, at the age of 74 years. He was the head of an old Cheshire fargily, and the son of Roland Egerton Warburton, the famous hunting poet. He was educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford.

He owned the Cheshire estate, on which his father's rhymes adorn inns wells,' cottages, and signposts. He was a Deputy-Lieutenant and Justice of the Peace for Cheshire. He was a Member of Parliament for the Mid-Cheshire Division from 1876 to 1885, was Colonel of the. 'Earl of Chester's Yeomanry, and formerly head of the Arley Troop. He was a clever amateur water-colour artist. He married a daughter of the third Baron de Saumarez.

REGEN'

Musical ,comedy will be the attraction at the Royal Court Theatre next week, when Messrs. Macdonald and Young are sending us the charming musical comedy "Princess Caprice." The story, which is an adaptation by A. M. Thompson of "Der Liebe Augustine,", is simple yet interesting and coherent, and above all can claim a plot. Thessalia was in a very bad way. Bogumil, the Regent, had run through all the available funds, and the treasury was dry. Gjuro, the Prime Minister, proposed that the Princess Helen, the Regent's niece, should be given in marriage. to Lienla, the wealthy prince of Micholies, who would replenish the treasury and grant a substantial pension to the Regent. This suggestion is particularly welcome to Bogumil. The servants Of the palace" are clain- ouring.for their wages, and a certain individual who had been mistaken for a wealthy banker, turned out to be nothing more than a bailiff, whom certain creditors had put in possession. As the banker, the man was feted by the eccentric Regent, given a special cigar to smoke and the choicest wines to drink. As the bailiff, however, he found the Regent's attitude towards him very much changed. The cigar and the wine were taken from him, and he was turned out of the august presence. Under these conditions Gjuro's scheme would have gone through, but it so happened that the Princess Helen was in love with Augustine Hofer, her music master. Besides she detested, Licela. Further aggravated by the Prince's flirtation with her own attendant, whom he pro-

moted to the position of maid-of-honour, she refuses to marry Licola. Matters were at a deadlock when it was dis- covered from'an old book in the archives of a monastery, formeily the home of the Princes of Thessalia, that Helot was not a princess at all; that the real princess was Anna, her foster- sister. Thus the road of love was open to Helen and her music master, while Lieola was free to marry Anna, the real Princess of Thessalia. The cdrapany includes many well-known and popular musical comedy artistes. Miss May Stevenson is Helen; Miss Nan Rose, Anna; Mr. Aubrey Millward, Augustine; Mr. Myles °- Clif- ton, ie 1 L—a and the irresistibly funny come- dian; Mr. Coningsley Brierley, the 'Regent. The production which is being brought is that which was used at the Shaftesbury Theatre, London, 11l its entirety. The orchestra is being specially increased by musicians travelled by the company, and with a full operatic chorus, will be under the direction of Mr. Frederick Y Rosso. The engagement is for six nights, once nightly, with the usual matinee on Monday at 2.30.

"PRINCESS CAPRICE" NECKWEAR. The "Princess Caprice" Neckwear is a dis- tinct and useful novelty, made up in a wide range of choice colours, and bearing a dainty design from the musical comedy. Mr. .BANrii, of Horscmarket-street and Sankey-street, is the sole agent, and is this week making a Special Display of these goods in the windows at both shops.
