div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914. WORKERS AJID THEIR MOVEMEJITS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914. WORKERS AJID THEIR MOVEMEJITS.
THE RAILWAY CLERKS. The Local Men Carry On Active • Propaganda Work. AGE OF TRADE UNION FUSION.
BY "A WORKER."

The local branch of the Railway Clerks' Asso- ciation is an energetic body which deserves to meet with success. They are keen on propa- ganda work, and do it with an enthusiasm and thoroughness which constitutes an example some other local unions might copy. One of their meetings was held on Saturday, and some pointed remarks were made about the treatment the clerks receive. One speaker stated that a dray horse was of more value in the eyes of the railway companies than were the clerks. We have heard this.story from other railwaymen's unions, and it has even been stated in the House of Commons that the human element in rail- way matters is the least valued. In time trade unionism may be strong enough to change such a condition of things, but it will take time. Fusion Schemes.

We seem to live in the age of amalgamations. Employers are uniting into larger and more powerful federations, and the workers are be- ginning to realise the value of one large union in preference to a number of small and less powerful bodies. The railway unions were the first to set the example in fusion. The different unions who cater for unskilled and semi-skilled workers are now considering a scheme for fusion and there is every indication that the amalga- mation will be carried into effect, although some time must elapse before the new union is ready for work. To unite the three railway unions was a comparatively easy matter, but with the latest schemes there are far more in- terests to be conserved, and it will take time to construct a nea° union. The Dyers and Bleachers and kindred unions are also on the point of amalgamating and providing one strong body in place of numerous small ones scattered all over the country. There can be no question but that such unity is greatly to the interest of the workers. • The Carters' Strike. _

Manchester in the past has been notorious for the number of carters' strikes. 'Why strikes should be so frequent it is difficult to say, ex- cept that there is not the spirit of give and take between employers and employed in Manches- ter as there is in other places. The strike of last week was short anti decisive. The men came out, after weeks of futile negotiations, for a rise of 2s. per week in wages. The teamowners said they could not give that sum—it would make them bankrupS. The carters refused to budge front their terms and the offer of is. week advance did not sway them. Matters came to an acute crisis when the President of the Chamber -of • Comnierce brought the parties to- gether, and the dispute was promptly settled. The carters got the 2s. per week increase, and gained the most decisive victory they have ever secured in connection with any strike. The downing of tools is not always a profitable Policy, but in this case it has proved so.

Engineering Trade Trouble; A close observer will be able to note the like- lihood of trouble in the engineering world, and the position has become more serious through the employers' federation and the A.S.E. fail- ing to come any conclusion about the suggested new agreement to take the place of the old one from which the men had withdrawn. When it was seen that agreement could not be arrived at, an effort was made to patch up a temporary working arrangement. The scheme proceeded until the last clause was reached. This is: "There shall be no stoppage of 'work, either of a partial or a general character, but work shall proceed under the current conditions until the procedure provided for lia9 been carried through." The men's representatives could not agree t'o this, the conference broke up, and now the position is critical, and one dare not fore- cast what may happen.

STRENGTH OF RAILWAY UNION. The annual statement of membership of the National Union of, Railwaymen was officially issued on Wednesday, and it shows that on 31st December last the membership stood at 267,611, as against 132,002 for the previous year, or an increase of snore than 100 per cent. Since the returns were made the union membership has increased at the rate of from 1,000 to 3,000 per week, and it is now believed to be at least 280,000. t

Making allowance for members of other unioim and men who are ineligible, the "Railway Re- view" estimates that about 100,000 railwaymen of all grades are still outside the union. The National Union is now the largest single union in the United Kingdom, the next largest being. the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, uith a membership of 170,000.

SWEATED WOMEN WORKERS. The wages of women engaged in sweated in- dustries was dealt with by Miss Basnett, of Man- chester, who gave an address on "Home Workers" to the Manchester Society for P‘ oruan Suffrage on Wednesday._

There were women, she declared, who toiled for 10 or 12 hours every day, often in basement rooms. Sometimes they worked in one room, where the family slept and ate, and where, if anyone died, the body would have to lie until it could be buried. There were over 100,000 home workors in the kingdom, and a very large number of them earned considerably less than the 10s. 10d. per week which it had been computed was the sum needed for a single woman to support herself in Glasgow; or the lie. 10d. minimum for London, or the lls. which her own inquiries led her to believe was the figure for Manchester. Miss Basnett gave instances. In the chain- making industry she had known of women. earning only Bd. per day; in shirt making there were workers paid at 9d. per dozen; and, cruellest irony of all, the Red Cross badge on tHe Red Cross sucks, waggons and other equip- ment was often made by workers Who could not earn 10s. per week, and out of that they had to find so much money- for wool. The competition of women who were perhaps comfortably off, but who had no margin to spend for extras, helped to pull prices down, because they could afford to do the work for less than the woman who was obliged to work. The Trades Board, she added, was, not a panacea; it was only one step. The desirable wage for women would have to come by the vote. Replying to a questioner, Miss Basnett said it appeared that the only thing which could be done by Way of remedy at present would be the extension of the Trades Boards.
WORKHOUSE OPERATlONS—continued.

div.head: HORSES BEFORE CLERKS. Equines Better Treated Than Railway Scribes.
div.p: HORSES BEFORE CLERKS. Equines Better Treated Than Railway Scribes.
BANK PASS-BOOK _AS A _ GOD.

The Warrington branch of the Railway Clerks' Association are at present very active, and on Saturday night they listened with interest to an address on The Spirit of the R.C.A.." from Mr. A. E. Townend, of Manchester. Mr. G. Merrick presided, and he was sup- ported by Messrs. Ifyilton and Pearce. Mr. Townend, referring to superannuation, said he was pleased to see that the Warrington branch was in favour of the contributory system (hear, hear, and applause)—because that showed they thought they were capable of managing their own affairs. The first sense which mani- fested itself in the spirit of their association was that of exankination. This sense of exam- ination had got to work, and, as a result, they had found the sense of environment. He was sure they would agree that they had not yet reached the 'normal standard, and that their value was not so high as they were determined it should be. (Hear, hear.) Less Valued Than a Horse.

There was, however, the directors' point of view, and the best way to find it was by com- parison, and they found that the clerk's varue to the company was 80 times less than the horse. If a horse was ill it had every care and the best attention, but if a clerk was unable to follow his work there was no care from the railway directors.

They were not going to allow that; for they wanted a little humane consideration on behalf of the men, equiilly as much as that given to the horse. (Hear,. hear.) The best thing for the clerk to do was to set a value on himself.

This they had done, and had set it at the very moderate sum of £l5O. He had ideals that some day they, in return for what they 'did, would enjoy all that had been created. Ha agreed they had a long way to go before it was attained. Having set their valuation they ran up against one or two things detrimental to themselves, including "toadyism," so therefore they would have to be determined and rely one upon another, for nothing on earth could deter a determined body of men. (Hear, hear.) " Infra Dig."

Some head office men, and he believed they had some in Warrington, would not come into their association because they considered it infra dig. to be a trade unionist. The doctors and the lawyers were compelled to be members of their trade unions, and they did not consider it infra dig to be trade unionists. Among the R.C.A. there waS the spirit of unity, and they were bearing down on the arena in a united body ready for battle. lie appealed for more support and asked the men 'to give the leaders all the support they could, for out of unity and out of loyalty sprang the real spirit of the R.C.A. If the spirit was developed upon the proper lines it would not be very long before, when the R.C.A. was men- tioned, that there would be nothing but dismay in the opposition camp. Life, as they knew, held for them all an abundance of happiness and joy, which, unfor- tunately for the movement, they were unable to enjoy. They had only to demand it and they would get it, for it *as theirs by right. At present they were in the valley, for no matter where they went they were met with blank refusals from the railway companies, so that it was quite evident the companies refused to give them anything, but if the workers fixed their ideals on the mountain tops they were bound to get there, where the free winds of heaven blew for them. •
There was not the slightest doubt that they were prepared to fight those nten, whose only prayer was a balance sheet and whose only god was a bank pass-book. (Applause.)
A POINTED RESOLUTION. The following resolution was unanimously carried :

"That the Warrington branch of the Railway Clerks' Association, approximately 140 strong, hereby expresses its disgust and dissatisfaction with the negative reply given by the Home Secretary to the deputation from the Trade Union Congress, which interviewed him on the 9th ult., upon the question Of Government in- spection and regulation of unhealthy railway offices, and urges the Home Secretary to intro-. duce thorough-going legislation on this subject during the present session of Parliament."

div.head: FOR RELIEF OF MINERS.
div.p: FOR RELIEF OF MINERS.

The 41st annual report of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Pernnent Relief Society shows that on December 31st, 1912, the society had 60,157 members enrolled, and at the close of increase of the members numbered 62,231, an of 2,074. In 1893, when the membership was 51,451, the number of accidents totalled 6,477, being a proportion of 127 per 1,000 members per annum, and last year, with a membership of 62,231, the accidents numbered 14,587, showing 234.4 accidents per I,ooo_ members per annum. Referring to the, mining disasters which have i occurred during the year, t is added that the heavy record of colliery explosions during recent years shows the urgent necessity for the provi- sion made by the Permanent relief societies for the sufferers by mining accidents, and especialry for the extension of their operations to the min- ing districts where they have not hitherto been established.

div.head: MORE UNIONS UNITING.
div.p: MORE UNIONS UNITING.

A conference of the representatives of societies whose members are engaged in the dyeing, bleaching, and similar trades was held at the Deansgate Hotel, Manchester, on Saturday. It ' was called by the National Federation of Bleachers, Dyers, Finishers and Kindred Trades for the purpose of considering a policy for amalgamation. Mr. Edward Verity, president of the Federation, was in the chair, and twenty societies, with a membership of 160,000, were represented by 84 delegates. The societies are established in Lancashire, Yorkshire, Cheshire, Leicester, Nottingham, and Dundee. . After several hours' discussion the conference decided to form a committee to represent all the various unions, the committee to formulate a scheme for atualgtehation, . which shall be printed and submitted to the societies. ''A fur- ther conference will then be called, and ulti- mately a billot of the members taken if the scheme is adopted. It is apparently anticipated that amalgamation will be successfully carried out, although a great deal of work is necessary before that end is attained.

div.head: HOW TO FIND HUSBANDS.
div.p: HOW TO FIND HUSBANDS.

The midinettes of the famous dressmaking establishments of the Rue de in Paix have de- vised an ingenious plan for •finding husbands. They have founded a mixed club, called the Trente et Quarante (thirty And forty), which consists of fifteen girls and fifteen young men, with ten additional honorary members. ,The number of young men members is strictly limited to fifteen. The result has been fierce competition among many of the most eligible young bachelors of Paris. A• well-known bar- rister, a rising young author, a famous sports- man, all men of considerable means, are already elected.
David Wishart and Samuel Young, cabin boys, each aged 15, were cut to pieces as they were walking towards home along the .railway between Glasgow and Paisley.
At a conference on the rent-question, called by the Trades and Labour Council at Leeds on Saturday, it was decided to establish a perma- nent housing council in the city.

div.head: RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RURAL COUNCIL.
Question of Dangerous_ County Roads
Discussed.
LUMB BROOK CORNER AGAIN.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton en Tues- day, Mr. C. E. Linaker presiding. The Local Government Board forwarded copies of the Provisional Order which they have issued for enabling the Runcorn Rural Council to put in force the compulsory clauses of the Land Clauses Acts with refeitence to the lands required for the purpose of providing access to certain lands to be used for the disposal of sewage of the contributing places of Grappen- hall, Latchford Without and Thelwall. The Order would be submitted to Parliament for confirmation in due course. The Clerk said that copies of the Order had been served on the owners and occupiers c9ll- -

A DANGEROUS SPOT. The Clerk to the Halton Parish Council wrote stating that at a recent meeting it was decided to call the attention of the County Council to a dangerous spot known as Astmoor Bridge. Some time ago the County Council went -so far as to provide plans for the construction of the new bridge, and from what has appeared in the local papers quite recently, it appears that they have this matter again under their considera- tion. We think that your Council could do good service by writing the County Council in re- spect of this new bridge, or necessary and im- portant alterations and improvements to the old. We think it imperative that this matter should be taken seriously in hand at an early date, and we hope the Rural District Council will see their way to assist by calling the at- tention of the County Council to the necessary improvements. We have also written to the County Council respecting n Rucorn-lane, that was the road leading from Halton Brook up into the village of Halton. There was no doubt most of the members of the Council would be aware that half-way down there was a very ugly curve and then the road narrowed considerably, and it was a soarce of great danger. It should be widened and straightened more or less from top to bottom 4 and also whilst this was being done, a footpath should be made, as the old footpath leading by the fields was unsatisfactory. They respectfully asked the Council to do their best in these matters. In regard to the village road, the Chairman said that if the price of land for widening pur- poses was prohibitive it was not worth while considering the matter. At the same time they were always wishful to do what they could to meet the wishes of the townships. It was a matter they might consider when they went through the estimates for the next year.
BOTH COUNTY ROADS. In rePIY to questions, the Clerk said hotb Were county roads. Mr. Antwiss: Who does the land belong to?

Mr. Wright: Sir Richard Brooke. Mr. Linaker, jun.: I have never met-any fast traffic on the road. Only an occasional coal cart. It was agreed the Clerk write. the County Council, urging for the immediate considera- tion of the Parish Council's recommendation in regard to Astmoor Bridge. Mr. Britch : Embody both. We might as well be killed for a sheep as% lamb. Mr. Linaker : Which are the sheep, and which are the lambs? • Mr. Mclntyre: We are assured that if we apply for the land we shall get it given to us. The Chairman: Oh, no ! Mr. Britch : Send the second paragraph to the County Council as well. This was agreed to.

SURVEYOR'S WAGES. On the proposition of the Chairman, it was decided to pay the surveyors, Messrs. Wright and Damlyn, Warrington, £212 for their ser- vices. Reference was made to the excellent work they did, and Mr. Woodward said that good surveyors were, going to be very important to Rural District Councils.

div.head: LUMB BROOK CORNER.
div.p: LUMB BROOK CORNER.

Mr. Whitlow said there was a very dangerous hedge at Lamb BrOok-corner, and on Saturday night two conveyances collided. The hedge was too high, aml he had expected an accident there before. Could they, he asked, get the owner to out the hedge? Mr. Swinton : It is a high hedge, about six feet.
Mr. Mclntyre: It is very dangerous.. It was decided to call the attention of the owner to the spot and reonest Jilin to cut the hedge down and so make it less dangerous.

div.head: WORKHOUSE OPERATIONS.
div.p: WORKHOUSE OPERATIONS.
Discussion at the Runcorn Board of Guardians.
"IMPOSING" ON HOSPITALS.

Mr. Linaker : Would it not be possible to provide this room out of our own accommoda- tion?

Aforris: That would mean an extra fee fore another doctor, whereas they have all the necessary persons at the hospitals. But this Warrington deputation, although as will be seen they admit having tra- velled over a thousand miles of Irish gromad,l never so much as saw a idemand for Home .111 e. All they saw were slums and high rates 14 Places controlled by Nationalists, and bright- low rates and Union Jacks where Orange- rule. places visited, and eliciting whatever infor- mation we could gather from both Nation- alists and tinionista to enable us to arrive at an unbiased opinion formed from our inquiries. Our tour commenced at Dublin, and from there we went to Longford, afterwards mak- ing a long journey to the South, visiting Cork, Queenstown, Limerick, and Ennis. Our visit concluded with two days in Bel. fast. In Dublin one of the most striking features was the squalor of the slums we visited. A large proportion of the working- class population are simply dragging out an existence in filthy dens and under conditions which would not be tolerated in any third- rate municipality in Great Britain. The rates are high, and the very many evidences of civic mismanagement cannot be contra- dicted.

The undeniable bitterness and disloyalty to our country and our King are greatly to be regretted. In Longford the Nationalist control of the town cannot be said to have produced a satisfactory condition of affairs, the worst element being the campaign of boycotting and intimidation, of which ample proof was forthcoming. In Cork, Queens- town, Limerick and Ennis we inquired into further cases of boycotting, which were even worse than those into which we had pre- viously inquired. The day we were in Cork we had a prac- tical instance of the feeling which prevails among the Irish Nationalists. A monument erected to the memory of the officers and men of the County and City of Cork who lost their lives during the South African Wai was subjected to a disgraceful outrage. The southern panel, which contains the inscrip- tion and principal names, was completely while other portions were blackenedsimilarly by tal disfigured..: We understand about eight mouths ago a similar outrage was per- petrated. Throughout the course of our journey we made a point of interviewing all classes and conditions of the people—in the train, in the streets, and wherever we could hope to gain any information. We have ascertained and we are fully convinced that the demand for Home Ride is not so real, as has been urged by the leaders of the Nationalist party. The farmers are prospering, the Unionist Land Purchase Act having wrought great changes in the country, which apparently was never in a better condition. We concluded our tour in Belfast, and on our arrival there were much struck with the appearance of this great city and the evi- dences of prosperity and efficient govern- ment, which formed a sharp contrast to what we had previously seen in towns where the Nationalists had control. We were given an opportunity of inspect- big several of the great industrial concerns in Belfast, notably shipbuilding, engineer- ing, and linen manufacturing. We ,were allowed to talk to the workers, and in every case we found them contented, industrious, and prosperous. We also interviewed Mr. D. R. Campbell and the deputy-chairman and the assistant secretary of the Belfast Trades and Labour Council, and also some leading members of the Ulster Liberal Asso- ciation, including Mr. James Wood, ex-M.P. for East Down, and Mr. H. 'H. Graham, secretary and agent of the association. Our many inquiries only confirmed the opinion that the opposition to the present measure is one of great earnestness and determination. In conclusion, we desire it to be known that our opinions have undergone a com- plete change in consequence of what we have heard, and seen, and we have not the slightest doub't that if the present Bill be- comes law it will be resisted to the bittei end by the loyalists of Ireland. We are therefore unanimously of the opinion, after having visited both Nation- alist and Unionist districts and having had ample opportunity of hearing the arguments of both sides, that to force the present Home Rule Bill upon the Statute Book without an appeal to the electors of Great Britain will bring about the greatest calamity that has ever befallen the people of this country. (Signed) E. E. Pester (Liberal). Edward Devonport (Liberal). James Bramhall (Liberal). Joseph Payton (Liberal). William Woodcock (Liberal). Walter Hall (Liberal). Isaac 0. Roberts (Liberal) (War- rington). G. D. Howarth (Liberal). S. Evans (Liberal). A. Wilkinson (Independent). Harry Douse (Conservative) Hyde). Mr. W. H. Bellian, of Warrington, acted as secretary for the tour.

AiLa!, following report was supplied to us on i.et' by Mr. Herbert Hayes, organising •see- -17Q, of the Conservative Party even Liberals returned to Warrington l'alerday from Ireland, whither they had ee/1 sent by Lady Greenall, of Walton Hall, i° study the Home Rule question at first 4-,atal• A previous deputation sent by Lady I:treenail in January decided that Home ule would be not only a blunder, but a • fri:l'e party were accompanied on their tour sPeetion by a deputation from the Hyde tPaien of Cheshire, which consisted of two ,10erals one Independent, and one Comer. l'atiNre• They also signed the following e have and now finished our week's tour in undertaken at the invitation of , TtlEalY Greenall, of Walton Hall, Warrington, purpose of studying the Home Rule —estiGn, of observing the conditions in the

div.head: LIBERAL OFFICIAL VIEW. The Real Liberals Will Remain Liberals
div.p: LIBERAL OFFICIAL VIEW. The Real Liberals Will Remain Liberals
- --- - In Spite of Tory Trips.

We have interviewed a prOminent official of the Liberal Association respecting these _free excursions to Ireland, and found that little at- tention is being paid to them. There is a feel- ing that at a time when so much real work is on hand there is but little time to waste upon play. However, we were accorded a few minutes .in which to discuss the least trivial points about the mattei.
"What is your opinion about this latest trip?" asked our representative.
"Well," was the answer, "to tell you seri- ously, I have not troubled much about it, seeing how effectively the previous trip was knocked on the head by ridicule and exposure."
" Are the men who went Liberals?" "I believe three of them are, but I have no knowledge of the other four." " D 9 you blame them for going?"

" Ce.riainly not, and it i; quite certain the programme arranged for them would impress them. There would, however, be a different tale to tell if a prominent Liberal were given full power to convey the trippers to Home •Rule quarters. Even the Tories would be converted. Do you think the Liberals, if they desired to convert a Tory, would take him to one of the Universities?" 'Do you think any of the Liberals you know will vote against you?"
„ 'I have not the slightest hesitation in saying that, so far as the men I know personally are concerned, it will take a good many Tory trips to convert them to Toryism.”

" Does that expression of opinion refer to both sets of trippers?" yes:, " And includes Mr. England?" "Certainly not. We never acknowledged him as a Liberal." "But he was a member of the Liberal Club?" "Yes, but that does not mean he was a mem- ber of the Association." "Then why did he join the Club?" "That is best known to himself. I believe he was sincerely repentant at again leaving the Liberal party, and had certainly given opinions to friends that he was on the wobble again, and anxious to get back, but I am afraid it would have been a difficult thing to get the membersl of the Association to accept him. Our workers think that it would be best for Liberalism if he remained with the Tories." " When did he join the Club?" "On 24th of October, 1913, when this Home Rule question was continually being discussed." "It is rather a sudden change round again in three months?" "Yes, it is, but when you become better ac- acquainted with Mr. England, you will under- stand." "'Surely he could not go over to the Tories again without some strong reason, seeing the
Home Rule question was before him when he joined the Club?"

"I cannot say what the strong reason was. He certainly never gave the Club members any impression that he was about to change his politics again. It was only when we saw his name in the list of trippers that we recognised that he had again made his escape."
" Is there any other aspect of the question to which you care to refer?"
"Only with reference to Alderman Bennett."
"What about him?"

"Well, we are surprised that he should allow his name to go forward to all constituencies as an Independent chairman. Our people had the greatest respect for him until this happened. We consider, and rightly so, there can be no Independent chairman between the two parties, who is connected with either party. lam afraid he has not quite acted fairly in allowing his name to be used in this way. No man can be independent in any matter when his mind is already made up. It is not playing the game."

div.head: _EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914.
div.p: THE _EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914.
JUNIOR LIBERALS.
Ulstr Does Not Want to be Over- Ridden by the Clerics.
MR. C. E. PARKER AND HOME RULE.

A meeting held under the auspices of the Junior Liberal Association is always popular, and when one of the excellent public entertain- ments and meetings was announced to take place in the Co-operative Hall on Monday night it was little wonder that the spacious building was crowded long before the programme was entered upon. The audience were extremely delighted with the accomplishments, of the artistes and ap• plauded vociferously. Mr. C. E. Parker pre- sided, and he was supported by Mr. J. B. Mar- tindale (prospective candidate for the Widne4 Division), Mr. E. Lloyd Jones and Mr. Hughes (secretary of the. Association). . _

As to the artistes who entertained in such an, admirable fashion, Miss Ethel Austen (Liver- pool), who has on previous occasions merited, .the approbation of Warrington audiences, used her sweet soprano voice to advantage in "The farewell song" from "The Daughter of the Regiinent," "It was a dream," and other num- bers. Miss Ellen Reed (of the Manchester, Leeds and Liverpool concerts) is a contralto vocalist with a rich, full-toned voice, and whose enunciation is perfect. She made the happy choice of " Fleurette" (a), "Happy summex song': (b), and "The reason." Miss Margaret Baron is indeed a clever elocu- tionist, and the items she gave were character- ised with a skill and cleverness which was highly commendable. Sheridan's "School fox Scandal" and "A Venetian Revenge," by H. Saville Clark, treated in her artistic style, pleased the audience immensely. Mr. John McArthur sang "The Rosary" and "Absent" in a pleasing manner, his baritone voice suiting both songs admirably. The audi- ence could not restrain itself, however, when, in sprightly, dashing manner, he rendered "Gal- loping Dick." He was equally successful in all his songs, and many were those who expressed a desire to hear him again. Miss Gertrude Jones was an efficient accompanist.

div.head: NO ORDINARY TIMES.
div.p: NO ORDINARY TIMES.

T 4 CHAIRMAN, who received a hearty welcome, said !fiat if these had been ordinary times he would have been satisfied to have said very little, but they lived in stirring times. (Heart hear.) The events of the last few days had been like a cinematograph. Ulster had filler; the whole sheet, and he was afraid there was a danger of Ulster filling too much of the sheet. Because the trees of Ulster were made so large there was .a danger that they would not see the Irish wood. They could not see the wood for trees. „ They could not see the larger ques- tion than Ulster, and that was the Irish ques- tion. His association with Ireland had been pretty close for 30 or 40 years, and he thought he could claim that for every day the deputation —(great laughter)—had spent there, he had spent at least a month.

-They in Ulster seemed to have conferred a special title on a Warrington gentleman. (Laughter.) They had heard of "Galloping Fred," but he saw in the " Dispatch" that morning that they had Colonel Broadhurst. (Great laughter and applause.) Still he was sure they would all congratulate Councillor Broadhurst on the great honour conferred upon him in Ulster, and he hoped Councillor Broad- hurst would live long to bear the honour con- ferred upon him. (Laughter.) His (Mr. Parker's) association with Ireland ex- tended over many years, and, curiously enough, his association had been with those who were anti-Home 'Rulers. When lie was in Ireland on the last occasion he was requested to go to Belfast to see some of the leaders. They then saw several gentlemen and had several hours' talk with them. They were very kindly disposed, but the sum and substance of it all seemed to be suspicion and distrust. They did not fear persecution or anything of that sort, but they feared that the Catholic Church would so in- fluence the legislation passed in the Irish Par- liament that their, section—the business section —that is Ulster, would suffer.

div.head: " Influence of the Priest."
div.p: " Influence of the Priest."

They talked about the influence the priest might have, and certainly he found that the fear of the Roman Catholic Church was in the minds of many. Talking to a Protestant gentleman and a Home Ruler, he mentioned that phase of the question to him, and he said, "Yes; it is a fear in the minds of a considerable number of persons, and for my own part I very much object to the influence of the priest, or; for that matter, a Methodist parson, in regard to eivil affairs. We don't want the influence of the Church brought in to influence matters outside. I don't say that the man who is a priest, a Methodist parson, Or a minister, should be disenfranchised like lunatics, but they must come in, not as parsons, priests, or Church of England ministers. We don't want these men to come in with this influence behind them. It is an obectionable thing. Whatever influence we had is passing away."

Not Disloyal. They were not disloyal, but held the opinion that the influence of the priest and :the Church should be kept in its proper place. Thb, gentleman said that one of the greatest benefltb that would come to Ireland from Home Ruk would be that whatever was left of the undue influence of the Church, whether CatholiToi Methodist, would pass away. He thought that was a thoughtful and intelligent way of looking at the matter. The gentleman said "there had been influence in the past. Supposing you put the responsibility on the people, they will rise to their responsibilities and discharge their duties and keep out undue influence from out- side." _

He also said: My hopes in regard to that particular matter have better foundation than those of the people on the other side." He (the speaker) thought, however, that if they would look back on the history of the Horne Rule agitation they would find evidence that the Nationalist party were not controlled by their Church. It was, however, a fear that many people had, this influence of the Church; but it was a fear that was absolutely groundless. They had to recognise that the demand for a form of self-government for Ireland was just and legitimate, and in regard to dealing with Ulster, although one was anxious to meet a reasonable demand, the meeting of such demands should not jeopardise the solving of the question that the Liberal party had in hand in regard to Ireland. (Applause.)

RESISTANCE BY TORIES. Hampering Liberal Measures. Mr. J. B. MARTINDALE said there was not a single Liberal measure passed in the last few years which the Tories had not resisted with all their power. But now they had a tolerably fair chance of putting their measures on the Statute Book, and yet the Tories were adopting the most contemptible measures they could find. The fight they were making against Home Rule was not so much an attack on the Home Rule Bill as it was an attempt to do away with the
Parliament Act. (Hear, hear.) The passing of that Act would mean religious freedom to Wales. They knew that when dealing with the Conservative party they took everything to themselves.

The Government had not done anything to induce those people who held strong views in Ulster to take the absurd course they had. The Government had done nothing to induce them to believe that the Army should coerce Ulster, As a matter of fact that was farthest from their ideas. But if the Ulster Volunteers were about to break up public peace and property; then that Army must be called in. (Hear, hear.) Sir Edward Carson seeded to imagine that the Army was to coerce Ulster. If there was one man in the country who knew what coercion meant it IN-as him. (Hear, hear.) He was one of the coercionist party, who did more to quell and crush the national spirit than any man in the kingdom. Coercion was something wholly antagonistic to the Liberal ideas, and the Liberal party had no idea in regard to coercing Ireland. But they were determined that if a great majority of the Irish people demanded that measure and showed they were worthy- of it, the great majority should have their will, despite the loud and clamorous opposition of a part of Ireland. If they denied Ireland Home. Rule now they would be lighting the fire that no Government would be able to put out. If such things as were threatened in Ulster were allowed to go on they would strike at the root of the discipline of the British Army and bring about an early fall. The duty of the Army was to do its duty without any bias or prejudice, .and he asked them to stand solid by the Gov- ernment when they had to face a situation like the present. If they stood by the Government they would be standing by their fellow Liberals in the North of England. div.p: TRIBUTE TO MR. PARKER.

Mr. E. LLOYD JONES proposed a comprehensive vote of thanks. After expressing their grati- hide to the artistes and Mr. Martindale, he said that to Mr. Parker they owed more than ever they could repay. He did a splendid work for the party, which he led so magnificently, espe- cially by his excellent articles in "The Exam- iner." He was the greatest asset to intellectual Liberalism they had in, the party in Warring- ton. (Hear, hear.) He had been the means of formulating Liberal, Progressive and public opinion in the columns of "The Examiner" more than any man. To a very great extent

div.head: POLITICS IN THE ARMY.
div.p: POLITICS IN THE ARMY.
The Claim of Officers to Choose What They Shall

div.head: and Shall Not Do.
div.p: and Shall Not Do.
LEADING POINTS IN THE GREAT CRISIS.
We give below the chief points in the military- political conspiracy which reached a dangerous crisis this week :

GENERAL PAGET AND A SOLDIER'S DUTY. Lieutenant-General Sir Arthur Henry Fitzroy Paget, Commander-in-Chief of the Forces in Ireland since 1911, made a speech at the Corinthian Club, Dublin, on February 24th, from which we extract the following striking passages :7

. - I have been assured over and over again that there is no intention on the part of the Govern- ment to make use, of troops in this country, except for one purpose—a very proper purpose— to maintain law and order. I can assure you that I cannot be told that too often, because my feelings are very strong on that subject. . . . It is not thinkable—it is not possible—for me to contemplate even being asked to concentrate my men to move against the forces .that are, I believe, in being in the North of Ireland. But at the same time you must remember that in our lives we soldiers have to ,do things that we do not like. We have, too, a small Army. It is very efficient, and that comes because the Army is• in a very high state of discipline, and when you have to deal with large bodies of men who understand the meaning of the word discipline, it means that, however distasteful it may be to , them, they will -carry out any orders given to them by their King, and it may be—God forbid it should be—my lot to be ordered to move to the North. I should regret it. I have no doubt that many officers—friends of you all—would hate the very idea of moving one , mile north of Dublin; but if that order comes ' that order must be obeyed, and if the order was not obeyed, it would mean that the Army is not in that state of discipline in which you would wish to see it. I do not for one moment believe —not for a single moment—that there can be any question of such a move being made,. but should it happen you must take into considera- tion what we soldiers are, our training of years, our stern sense of discipline, and how vital it is —how important it is—that we should carry out such instructions as we may receive, and al- ' though you may condemn us in any act of ours, at the same time you would say to yourselves, "Well, after all, they only did their duty."
TROUBLE FORESEEN, : AND .A WARNING.

On December 16th Colonel Seely, Secretary. of State for War, saw the General Officers Com- manding-in-Chief, and made to them a state- ment with reference to the duty of soldiers when the possibility of resignations of their Commis- sions e notice.ralsa fficer to private, He pointed out that h s n o brought one, is entitled to use more force than is required to so io from o maintain order and the safety of life and pro- perty. If men in the Army were led to believe that there was a possibility that they might be called ' upon to take some outrageous action for instance, to massacre a demonstration of Orangemen who were causing no danger to the lives of their neighbours, bad as were the effects on discipline in the Army, nevertheless it was true that they were, in fact and in law, justified in contemplating refusal to obey. But there never had been, and was not now, any intention of giving outrageous and illegal orders to the troops. The law would be respected, and must be obeyed. What had now to be faced was the possibility of action being required by His Majesty's troop q in supporting the civil power, in protecting life and property when the police were unable to hold their own. .
Attempts had been made to dissuade troops from obeying lawful orders given to them when acting in support of the civil power. This
much fear same conditions in 16th Lancers. Fear men will refuse to move."
And later same day :—" Regret to report Brigadier and 57 officers, 3rd Cavalry Brigade, prefer to accept dismissal if ordered North."
OFFICERS MAKE STIPULATIONS.

The Secretary of State for War instructed General Paget to suspend from duty any senior officers who have tendered their resignations or in any other manner disputed your authority. Direct Gough and Offictrs Commanding sth and 16th Lancers to report themselves to the Adjutant-General at the Wal• Office without delay. They should leave by first possible boat. They should be relieved of their Commands, and officers are being sent to relieve them at once. Resignations of all officers should be refused. General Gough, General Officer Commanding 3rd Cavalry Brigade in Ireland, reported The officers are of unanimous opinion that further information is essential before they are called upon at such short notice to take decisions so vitally affecting their whole future, and especially that a clear definition should be given of the terms "Duty as ordered," and "active Operations" in Ulster. If such duty consists of the maintenance of order and the preservation of property, all the officers in this brigade, including myself, would be prepared to carry out that duty. But if the duty involves the INITIATION of active military operations against Ulster, the following numbers of officers by regiments would respectfully-and under protest prefer to be dis- missed (list follows).

General Gough and other officers reported themselves, and Mr. Asquith made it known that they had honestly misunderstood their in- structions which had been tactlessly handled. General Gough, however, wrote to the Adjutant-General on March 23rd On thinking over the points raised by the Secretary of State this morning, the question has arisen in my mind, and it will undoubtedly be one of the first questions asked me by my officers, when I see them, viz.:— In the event of the present Home Rule Bill becoming law, esti we be called upon to enforce it on Ulster under the expression of maintaining law and order? _ .

This point should be made quite clear in your draft letter, otherwise there will be renewed misconceptions. The following document was then handed to General Gough, but its terms were not made known till Wednesday, after they had leaked out and caused a great sensation : Brigadier-General 11. De la P. Gough, C.B. You are authorised by the Army Council to inform the Officers of the 3rd Cavalry Brigade that the Army Council are satisfied that the incident which has arisen in regard to their resignations has been due to a misunderstand- ing. It is the duty of all soldiers to obey lawful commands given to them through the proper channel by the Army Council, either for the protection of public property and the support of i the civil power n the event of disturbances or for the protection of the lives and property of the inhabitants. This is the only point it was intended to bc put to the officers in the questions of the General Officer Commanding, and the Army Council have been glad to learn from you that there never has been and never will be in the Brigade any question of disobeying such lawful orders. His Majesty's Government must retain their right to use all the forces of the Crown in Ireland, or elsewhere, to maintain law and order and to support the civil power in the ordinary execution of its duty. But they have no intention whatever of taking

div.p: AN ATTEMPT AT RESTORATION.

ONLY DID HIS DUTY. Air. PARKER said that in whatever he had done t 2 do his duty, and that ought in connection with Liberalism in Warrington he triedof all of them. They should all use their capacities and opportunities to the best advantage, and so do what they could te thoae o n they aim assist in the progress of this great country. He thought they ought to pay their tribute to Mr Jones and those who had assisted him in the series of meetings they had held, and which had been enjoyed by everyone who had attended. (Hear, hear, and applause,)
a amounted tb a claim that officers and men could pick and choose between lawful and reasonable orders, saying that they would obey in one case and not in another.

_ The Army had been quite steady. During the past year there had not been brought to the notice of the authorities one single case of lack of discipline in this respect At the same time, in view of the statements in the Press-and else- where, it was well to make the position clear. I informed them, concludes Colonel Seely, that I should hold each of them individually respon- sible to see that there was no conduct in their commands subversive of 'discipline. They could let it be clearly understood that any such conduct would be dealt with forthwith under the King's Regulations. If any officer should tender his resignation, they would ask for his reasons, and if he indicated in his reply that he desired to choose which order he would obey, I would at once submit to the King that the officer should be removed.

NECESSARY PRECAUTIONS LEAD TO " RESIGNATLONS." On March 14th General Paget was informed by the War Office that the Government had re- ceived reports that attempts might be made in various parts of Ireland by evil-disposed persons to obtain possession of arms, ammunition, and other Government stores, and it was considered advisable that the General should at once take special precautions for safeguarding depots and other places where arms or stores are kept, as he might think advisable. General Paget wired to the War Office on March 20th :—" Officer Commanding sth Lancers 'states that all officers except two and one doubt- ful, are resigning their Commissions to-day. I
advantage of this right to crush political opposi. tion to the policy or principles of the Home Rule Bill. -

J. 8. J.1,.1 23rd March, 1914. J. S. E. [lt will be noticed that the initials of Lieu- tenant-General Sir J. S. Ewart, Adjutant. General of the Forces, are appended to the last document, in addition to those of Colonel Seely and Sir John French.] The paragraphs in black are those which Colonel Seely stated later in the week had been added unknown to the rest of the Cabinet.

CONSERVATIVES SIDE WITH OFFICERS. Mr. Boner Law, Leader of the Opposition, in the House of Commons on Monday night, justi- fying the action of the officers, said : lam going to read—l have permission to read —a statement, taken by one who heard it, of what was said by the General Officer Command- ing the Troops in Ireland to his Commanding Officers. This is what he said : "Sir Arthur Paget said that active operations were to be begun against Ulster, that he ex- pected the country to be in a blaze by Saturday" —(Opposition cries of "Oh ")--" that he had been in close coMmunication with the War Office and that he had the following instructions from the War Office to convey to the officers: 'Officers domiciled in Ulster will be allowed to disappear, and would be reinstated in their position, but they must give their word of honour that they would not fight for Ulster.'" A perfectly fair proposal. "Officers who are not prepared to undertake active operations against Ulster for conscien- tious or other scruples were to send in their resignations, and would be dismissed the Army. It was to be fully understood that the officers,

div.head: BOVRIL BEATS HOT RUM.
div.p: BOVRIL BEATS HOT RUM.
Colonel Ross Was giving an account of a four days' cammtign before a meeting in the Chateau Laurier of the Association of Officers of the Medical Officers of Canada:
"How did you find Bovril for your men dur- ing the campaign?" asked a member of the audience.

"The best ration we took with us. We took a supply of rum, but after a day's hard work the men said-that a cup of hot Bovril was the best stuff they could get. We found it znuch better than hot rum," answered Colonel Ross.
brigadiers, and any officers who .avoided service on an incorrect plea of domicile in Ulster would be tried by Court-martial."

I ask the Prime Minister, said Mr. Bonar Law, to say openly that he [General Gough] has been reinstated on the distinct understanding that he will not be asked to use the troops to enforce the Home Rule Bill in Ulster. (Loud Opposition cheers.) Unless this were regarded by the Government as the possibility of civil war, they had no right Lo make such an exception to Ulster officers, and it does prove that they did so regard it. (Oppo- sition cheers.) To coerce Ulster is an operation which no Government under existing conditions has a right to ask the Army to undertake— (Opposition cheers)—and in our view, of course, any officer who refuses is only fulfilling his duty. (Renewed cheers.)

Mr. Asquith said : The judge or the magistrate is often called upon to interpret and to administer and to enforce a law which his judgment, perhaps even his conscience, disapproves. He holds his office by a tenure to observe his duty to the Crown in that matter; and in the sane way the naval and military forces of the CMwn, when they are called in to assist the civil power, have no more authority than a judge or a magistrate to dis- -1 criminate between this law and that. If it is the law of the land, it is a law which they, like other subjects of the King, must obey. If the doctrine of Mr. Bonar Law is going to be recog- nised and adopted, how is it going to be applied? If this dispensing power, alleged to reside in the bosom of an individual officer or soldier, to appraise at different degrees of value different injunctions of the law, became the law, then the whole fabric on which law is built would disappear. THE GENERAL'S "TROPHY." In the meantime a rumour gained currency that, contrary to the Premier's assurance, the officers had returned conditionally and on their own terms, and on Tuesday it was announced that General Gough "resumes command of his Brigade, with a written assurance from the Gov- ernment that the troops under his command will not be used to coerce the people of Ulster into acceptance of the Home Rule Bill." General Gough is said to have made a display of his " victory " over the Goveriiment. LABOUR MEMBERS AND THE PEOPLE'S. LIBERTIES. • In the House of Commons on Tuesday night Mr. Ramsay Macdonald asked the Premier whether General Gough had gone back with a "trophy," but Mr. Asquith declined to make any statement on the question until Wednesday. A scene of enthusiasm, without precedent for many years, occurred in the House of Commons when Mr. John Ward, the Liberal-Labour Member for Stoke, declared : We rejoice that you (the Tory party) have made the issue plain. It is: Are the people of this country free to make their laws absolutely without interference from either King or Army? Liberal, Labour and Nationalist Members gave vent to their emotions by cheering for three minutes. Later, Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labour Member for Derby) also made this striking declaration : There is no institution, however great or sacred, in this country that I will not take my stand in smashing if it attempts to interfere with the constitutional liberties of the people. LIBERAL ATTITUDE. The temper of the Liberal party throughout the country was admirably reflected by the "Westminster Gazette" on Wednesday in the following passage "The General who has been given an inch takes an ell. He takes the public into his con- fidence; he gives the Government no quarter. He interprets the phrase about crushing poli- tical opposition' in the light of his own letter, which clearly demands an assurance of a much more sweeping kind. "He means to intimate that in the struggle between the Army and the Government the Army have won. 'The object of ray journey to London has been fulfilled'— the object which tll'e public had taken to be ,simply that of rendering explanations to the authorities of the unprecedented occurrences at the Curragh. "We say quite frankly that rather than that this should go on the record we would cheerfully ' see the Government out of office and the Liberal party sent into the wilderness, there to work as free men in defence of their liberties. An Army which can dictate to a Government is a menace to liberty; air a menace, let us add, to public order."

In the House, REPUDIATED. , Colonel Seely admitted that he had, unknown to the Cabinet, added the offend- ing conditions to the letter to General Gough and resigned. The Prime Minister repudiated \ the conditions, and laid down with emphasis the following rule, So long as we are responsible for the govern- ment of this country, whatever the consequences may be, we shall not assent to the claim of any body of men in the service of the Crown, be they officers or be they men, to demand from the Government in advance an assurance of what they will or will not be required to do in cir- cumstances which have not yet arisen. It is a new claim which, if once admitted, would put the Government and the House of Commons, on whose confidence the Government depends, at the mercy of the military or the Navy. An outburst of tremendous excitement took place on the Ministerial and Nationalist benches I after this repudiation. On both sides of the house members were to be seen on their feet clamouring approval at the top of their voices !. land excitedly waving their handkerchiefs. The solidarity of the Coalition in support of the 'Ministers, which appeared to be in peril at the opening of the debate, was consolidated anew. The Prime Minister had handled a situation most dangerous for the Government with con- , summate discretion and tact. The relief of every sectio, of tia, ktiatsteTialiste was intense,

div.p: THE CHALLENGE TO DEMOCRACY.

This has been a week of crises—and hard lying. Our readers will be able .to form their own judgment upon the facts as set forth in another column, and we venture to think that there will be few who will not come to the con- clusion that a most desperate attempt has been made to undermine the funda- mental principles upon which our liberties as a people stand. The demo- cracy are gradually but surely working out their own salvation, and the ' aristocracy do not like the idea.. up to the present Parliament, Tory measures might pass, but the Radical and Labour men Were kept in their Proper places. If they happened to come into, office the House of Lords stood by, and, laughing at the efforts of the people, threw their attempts to free themselves to the wind. The ilarlia- ment Act was designed to change all that. The Tories, seeing their old champion crippled, sought another. They ,encouraged the setting up of a hostile army in the KING'S Territory, and then intrigued with the officers of

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 28, 1914.

the KING'S Army to'refuse to keep the KING'S peace. The l'evolt we have witnessed this week is „ merely the Lords' Veto disguised as a General, as is so admirably shown in our cartoon by GOULD. Fortunately, the hideous game has been prematurely exposed, and we see the designs of the patriotic, constitutional party in their ugly nakedness:

There Can be no mistaking the game. A General who was given the chance of escaping from . an untenable position under shelter of • a misunderstandini, came again to the charge, and insisted upon, and actuallY received, a guaran- tee that he, would, not be required •to serve in -Ulster. The Tories supported him in the House. Only on one hypothesis can the action of the gentle- manly party be understood. If they ruled that officers might ,be excused from the duty of assisting to keep the peace in the neighbourhood of Belfast, in what plight would they be; should they come into power, and a National- ist Volunteer Army made its appear- ance in the neighbourhood of Dublin? But, .according to Mr. BONAR LAW, they do not expect to come into office for forty years. And so they are desperate and inclined, in the eloquent language of one of their number, to damn the consequences. It is well we have had this warning: Liberalism and Labour, all the stronger for the start- ling experience, will know how to act.

div.head: " SOCIETY " AND POLITICS-WITE
div.p: " SOCIETY " AND POLITICS-WITE
A LOCAL APPLICATION.

The "Warrington Guardian pro. claims, with quite a "flourish of trumpets," the " conversion " of more Liberals into Anti-Home Rulers, and seems to infer that Toryism in Warrington is strengthened in conse- quence. There are at least two factors which materially affect the value of such conversions, and must not be overlooked. The first is that LADY GREENALL, in her desire to ascertain, for the .benefit of the Warrington electorate, only the truth about "Ulster." and without the slightest shadow or shade of a desire to make political capital out of the venture, has very generously " financed " the expe- dition. The very idea of an "impar- tial ", inquiry •by so-called " Liberals," led and conducted by Mr. W. H. BELLIAN, and paid for by their strongest political opponent, is so farcical as to destroy in advance any value to .‘'yhich the " unanimous " report of the deputa- tion might otherwise be entitled. Secondly, " signatures " should be "weighed as well as counted," and on this point also very ilittle " grist " will come to the Tory "mill." On the other hand, if the Tories in Warrington fondly imagine that their cause is gaining ground here, they are in for a rude awakening, whenever the General Election takes place. That their candidate has not strengthened his "persona! "• hold on the constituency is admitted, whereas the Progressive forces In the borough have been I materially strengthened during 1913, and, in addition, the circumstances of the past few days have shown up the arrog,ant pretensions of the " Society " element in the Tory party in such a " lurid " light, and have disclosed such, a " menace " to the rights of the people , as will weld together all sections of the. Progressives to such purpose that at the next General Election the Liberai party will return to power with a majority very little, if any, short 9f that I of 1906. Our all-conquering programme I will include Land Reform, both urban and rural, as defined by Mr. ' LLOYD GEORGE, and the purging of the Army of all backstairs and petticoat influence, the absolute elimination of all preferment otherwise than by merit—in other words, the thorough democratisation of this great Service, in such a manner as will make it possible for " rankers " of ability to rise to the very top of their profession. The Tories, presuming upon the far too generous sufferance of the Govern- ment, have, in their insensate folly, threatened the very citadel of the People's liberties, never dreaming that their assaults would be so overwhelm- ingly repulsed, and that the never-to- be-forgotten words of JOHN WARD— " We, as a people, demand the right to , make our, own. laws, without interfer- ence from either KING or Army would find such a unanimous, exuber- ant and thunderous echo from the heart and voice of every patriot in our land. Verily, how little difference there is between the Toryism of to-day and that of centuries ago. It is quite a common- place to hear the remark that the Tory of to-day—or Conservative, as he prefers to be called—is what the Liberal of a few years ago WAS. Never was A greater " fiction " uttered. Whiggism and Liberalism both have always recognised a man's rights; and political, ; religious and civic freedom have been fought for and granted upon the basic principle of the equality before the law of every man. Toryism has always meant, and still means, the recognition and enforcement of class distinctions and class 'privileges, and so deeply engraved is this condition of mental conceit that it finds expression in such incidents as we are daily witnessing in connection with Ulster, incidents that have indelibly stained the hitherto unblemished record of the Army for unquestioning obedience to orders and unswerving loyalty to the KING and the Parliament. To the younr, men of the Liberal party the call Co arms in ,the coming fight is irresistible, and it will be answered by them with all the joy and ieal which is begotten of a righteous cause and the. confidence of Victory with which it is accompanied. ,

div.head: PASSING WEEK.
div.p: THE PASSING WEEK.
OUR INFIRMARY.
Facts brought before the annual meeting of - - -
he friends of the Infirmary yesterday proved

_ that in spite of the benevolent work that is now being done under the provisions of the Insur- ance Act, the calls upon the good offices of the institution continue to multiply. Not only do patients increase with the natural growth of the town, but the cost of maintenance rises in sympathy with the increasing costs, that are felt so- keenly by many sections of the com- munity. An adverse balance of a few hundred pounds at the beginning of the year grew into more than a thousand pounds, and ways and means will have to be found of stemming the , threatening tide. There was a falling off in . income because the Million Penny Fund Com- ' Mateo had finished their work in the previous year, but we hear that during the coming summer that most vigorous and determined .band will Come to life again and hold another Old English Fair in Victoria Park. May they have a prosperous time, and, incidentally, may the Infirmary be relieved,of its debt!

ITS EFTICiENCY. There can be no .doubt about the efficiency with which the Infirmary is conducted, one of the latest indications of the desire of the Board of Management to place its administration on a sound footing being the appointment of a per- manent senior house surgeon, in the person of Dr. Law, to replace the procession of promising, but young and restless, men Who! have in the past occupied the position with varying success. The House Surgeon's report presented yester- day is a record of 'successful work- against disease and accident, deaths in the house, averaging, only four per cent.., which is very ! low, considering the number of desperate cases such as burning, scalding and motoring victims who are rushed to the Infirmary in SO hopeless a state that they die within a day of admission. Warrington is particularly liable to anthrax, owing to the share it takes in the tanning industry, and special facilities exist at the Infirmary for meeting that danger. , Special emphasis is laid upon the importance of prompt action on the .part of master and man when anthrax is suspected. ..The Infirmary should at once be communicated with and the suspect placed under observation. The difference between speed and, lethargy in anthrax is the difference between life and death. •

RADIUM AND THE CURE OF CANCER. Mr: .1. 11. Smethurst told the Working Men's Committee a fortnight ago that the Board made every effort to provide the staff with the best Possible implements; and the House Surgeon draws attention to the first-class X-ray installa- tion which, through the services of the Million Penny Fund Committee, is now available for the inspection of every fracture, or suspected fracture, that *calls for treatment. When Mr. Smethurst hesitated as to our ability to purchase radium for the Infirmary, in.. Joseph exPresso4l the opinion that if radium were proved to be of Paramount importance for the treatment of Patients, radium should be provided. Radium at the present time is practically priceless. It is between 1:20 and DO a milli- gram, and such large places as Manchester and Glasgow are making big efforts to raise funds of £6,000, which will buy the least .quantity •needed for practical purposes. It will be seen at once that Warrington would take upon itself a hopeless task 41 an attempt were made to provide the Infirmary with radium, for it xvotal be patting more than a year's income in the compass of a teaspoon. The Use of radium at the present time is but in the experimental stage, and it is for experimental work that Manchester is moving. Wou/ti it not be best for Warrington to help Manchester to raise the necessary money, and so give the town a title to participate in the benefits that our big neigh- bour will be able to bestow? Besides, War- rington pride would be duly satisfied if the town were allowed to take a part in pioneer work that medical men believe will result in placing another blessing at the disposal of suf- fering humanity. Radium . has been proved to be a complete cure in small tumours, and the treatment of scar tissue and Skin diseases and, while not a cure, still a great ameliorative agent in the treatment of malignant diseases, including all kinds of cancer. If we subscribe to Manchester we should he entitled not only to send patients there, ,but to receive radium " emanations " for use locally. A liberal supply of " emanations" is available at London, 'where there is a stock of radium worth £20,000 or £30,000.

To WAKES, OR NOT To WAKES? His Worship the Mayor has called a meeting to be held at the Town Hall on Tuesday after- noon, to consider the question of establishing a Warrington Wakes. In the settlement of this question, the interests of all, as is ,so forcibly pointed out in the letter from Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, will have to be consid- ered. The institution of a Wakes Week would necessarily mean the abolition of Walking Dab, and there are sentimental, as well as business, considerations that weigh heavily in favour of perpetuating old and established custom. Still there is no harm in discussing the situation, and the Mayor has acted with his usual good judgment in calling the meeting of the parties concerned—representatives of firms, clergy, heads of Corporation departments, trade union ,representatives—while all others interested are invited to attend. It will be best to enter such a conference with an open mind, and we refrain from expressing an opinion at the inoinent.
