We have got several persons in Ireland to deal with it, too, but pressure on our space in this critical week prevents our publishing the comments of these correspon- dents till next week. It will be noticed that

the " report " of the deputation mentions names of Liberals and Home Rulers in such a loose fashion as to lead the unthinking to . believe these gentlemen had given -unfavourable opinions as to the claims of Home Hula. A repudiation of this and some caustic remarks by Home Hula journalists are among the material we can promise our readers for next week. .In the meantime we say: Read the report ;. it proves too much and is its own refutation.

EUGENICS AND ALCOHOL. . The Medical Inspector under the Inebriates Act—Dr. Branthwaite—has expressed the opinion, in his last report, that alcohol is only a medium for revealing certain weaknesses in the race. The question of an alcohol-proof race was touched upon by Dr. Manson in his re- marks to the Sankey Bridges Adult School last Sunday on "Eugenics." He stated that the logical outcome of a rigid temperance,policy— that is, the abolition of alcohol as a beverage— would be to raise a race whose weakness to- wards alcohol would still be potentials although not manifest. This inherent weakness is a great Obstacle to the extensive use of . alcohol as a source of energy for industrial purposes. Some of those who believe that the use .of

alcohol is the solution of the liquid fuel problem are of the opinion that the weaklings towards alcohol and their offspring would gradually die out if alcohol were freely obtained at its'natural price, which is relatively cheap, and in this way an alcohol-proof race would grow up. Sup- porters of this view, however, forget the com- plexity of human character, and in raising an alcohol-proof race by this means they would certainly destroy some very desirable qualities that seem to be associated with a weakness towards seductive drugs like alcohol. A survey I, of the ,history of literature And art brings this out very clearly. The solution of gip problem is in the nature of a compromise`, Alcohol should be put to its fullest uses industrially, and means taken to lessen its seductive influence on humanity. On the other hand,:man should be trained md strengthened to resist its tempta- tions. Where measures of this kind are seem- ingly adequate, and yet hopeless inebriety persists, in certain stocks, these stocks should be gradually eliminated by methods of rational selection.
GOOD LUCK TO " THE EXAMINER." The "Chester Chronicle," the Oldest and most influential newspaper in Cheshire, had the following editorial note last week :

At the annual meeting of the Warrington Liberal Association last week the President of the party referred in complimentary terms to the success and growing influence of the local party organ "The Warrington Examiner." For the energy, intelligence, and improvement brought into the paper he warmly thanked the editor (Mr. Weston). Mr. Weston was at one time a highly-esteemed Chester journalist, and nobody familiar with his grit, energy, and con- scientiousness will be surprised at this hand- some acknowledgment. As an old colleague, I .wish him and "The Examiner" all good luck.

div.head: WHAT WE ALL WANT To SEE.
div.p: WHAT WE ALL WANT To SEE.

Some of us who have travelled must have seen two kinds of rivers in different countries. There is the river which rushes tumultuously along; dashing against rocks, a grand spectacle! You can stand on its banks and enjoy it; but it never fructifies the banks; they are arid—a , wilderness. Ancl no ships ever pass along it to carry good things to the people who live there. , Then there is the other river, the great, tran- quil, broad stream irrigating the banks, carrying great ships with cargo to the people who live there. Politics up to the present have been too much:like the former. Tempestuous, rowdy, full of life, dashing along—a great spec- tacle to watch from the banks—to see the struggle of the torrent dashing against the rocks! And we say, Is not this fine?" But the banks are arid. There is nothing being carried along. I want to see the political stream carrying its cargo to the people on the banks. I want to see the political stream irrigating the soil so that there shall be a harvest on it a hundred-fold to the hungry children of men. Tins was the last passage in one of Mr. Lloyd George's speeches last Saturday at Hudders- field. It is a fervid plea for social reform put in a way calculated to soften the hardest Of re-actionaries.

div.head: DIARY OF AN OLD MAID.
div.p: DIARY OF AN OLD MAID.
Brief Record of a Woman's Opinion of Men
and Their Manners.

The following truthful and touching history of an old maid, dating from about 1843, is one of the briefest, yet at the same time most complete, records of human experience in print. Those who can read between the lines will have full sympathy. History proverbially repeats itself kth.d human nature, especially feminine nature, is still the same. out.
At fifteen years, anxious for coming Sixteen, began to have some idea of the tender passion. Seventeen, talked of love in a cottage, and dis- interested affection.
Eighteen, fancied myself in love with some handsome man who flattered me.
Nineteen, was a little more difficult, in conse- quence of being noticed: _ _
Twenty, commenced fashionable and dashing. Twenty-one, still more confidence in my own attractions, and expected a brilliant establish,. „ment.
Twenty-two, refused a good offer because he was not a man of fashion. _
Twenty-three, flirted with every young man I met.
Twenty-four, wondered why not married. Twenty-five, rather more circumspect in con- duct.
Twenty-six, began to think a large fortune not quite so indispensable.
Twenty-seven, preferred the company of rational men.

Twenty-eight, wished to be married in a quiet way, with a comfortable home and children. Twenty-nine, almost despaired of entering the marriage state. Thirty, was rather fearful of being called an vld maid. Thirty-one, an additional love of dress. Thirty-two, professed to dislike balls, finding it difficult to get good partners. Thirty-three, wondered how men could leave the society of sensible women to flirt with chits.

Thirty-four, affected good • humour in conver- sation with men. Thirty-five, jealous of the praises of women. Thirty-six, quafrelled with friend who had been lately married. Thirty-seven, thought myself slighted in com- pany, 1 Thirty-eight, liked talking of my acquaint- ances who are married unfortunately, and found endless consolation in their misfortunes. Thirty-nine, ill-nature increased. Forty, became a confirmed scold. And so on up to 50, when the lady seized upon lap dogs, and talked largely of philanthropy. After that age, grey hairs start out upon the temple, and " old lady " becomes the tune—no longer old maid.

div.head: SNIILE OF A LITTLE CHILD.
div.p: THE SNIILE OF A LITTLE CHILD.

There are things which not all the money in this world can buy, which yet are given freely, and on all sides "without money and without price " ; and not least among them is the sweet, trustful smile of a little innocent child. There is such exquisite loveliness in it as even angels must delight in. I keep in my heart many such priceless treasures to help me onward in Life's ceaseless warfare. WALTER CARTER. Latchford.
A CLARION CALL.
Mr. Llogd George and the Fight for
CiliC Libertg.
A GRAVE CRISIS.
To be Confronted With Resolute Unwavering Determination.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir, I am not writing you, ' Mr. Editor, to ask you to allow me to encroach on your space this week myself, but having just read in the "Manches- ter Guardian" of Monday an admirable report of Mr. Lloyd George's characteristic and in- imitable speech at Huddersfield on the Irish question, it does occur to me to send in a plea for space for such extracts from this speech as you may be able to find room for in next Satur- day's issue. True, it will already be familiar to most of the readers of "The Examiner," but it may have escaped some, and this speech is such an incomparable answer to all the frothy non- sense with which sensational mischief-makers in the "Daily Mail" and other papers of that description pursue their heedless and reckless attempts to hinder a settlement of the Ulster problem, and extract some further wretched party capital out of it. The speech is as irrefutable as the masterly demonstration of the ' Government's position delivered by Mr. Churchill at Bradford, or the brief but not less admirable address delivered the other day by Sir John Simon in Manchester. Every step taken in this great controversy shows the wis- dom, the absolute fairness, and the great con- sideration towards the Protestants of Ulster with which the Government has acted under the Prime Minister's superb leadership.— Yours, 4c.,
ARTHUR CROSFIELD.

div.head: GREAT SPEECH.
div.p: A GREAT SPEECH.

Mr. Lloyd George, speaking at Huddersfield last Saturday, said: A grave crisis has arisen in the history of democratic government in this country. we are confronted with the greatest issue raised in this country since the days of the Stuarts. Representative government in this land is at stake. (Cheers.) In those days our forefathers had to face a claim of the Divine right of kings to do what they pleased. To-day it is the Divine right of the aristocracy to do what it pleases. It is a question of whether progressive Bills, supported by the democracy of this kingdom, if opposed by the Tory party, are to be honoured or whether they are to be flung in the waste- paper basket. (Cheers.) Tie Tory party have two answers to that question. The first is, "We will not allow the Liberal progressive measures to pass." The second answer is, "If they do pass we will refuse to obey them." I have some- thing to say about both to the Liberals of this great county. If Liberalism flinches one inch before either of these insolent and arrogant claims it is not fit any longer to be an instru- ment of government in a great Empire, and it is time that it made way for a sterner, a more highly-merited body of British Progressives. But you need not fear. That is why I am here this. afternoon on behalf of the British Government to say this to you—that they mean to confront this defiance of popular liberties with a most resolute, unwavering determination, whatever the hazard may be. (Cheers.) We are not fighting about Ulster. ("No.") We are not fighting about Home Rule. We are fighting for all that is essential to civil liberty in this,land. The Parliament Act has abolished the Lans- downe House Legislature. (Laughter.) It is one of the great charters of popular rights. It is a great landmark on the road to freedom; and now they are attempting to abolish it by force. That is what we have to face. (A Voice: "We will face it.")

div.head: ARISTOCRACY AND RETAINERS ABOVE
div.p: ARISTOCRACY AND RETAINERS ABOVE
THE LAW.

We were under the impression that it was the basis of all civilised government that the sub- ject must obey the law until you alter it. But that is where the unwritten Constitution comes in. (Laughter.) There is just a little proviso that has been written in by the Peers, that in this connection "subject" means the common people. It is not intended to apply to highlyplaced persons like the Duke of Abercorn an the Marquess of Londonderry and Lord Wil- loughby de Broke—(laughter)—or to a great lawyer like Sir Edward Carson. This is ow the Constitution should read if it were a written one: "All subjects must obey the law. whether they like it or not, unless they be members of the British aristocracy, their associates, or re- tainers." (Laughter.) I am giving you a lec- ture on law up-to-date. It is the new doctrine i . know much t that is for owl). ttiho the aple oopbleedai et ntchee. t o(pL aut o o)t t top hear.) through the various t about fashions, but there s one thing I know about them, and that is that fashions have a from bottom. t he ( Ti ea rs habit of percoilaattiang to thedown And what may be the fashion for a duke to-day may be the fashion of a poacher to-morrow. (Laughter.) What may be the fashion for a baron may 'be the fashion for a burglar. It is all law. If it is on the Statute book it is law. Why should there be one law for the poor and another law for other people? Of what right of citizenship does Home Rule deprive any man in Ulster? So far froui de- priving them of their votes it gives them a vote for two Parliaments. They can vote for the Home Rule Parliament; they can vote for the Imperial Parliament; they have their rights as citizens of the Empire, as British citizens. There is no right they are deprived of. They "[the Conservatives] are on a slippery slope, and they themselves have most to lose by it; but, believe me, the whole foundation of civil liberty is at stake. They are fighting the battle of the British oligarchy with the Orange army, but the issue is broader, wider, than the domain of Ulster. It reaches to the uttermost boundary of British freedom and democratic government in this country. (Cheers.) •

div.head: REAL MOTIVE FOR RESISTANCE.
div.p: THE REAL MOTIVE FOR RESISTANCE.

If you want to prove the real motives for this armed protest there are two or three facts I should like to get into your minds. If they are afraid of the persecution of Protestants' in Ire- land, why are they in Ulster prepared to aban- don their fellow-Protestants where the Protest- ants are weakest? They say, "Exclude Ulster and we will accept your Bill." But excluding Ulster means that you leave the small Protest- ant congregations scattered through the South, the East and the West without any of the pro- tection which they get from the powerful Pro- testant community of the North. Why are they doing that? Because they do not believe there is any danger. (Cheers.) All they ask for is— and I want to impress this upon you—that their pride should not be lowered by having to meet Catholic Irishmen on equal terms in the land which their race has lived in and suffered for throughout the dark centuries of Irish history. Now we are getting at the real reason. They have constituted the dominant caste in Ulster for centuries. Their ideas have governed Ire- land for centuries, and what ideas! They have governed it ruthlessly. There is no country in' the world which has been governed so relent- lessly, so brutally as Ireland has been governed. (Cheers.) The gibbet, the crowbar, fire and sword have been the weapons of ascendancy in Ireland. The Orangemen of the North profess to be very shocked at the idea that any force should be used for the purpose of setting up a free self-governing Parliament in Ireland. When did they acquire this detestation of coercion? (Hear, hear.) Coercion presented no horrors to them when used to evict Catholic peasants from houses they had built with their own hands for non-payment of rents which are ac- knowledged now by both parties to have been extortionate.

They did not object to coercion. On the con- trary, they supported it when the forces of the Crown were used to fling out Catholic peasants on the hillsides, used to drive them by the mil- lion into exile. When the protests of the majority of the inhabitants of that island were choked in blood, no protest from Ulster. 'Ulster supported every' coercive effort ever made, and

div.head: l'arish Church Services.
div.p: l'arish Church Services.

Under the auspices of the Warrington Church Society, the Yen. Archdeacon Madden preached yesterday at the weekly Lent services in the Parish Church. The service in the afternoon was for women and the one in the evening for men.

Bewsey-road Wesley Guild. All those who entertain the idea of visiting Switzerland got an added stimulus from Miss Massey at the Guild meeting on Monday even- ing, when she gave her lecture on "A Guilder's Holiday in Switzerland." Views, which hei brother and she had photographed, were thrown upon a screen, and these illustrated the plates of interest visited. The lady proved to be a competent lecturer, and interested her audience from start to finish.

IVarrington Market Prices. The market prices on Wednesday were: Wheat at late prices, viz., 4s. 6d. to 4s. Bd. per 701 b.; a steady tone prevailed. Oats slightly easier, demand not so strong; prices, 2s. 6d. to 2s. Bd. per 451 b. Oat straw, 255. per ton. Wheat straw, 255., with very little demand. Hay: Best clover hay, 655. to 70s. per ton; meadow hay, 55s to GOs. per ton. XX flour, 235. per 240th. Bran slightly dearer, firm, at late prices. The Bev. W. Braceeamp at 'Wycliffe. . . _ .

_ Last night the Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's, delighted a large audience at the Wycliffe Memorial Building, called together by the Wycliffe Young People's Society, to hear him lecture upon his holiday in Palestine, illus- trated by lantern slides. The kindness of Mr. Bracecamp was highly appreciated, and, on the invitation of the Rev. T. T. James, he promised to give a lecture on "A trip on the Nile" next winter. ,

Clever Sunday Scholars. The teachers of the local Sunday schools showed their interest in the new methods of teaching by the good attendance at the primary demonstration given by the Wesleyan scholars of the Sunday School, Silver-street, in Wycliffe Memorial Hall, on Saturday afternoon. Mrs. Henry Roberts presided, and Miss C. Gwen Parry, of Waterloo, conducted the demonstra- tion, which was followed by an animated discus- sion. After tea the teachers again assembled. The Rev. 'William Reid (the president of the local Sunday School Union) presided over the conference. A scholarly address on " The Teacher's 31essage" was delivered by Miss War- linrst, of Liverpool, and Miss Parry spoke on " The Sunday School Junior Department." Preachers for To-morrow. Warrington Photographic Society. "But thou last reserved the good wine until now" might almost be the motto for the last : lecture for the present session of the society on Tuesday. "Peeps at Life in the East" was the, title; and the lecture was by Mr. J. W. Had- field, of Dukinfield, and rarely can the society have heard and seen so much in one evening that was new and full of interest. During the voyage to Aden, Bombay, and the journey to Calcutta, many out-of-the-way scenes were visited, especially in Savoy, the Italian frontier, and the Adriatic seaboard. He characterised Port Said as the most wicked place on \earth. The voyage through the canal was anything but dull to an amateur with the camera. ' Aden, the town without a drop of rain, without a single green leaf, gave many views fresh to the audience. The lecturer had secured admission to one of the burning ghats of Calcutta, and there saw and photographed the whole process of Hindoo cremation of the dead. The first day lie had a companionl who had lived in Calcutta twelve years, and had never before seen inside the ghat; but one sight was enough for him. The second day's pictures may be imagined by those who were not present at the lecture. Mr 11. Holloway moved, and Mr. W. Daintith seconded, a hearty 1 vote, of thanks.
Reply on Messrs. Pearson and Knowles'

- Vakcsllleek Scheme. The following reply to the Mayor's circular has been sent to the Town Clerk by Messrs. Pearson arid Knowles : "Dear Sir,—ln reply to your circular letter of the 17t1\ instant, I am instructed to say that my directors, while fully sympathising with any movement which has for its object the im- provement in the everyday life conditions of their own and other workers in Warrington, in regard to recreation and such suitable holidays as may be consistent with the interests of ill.- dividuals and of the general business of the town, view with distinct disapproval and objec- tion the proposal to establish anything like ia ' Local Wakes Week,' which suggests to them what may not unfairly be described as an aim— less week of idleness called for by no common local object or celebration or reason for special holiday-making. "My directors consider that before any such far-reaching change in the old customs of the town ought to be even considered, the all-but unanimous assent, approval and wishes, not only of the 'Trades and Labour Council' and the employers, but of all whose social and busi- ness arrangements might be adversely affected by the introduction of such a scheme, should be obtained. At present there seems to be no evidence that such a feeling exists. '! Yours faithfully, For the Company, "(Signed) A. BROTHERTON, Secretary." St. John's Presbyterian Congregational Social. •

Mr. Warnock, with whom he had been asso- ciated in work on the Free Church Council.— The IRev. J. J. James congratulated St. John's congregation on their efforts and on the success which they had achieved in connection with

their bazaar. The church had a great worleto I do,, and an annual meeting of that kind was a time when they made up their minds to renew their devotion, so far as their own duty was con- eerned. They should make up their minds as to their own attendance at the church services, re- membering that if they wanted to convince people outside of the value of the church's work they must show that they believed in it them- selves.—Mr. J. 11. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
THE CRISIS,
A Strong Sense of Relief Last
Night.
MINISTER'S "WEEK-END"

The Central News, telegraphing late .last night, says that it is stated authoritatively that the decisions of Sir John French and Sir J. S. Ewart with regard to their resignations will not be officially made known until after the Cabinet has met, which it is understood will be to-morrow morning. The decision in the first instance will be formally communicated to the Secretary of State for War, who will in turn inform the Prime Minister.

In political circles if is stated with some con- fidence, that both officers will; if they have not already done so, withdraw their resignations. In certain quarters closely involved there is an air of optimism, and a strong sense of relief is apparent, as if some grave crisis had been averted. It i significant, also, that two promi- nent Cabinet ifinisters have made arrangements to spend the week-end out of town. The following announcement was issued fronz the National Liberal Club to-night :
"An eme'rgency meeting of members of the club will be held on Tuesday next or the pur- pose of considering the present grave rciitical situation and passing a resolinian t Lemon."

div.head: CINEMA EDUCATIOII.
div.p: CINEMA EDUCATIOII.
A Warrington Schoolmaster Makes a Novel Suggestion.
FREE SHOWS IN THE PARR HALL.

Speaking at the annual meeting of the War- rington branch of the National Union of Teachers, held in the Junior Conservative Rooms last night, the President, Mr. Newburn, made a suggestion that the cinema should be used for educational purposes.

After making various suggestions for im- provements in the teacher's lot and in the edu- cation of children, Mr. Newburn spoke of the appalling growth of criminology amongst the rising generation. The usual pegs on which to hang much of the blame were lack of parental control and kinematography, and the pros and cons of the latter were sufficient for a whole address. But the kinema had come to stay, and it was an invention which could be put to a great educational use, and the Education Com- mittee could do much by those means to help forward the education of the children.

div.head: SHOWS IN THE PARR HALL.
div.p: SHOWS IN THE PARR HALL.

The Parr Hall was at liberty every Satur- day afternoon practically, and he was certain it would be easy to evolve a scheme and arrange programmes that would put the children on a higher intellectual plane and appeal to their better instincts. It was naturally apparent to all that they should be up against vested inter- ests, but that was mere dust in the balance with them. They were out absolutely and entirely for the welfare of those committed to their charge, and he thought they were unanimous that close acquaintance with cowboy pictures and pictures which appealed to lower natural instincts, would, in no way, be beneficial for the rising generation. (Applause.)

div.head: CLERGYMAN CRITICISED.
div.p: CLERGYMAN CRITICISED.

After condemning the latest inspiration of the Board of Education in regaid to the endorse- nient of certificates, the speaker said that the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, who, besides being an acknowledged authority on education, was the guide, philosopher and friend of the local Guardians, an authority on Christmas glut- tony and harvest festivals. Ile said: "Qua of the greatest reforms called for in education is , the teacher. Far too many .adopt teaching as ' a means to a living and nothing more. This sort of teacher should be treated as one treats garden weeds." Other extracts of the reverend gentleman's statements were described by the speaker as a conglomeration of vituperation and misrepresentation worthy of a Cabinet Minis- ter. Perhaps it was wisest to treat the reverend gentleman with the contempt he deserved, and consign him to his weeds and other green things.

div.head: MORE FREEDOM WANTED.
div.p: MORE FREEDOM WANTED.

....... The teachers wanted more freedom and more encouragement from the inspector, the official and the manager, less rigidity of time-table and syllabus, consultative committees, not so much a lessening of curriculum as a longer period of carrying it out, or in other words,. a higher leaving age. They wanted satisfied teachers, less unrest and more real appreciation of a work that after all was second to none in its import- ance and far-reaching in its effects on future generations. (Applause.)

div.head: BENEVOLENT FUND.
div.p: BENEVOLENT FUND.

. - Mr. George Newburn, the hon. secretary and treasurer of the benevolent and orphan fund, submitted his report. lie was pleased to record another increase over last year's donations. Their total for the year was .253. The number of life members had also increased, and 37 life votes were in the hands .of the committee, the fund being built up by the committee standing at .2175 10s. sd. He had to again report that their strenuous efforts to untie the purse strings of certain teachers had met with little success, and he was becoming accustomed to the hand closed to charity. It was astonishing to find members of their profession going out of their way to injure the fund by not only trying to dis- suade others from joining, but actually trying to get present members to withdraw. There had been one local appeal for assist- ance, and substantial and sufficient help had been given. The following figures of the ex- penditure from the National Annual Report would show what the fund was doing to brighten the lives of some of their brothers and sisters: Annuities, £6,000; temporary relief, ..t11,000; home allowances, £2,000; maintenance of two orphanages, .Q 3,600. Concluding, the Secretary thanked Mr. Upson and the committee for their assistance.,

div.head: X7OO FIRE LAST NIGHT.
div.p: X7OO FIRE LAST NIGHT.
Outbreak In Congested Market Place.

A fire, which occasioned much excitement, occurred last night in what is perhaps the most congested area in Market Place. The preniises involved belonged to Mr. IL Ellis Vane, auc- tioneer and furniture dealer, and the outbreak seemed to start in the second storey. The flames had got a. good hold when the Fire Bri- gade got to Work, and their first attention was to prevent the fire spreading to warehouses behind and the premises of Messrs. Davies, solicitors. These precautions taken, they con- centrated with several lines of hose from the, steamer and the motor engines on the outbreak, and after an hour and a half's work quelled the fire. The damage is considerable, and was last night estimated at about £7OO. The cause is unknown.

div.head: MARCH 28, 1914.
div.p: A CLEAR ISSUE.
Liberal—Labour Member Voices the Democratic Ideal in the louse.

div.head: MR. JOHN WARD'S TRIUMPH.
div.p: MR. JOHN WARD'S TRIUMPH.
The Menace of the irmll's Interference in Ulster Politics.
BY C. E. PARKER.

In the political world the week just ending has been one of high tension. As Liberals I doll not think we have reason to regret the happen- ings. When the officers of the Cavalry Regi- ments at Curragh Camp went back to their posts they were received with acclamation. They had "beaten the Government"; "the civil authority had climbed down." It was at once recognised by the rank and file of the Coalition that someone had blundered, had blundered very seriously, and 'confusion prevailed. The only question was whether the blunder was the act of the Executive Government of the Cabinet. The trust we had in Asquith, which had become almost an article of faith, was strained to the breaking point. It was recog- nised that here was a great principle of demo- cracy which the Government had apparently definitely ignored, and the Executive had sur- rendered their trust and yielded to insubordina- tion. A Government that allows itself to be dictated to by the Army is a menace to liberty and public order.

The Foundations of British Liberty. At once there sprang into prominence an issue which overshadowed even the grave Home Rule foundations of British liber- tieswere endangered. When lieitcuytfejorjs rncesrealised this, their deter- minationstplrlbdaleennimd.oicnwrTsaeittr e quickly made; it was to maintain their principles at all hazards. These hazards were very grave. It meant rendering futile much of the work of the last three years, of sur- rendering the use of the Parliament Act for Home Rule, Welsh Disestablishment, and Plural Voting; and probably placing in power the reactionary party. It was an unwelcome course to take, but there was no thought of shrinking. If, ats it seemed, Asquith and his Cabinet were responsible and adhered to what appeared to be their position, then Asquith and his Cabinet must go. What form the appeal to the country precipitated by the action of the parties' trusted leaders would have taken it is impos- sible to irhagine. There is little doubt it would have meant a disruption of the Progressive forces as now constituted, the creation of a new party on a clear, democratic basis, and, in all likelihood, this party for a long time would have the Opposition seats as their resting-place. I was told in London on Wednesday by those who had long been Members that when the , Labour Member, John Ward, gave utterance to the words, "We have now to decide whether the people have to make the law of ihe country without interference from either King or Army," the demonstration made by the unoffi- cial forces'of the democratic party in the House of Commons was such as had never been wit- nessed in these Members' life-time. John Ward was fortunate in giving utterance to the ! principles of democracy at the right moment, in the right words, and with impassioned feel- ing. The scene must have brought home to the Government Bench the convietion that whatever sacrifices had to be made, the democratic forces would not tolerate any dictation from the Army, and it is well if this has been established. Law for Rich and Poor. Nor would it tolerate a different application of the same law to rich nn 4 poor. Was a little printer to be sent to gaol for distributing a leaflet among the privates of the Army while certain gentlemen were Made the heroes of every drawing-room for preaching to officers the same sedition and go scot free? In London I found the feeling intense, anl. even among Conservatives there were many ex- pressions of anxiety in regard to what seemed a weak surrender of the Executive power and authority, which they, as well as th,e Liberals, considered should be maintained at all costs. I was at the National Liberal Club on Wednes- day, the place of all others in which you can sense the pulse of representative Democracy. After lunch in the large, crowded smoke-room it was proposed by a member that cheers should be given for John Ward. Every man responded, amid a scene of great enthusiasm. The issue was clear, the course of the democratic party clear, but as we sat down and thought it over we began wondering what changes would occur; what conditions would be created when we were deprived of trusted leaders, and when there would be an appeal to the country, presumably against the action of these leaders. So in spite of the enthusiasm there was an after-glow of gloom. The Cabinet was then sitting. What would be the outcome? Did it mean resignation, dissolution, and a fratricidal political conflict? We could only "wait and see." The afternoon crept slowly on, the House assembled, and after tedious preliminaries the blundering was ex- plained. Members gathered round the Club news boards, slowly but steadily the ticking mechanism put on the sheets the details as they were being explained in the House. The parti- culars quickly spread, and a great sense of relief pervaded the Club. Seely had blundered, but had frankly taken upon himself all responsi- bility, and had resigned. The Cabinet were for some time in ignorance of, the blunder, the awkward corner had been rounded, and the situation saved, but with some loss of credit. And then we talked it all over while there 1 nnidwoolfaedllagtomef. With Colonel Seely there was a ensyt mpatily expressed. of which We had heard too m was a disposition to forgive; there was a fre- quent expression of hop 4 that this would be the last of the individual blunders and "frank acoako He is a general favourite in Warrington, as well as London, and on the admission of all parties a most efficient War Chief. 1311 t such blunders ought not to occur, and it is difficult to under- ssetarvnadntthoef the State in regard to a principle the application mind of an important application of which is of such fundamental importance. The Repudiated Document. The following were the critical conditions which Colonel Seely, on his own initiative, added to the draft 'approved by the Cabinet the civil power in His majesty's Government must retain their right to use all the forces of the Crown to maintain law :aiole‘lixetecolusioPine°Ort'ef.its duty. itanini ed,lßo. lordinary. eitil y have no intention whatever of taking icaolf t°ll:e Home Rule Bill." or right t o Policy o r prin- ciplesuslthti , It is possible that Colonel Seely, when he used polit the term " political opposition," had in his mind something of a vantage of of to the character of public demonstrations and the like, and he considered the officers would understand that in the event of Ulster's unlawful force, the Volunteers, using force to resist law, "His Majesty's Government," as stated ill the earlier paragraph, "should retain their right to maintain law and order," and expect obedience from the soldiers. But it matters little what exactly was in Colonel Seely's mind. The important thing in any document is, not BO much what is in the writer's mind, but what the words are likely to convey to the persons to whom it is written. Taking the two paragraphs together, and the circumstances out of which they arose, General Gough had good ground for thinking that he and his companions were allowed to be the judges under what circumstances they were free to refuse to co-operate if called upon to crush any active resistance which the 'Ulster forces took in connection with the Home Rule Bill. General Gough and his associates (whatever their pre- vious insubordination) have some claim to sym- pathy. They are now in a false position, through no fault of their own. They have a document which, under certain circumstances, relieves them from active service, and doing the duty they have ,sworn to perform; they know at the same time that this document has, in its vital part, been repudiated by the Cabinet.

div.head: LOCAL INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE LOCAL INFIRMARY.
Councillor Roberts Defends the Insurance

div.head: Act.
div.p: Act.
CRITICS CRITICISED.

' Many sweeping statements have been madb to the effect that the Insurance Act has affected the contributions to the Infirmary, but at the annual meeting of this worthy institution, held yesterday in the new ward, Councillor Roberts criticised insinuations of this character. Sit Gilbert Greehall presided.

The CHAIRMAN said they helped forward the work of the Infirmary in order that those whose circumstances rendered it difficult and almost impossible to have proper medical and surgical aid, apart from such an institution, should have proper treatment. (Applause.)

days and Christmas Day—with only four excep- tions. _ Recovery and Death-rate.—The recover; rate was 80 per cent, on all admissions, and the per- centage of deaths was 4.1. When it is consid- ered that of the 58. deaths, 19 occurred within 24 hours of admission, and that the majority of fliese cases were, at the time of arrival at the Infirmary, in a hopeless state, the death-rate will be accepted as a low one. Burns and Stalds.—A large number of burns and scalds (45) were admitted, and most of these were of a very serious nature. No less than 10 had a fatal termination; five within 24 hours of admission. Motor Accidents.—Accidents due to motor cars and other mechanically propelled vehicles were answerable for 10 admissions.

' Ant h rax.—Three cases of anthrax were treated, two of which were cured. Suspected cases of anthrax have been detained until a microscopic examination has been made. When this has not been entirely satisfactory, a• bac- teriological culture has been established and thereby a positive conclusion has been arrived at. AI cases of anthrax have with the least' possible delay been surgically treated, and have had Sclavo's serum administered. It is most desirable that employers of labour should send employes exhibiting a condition which may arise from anthrax infection to the Infirmary, if not for treatment, at least for ex- amination and observation, with the least pos- sible delay.

The Infirmary authorities fully recognise that Warrington is exceptionally liable to furnish cases of this dangerous condition, and conse- quently it is always equipped for dealing with it, and it is nnxious to secure the co-operation of those firms whose workmen are liable to be afflicted with this grave condition. Zymotic Diseases.—Beyond an outbreak of scarlet fever and one of measles—both of which occurred in the children's ward—the Infirmary has fortunately been free from zymotic diseases. X-Ray Installation.—The X-Ray installation —provided by the generosity of The Million Penny Fund Committee—has proved a valuable addition to the armamentarium of the Infirm- ary. During the past year 282 radiograms have been taken, all of which have been of the greatest assistance in arriving at diagnostic accuracy. It is now a routine practice for fractures and suspected ones to be submitted to the X-Rays. The radiograms are carefully preserved, indexed and filed, and are thus available for future reference, should this be required. Pathological Department.—ln the Patho- logical Department valuable microscopic and bacteriological examinations have been made, and the treatment of certain conditions has been aided by the manufacture of autogenie vaccines.

Markel, were ..t266 .58. 2d., an increase of £lOB 17s. 2d. Congregational collections were £233 is. lid., a decrease of 1:13 18s. 2d. The Board thanked the clergy, ministers and friends of the various denominations for their help, and trusted that their efforts in the ensuing year would meet with increased success.

-tl4B 11 0 • Although there was a decrease in the amount received, the Board expressed their most grate- ful thanks to the Working Men's Infirmary Committee for the splendid energy displayed in the face of many difficulties, and sincerely trusted that in the future an, even greater measure of success might crown their efforts.

div.head: Legacies Increase Endowment Fund.
div.p: Legacies Increase Endowment Fund.

The Endowment Fund was increased by the receipt of the following legacies The late Mr. Isaac Gilman, £1,019 12s. 2d.; the late Miss Emily Jane Massy, ..t100; and the late Mr. Edward Beck, four shares in his resi- duary esti.te. On account of this £1,280 was re- ceived in cash, and £1,694 108., representing the market value of certain stocks and shares, transferred to the institution. The Board de- cided to place the stocks and shares to a special account, to be called the "Edward Beck" Trust. (Note.—The balance ha S since been paid in cash, £384 10s., making the total value of the legacy, X 3,359.). The following qualified as life governors:— Mrs. Mary Florence Sainsbury, in respect of the legacy bequeathed by the late Miss Emily Jane Massy; and Mr. Roger Beck, as executor of the late Mr i Edward Beck. The Board recorded, with deep regret, their sense of the great loss the institution sustained by the death of the following: Miss Emily Jane Massy, a life governor; Dr. Edward Austin Fox, an honorary surgeon of the institution since the 28th April, 1876, and a life governor; and Mr. William Richardson, a life governor. The "Samaritan Fund" continued to be of the greatest assistance to poor patients who re- quired surgical appliances. The Board expressed their cordial apprecia- tion of the services rendered by the honorary auditor, the honorary surgeons, the honorary pathologist, and the honorary dental surgeon. The Board expressed their appreciation of the efficient manner in which the staff performed their respective services. The annual Christmas treat to the iiatients and staff was again provided without expense to the hospital funds, and a substantial sum was handed over to various special accounts.

Help Needed to Meet Increasing Deficit. The Board view with concern, concludes the report, which is signed by Mr. James Henry Smethurst, as chairman of the Board, the hict that the debit balance increased considerably during the year, and sincerely trust that the claims for greater financial support of this charity will be increasingly recognised as the services rendered become more widely known. The Board would welcome additional special efforts during 1914 to clear off the deficiency. The constant endeavour of the Board has been to increase the efficiency of the institution in every detail, and the most careful attention has been given to the expenditure. The Board sincerely hope that in every works in the district a systematic collection may be ' arranged, and earnestly appeal to all employers and employes to co-operate to bring about this ' most desirable result.

div.head: WORK OF DOCTORS HEAVY; RATE OF RECOVERY HIGH. Warrington's Liability to Anthrax.
div.p: WORK OF DOCTORS HEAVY; RATE OF RECOVERY HIGH. Warrington's Liability to Anthrax.

The report of the Senior House Surgeon (Dr. C. D. Law) for 1913 gave the following inter- esting details:— Operations.—The number of operations per- formed during the year 1913 was 930, being 347 in excess of those for 1912. A large proportion of the operations were of a major nature. During the year the operating theatre was in use every day—excluding Sun-

div.head: EXEMPTION FROM RATES.
div.p: EXEMPTION FROM RATES.

Moving the adoption of the report, Mr. J. H. SMETHURST said the expenditure included £B4 16s. for rates. Surely one might expect that with places of worship free from rates that an institution like that ought to be exempted. (Hear, hear.) They had also paid considerable sums for gas, and now that it was used mainly for sterilising they asked the Gas Committee to put them on the same footing as manufacturers, for they used it in a sense for the manufacture of the necessary things for sterilising. The GaS Committee said they had no precedent. No; they had no precedent from any other hospital that had been in the town for 103 years. In that small matter the committee might help them. (Hear, hear.) Those who said "Put the Institution on the rates" did not know what they were talking about. Going on as they were with an expen- diture of £5,000 or £6,000, it would mean an addition of threepence or fourpence in the on the rates.
Consumption Treatment.

After referring to the effect of the Insurance Act on the finances of the Institution, he said that if they had been in the same position as the Sanatorium, and gone to the local Health Authority and told them they treated all sorts of cases of tuberculosis, they would have re- ceived about .263. The Insurance Act did not provide for such treatment as was given in the Infirmary, and during the past year, according to a report prepared by Dr. Fox, insured patients had occupied 19 of the beds the whole of the year, and had cost .21.306 12s. 11d. They ought to be able to go to the Government and say they should be recompensed. They did not ask for a profit on the transaction, but that the expenses should be paid. (Hear, hear.) Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH seconded, and the report was adopted.

div.head: OFFICERS RE-ELECTED.
div.p: OFFICERS RE-ELECTED.

On the proposition of Alderman SMETHURST, seconded by Mr. HESKETII, the officials were re- elected, and Mr. A. C. Binks was placed on the Board of Management in place of Mr. W. Wat- son. Mr. E. J. ITAts proposed, and the Rev. H. OGDEN seconded, a comprehensive vote of thanks to the officers and the various committees, which was accorded unanimously. Mr. JACKSON HOLMES, Dr. Fox, and Mr. A. J. JOLLEY replied.
thanks 1
MR. RYLANDS' VIEWS.

Mr. P. RYLANDS moved a vote of thanks to the Working Men's Committee, as he said, for the work they had done under difficult circum- stances. Unfortunately, they had had a set- back in the ordinary revenue owing to the National Insurance Act. The result was satis- factory, considering that they had to contribute so heavily under the Act.' It was a serious matter when there was a deficiency in the work- ing of the institution of £7OO, and he asked the Working Men's Committee to render further service by bringing that pressure to bear, they could so well do, in the proper quarter, to see the Infirmary got an adequate remuneration for the public service it did to persons who were insured under the Act. Mr. J. A. RANSOM; seconded, and said he hoped the committee would not be discouraged. With the benefits under the Act the men would have more ready cash and probably they would raise £1,500 soon. (Laughter and applause.)

DIFFICULTY OF PERSUADING FIRMS. Alderman BiniToN, in reply, said that in some firms they could not prevail on the principals to collect subscriptions. He hoped that when the depression in trade had passed away, their sub- scriptions would be better. (Applause.) The Rev. W. BRACECAMP moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman. They had heard, he said, that they were losing money through the Insurance Act, and so they should appeal to the generous public to make up the deficiency.

div.head: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S VIEWS.
div.p: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S VIEWS.

Councillor ROBERTS, in seconding, said he was sorry that Mr. Rylands, with that pessimism somewhitt characteristic of him, had referred in unnecessarily depressing terms to the defl. ciency, which he attributed to the National In- surance Act. He (the speaker) did not agree with what Mr. Rylands had said. Too much was being made of the Insurance Act in regard to such matters. As a somewhat older man than Mr. Rylands, he would like to say that it did not assist them in their object to get what they could from working men in order that the wheels of the institution might be well oiled, and run as smoothly as possible. He did not think the 0t:1,306 12s. 11d, men- tioned in Dr. Fox's report was fairly charge- able against the Insurance Act, because a cer- tain number of people happened to be insured. That class of people were catered for in that in- stitution before the Insurance Act was thought of, and the same cases were dealt with in the same way as they were now. The Insurance Committee funds could not be used for the benefit of that institution. Until the institution was recognised under a certain section of the Act the Insurance Committee had no power to make any contribution to the In- firmary. Once they were recognised under the clause they would be able to make a charge on patients, just as. a Charge was made by the Corporation for the treatment of certain patients now. (Hear, hear.)
STRIKE NEGOTIKI lONS.
The Employers and Employes to Hold a Conference.

div.head: MEETING EXPECTED NEXT WEEK.
div.p: MEETING EXPECTED NEXT WEEK.

A fresh development in connertion with the strike at Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co.'s works was reported yesterday, when it was announced that a meeting was *to be held between the employers and the employes. - During this week Mr. Adam Bknnett (the sec- retary of the joint unions involved) wrote to the firm, asking if they were prepared to meet a deputation of the ;nen. . _

He informed "The Examiner" representative yesterday that the firm agreed to meet a deputa- tion and the date was being arranged. The men suggested Monday as the date of the conference if convenient to the employers, and, if not, any other day would suit the men's representatives. Whether the proposed conference leads to a settlement of the dispute remains to be seen, but the tone was more hopeful than it has yet been during the strike. At a mass meeting of the men on Sunday, Mr. Hutchinson said that only a miracle would get the men back without recognition. It was of vital importance to them that their unions should be recognised. Even if their unions were smashed, other more active and more powerful unions would arise in the works. Their fight was arousing much interest throughout the country, and he was continually receiving letters offering financial stpport.
Another meeting is to he 'held to-morrow.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
"LOVE AND A THRONE" AT ROYAL COURT.

This is a play teeming with romantic interest The situations are well worked out and excel- lently presented. Humour abundantly relieves the little tragedy which creeps into the play. Mr. Charles Whitlock makes an admirable King, and Miss Isla Garnet-Vayne makes a charming Helen. The rest of the company play their parts excellently. "Princess Caprice" comes next week, and a notice about this charming attraction will be found on another page.
EFFECTIVE VARIETY AT HIPPODROME.

Another first-class programme is presented at the Hippodrome this week. The Griffiths Bros. keep the company in the merriest moods. The Rangers give a quick, clever turn. Rudyer Bann is an amazing violinist, and Miss Edna Payne is an excellent mimic. , The other turns are excellent, and all combine to make a per- formance that should not be missed. Next Week's Programme.

„ Billy Williams, the "man in velvet,” is due next week and should prove a huge draw. He is a distinctive character. Agustin and Hartley present a whirlwind barrel jumping turn that is marvellous. Other good turns include: Owen and Wills, comedians; Myrtle Grove, come- dienne; The Days, second sight exponents; The Stellios, with their canine wonders; the Gerlandos, novel gymnasts; and Nellie Lewis, chorus singer.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY CONCERT. "The Hymn of Praise!'
div.p: THE MUSICAL SOCIETY CONCERT. "The Hymn of Praise!'

At the Warrington Musical Society's conclud- ing concert of the season on Wednesday there was a fairly good audience, by whom Mendels- sohn's "Hymn of Praise" was listened to with I manifest interest and pleasure. The society's vocal members sang, with appropriate zest and due restraint, those splendid choral portions of the work that have so greatly endeared it to those who know this masterpiece—and their name must be legion. Having regard to the society's serious handicap in working with a chorus very much out of balance in the various sections of the voices, we do not recall that members ever proved themselves more amenable to Mr. Crossle3r's baton, or ever scored so many good points in ensemble singing, as they did on this occasion. Amongst all that was thus good, it was noticeable that the members, one and all, were bent on "going for" (to use a strong if inelegant expression) " The night is departing," in which they worked up a fine climax after coming through the troubled waters of the middle portion in excellent style. Of the way in which they subordinated themselves in realising some delicate nuances, instances may be cited in "Praise thou the Lord, 0 my spirit," and "I waited for the Lord." Commendable taste and restraint were also shown in the softer choruses such as "lie counteth all your sor- mess." The duet in "1 waited for the Lord" was sung by Miss Elsie Wilkinson (a member of the chorus) and Miss May Huxley, the prin- cipal lady vocalist, and very sweetly and effec- tively their voices blended in a rendering of this number characterised by a strong devo- tional appeal. Miss Huxley and Mr. John Adams showed themselves in every way capable in the solos. The latter invested the trying recitative "We called through the darkness" with so intense a pathos as to demand for its artistic continuation an equally dramatic ren- dering of the telling little passage for the prin- cipal soprano, "The night is departing." This Miss lluxley vocalised in quite an ideal way. and fittingly introduced the big chorus to which reference has already been made. The orches- tral playing, while good in the cantata portion of the "Hymn of praise," was not so satisfac- tory in the symphony, ialhe long allegro move- ment of which, we are inclined to think, the marked metronome speed was considerably ex- ceeded, with disastrous consequences in the string section. The two succeeding and more leisurely movements were, on the other hand, quite gracefully and thoughtfully played by all concerned, the increasingly devout feeling en- gendered by the Adagio religioso arousing just that frame of mind which is so essential a pre- paration for the vocal part of the work. The overture to "Rienzi" in the second part of the programme unfortunately again showed the orchestra's conspicuous weakness. The opening of the overture was admirably , per- formed, but, as the tempo increased, the rag- gedness of the florid passages in the string l was seen to militate greatly against the success of the overture regarded as a whole. The strength of an amateur orchestra being that of its weak- est section, would it not be prudent to temper the difficulties of executants in the choice of pieces? Of the part-song, "Autumn Moon," by Dr. Lyon, it is not easy to form a sound opinion at a single hearing. While it had obviously been none too perfectly prepared in rehearsal it t was clear that the placid and tranquil flow of , its numerous' parts, and the soothing quality of s its harmonies would grow upon one on closer acquaintance and with the fuller realisation 'of . its possibilities in performance. The song was well received by the audience, who heartily acclaimed it. div.head: TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.
div.p: TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

The Parish Meeting was quite orderly. It was e, change from the last one: The stormy petrols were absent, And the meeting only lasted a short time. There was no burning question raised. The only breeze arose over the Suggestion to build workers' cottages. It did not last very long. The police have been making history again With several clever and effective captures. They did not believe the "fortunes" Told to them by a certain lady. The footballers were in a fine fix. They went to Weston without their Outfit and could not play the match.
Parish Council.—A meeting of the Parish Council was held on Thursday night. Council- lor Whitley- presided and the business was formal, and consisted chiefly of passing accounts.

A Visitor's Adventure.—At the Stockton Heath Police Court on Tuesday a somewhat strange story was told in a charge brought against Walter Harris, who said he had come from Leeds. It was alleged that he frequented London-road for 'an unlawful purpose.—lnspec- tor Breese said in response to a telephonic mes- sage lie went to London Bridge and found Harris detained by a Mr. Davies, who said Harris had been " round his house on the previous day." The Inspector further stated that Harris had offered .1:1 to a male servant at Mr. Davies' house if the servant would give him information respecting Mr. Davies. Prisoner admitted this, but said it was only "in fun." Asked to give his address, he said it was the Gothic Art School, Leeds, but afterwards admitted he wasp "on his own." He said he called at the house with the intention of taking orders for photo- graph frames. He said he was going to open a studio in Warrington.—A remand for eight days was granted.

div.head: POLICEMAN'S "GOOD LUCK." Amusing Evidence in a Fortune Telling Case.
div.p: POLICEMAN'S "GOOD LUCK." Amusing Evidence in a Fortune Telling Case.
LOCAL WOMAN FINED £2O.

There was amusing evidence in a fortune telling case which came before Councillor 11. Roberts and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes at the Stockton Meth Police Court. Elizabeth Ger- trude Kilner, married, of 16, London-road, was charged with pretending to tell the fortunes, by reading the hands, of Jane Wilding and Jane Richardscin and others. The two women named are the wives of policemen. Superintendent Owen stated that for some time it had been observed by the police that a number of young girls visited prisoner's house, chiefly on Saturday and S.unday nights. Pri- soner was visited by Mrs. Wilding and Mrs. Richardson. She pretended to tell their for- tunes, and it would be seen that the pretence and deceit of prisoner was clear. She charged the women is. each. On the 18th inst. Sergeant Davies and P.C. Oldham, of Runcorn, visited the house, and Kilner told them their fortunes for is. each. In one or two cases prisoner asked clients particu- lars about themselves, and enlarged upon them. If it was decided to convict he asked for such a penalty as would deter prisoner from ,again carrying on such a pernicious practice. He could not help considering the demoralising and injurious effect such work would have on girls and women.

div.head: "A TREACHEROUS MAN."
div.p: "A TREACHEROUS MAN."

Mr. Wilding, wife of Sergeant Wilding, of Runcorn, said, in answer to a question by Kil- ner, she stated that she was separated from her husband at present Prisoner said her husband was a treacherous man, and that he would come back to her, but she would not recommend wit- ness to live with him again. ' She also said her husband was a dock labourer. _ _
Prisoner interjected the remark that she only stated that the prophecies were probable.
SHOULD GO ABROAD.
Mrs. Richardson Richardson stated that prisoner said she would do well if she went abroad to any place that commenced with "A." She would succeed in a business where there was an off-licence..

At the age of 33 three men would come into her life, and one would have a great deal of influence over her. She also told witness she ' had been married two years. In reply to Superintendent Owen, Mrs. Richardson added that she had been married five months.

div.head: GOOD LUCK FOR THE SERGEANT.
div.p: GOOD LUCK FOR THE SERGEANT.

Sergeant Davies stated that he visited Miner's house with Constable Oldham and they found the woman smoking a cigarette. She told the sergeant he was employed by the Government, I and advised him to remain under the Crown. He would get married before he was 25; would travel, and find a nice-looking girl in a country lane. He would be married three times, and have five children. He would also receive a pension before he was 25. Prisoner, looking at his left hand, told him he was an engine driver. He had oiled his hands previously to make them look large and like a mechanic's. (Laughter.) He was also said to be a great elocutionist and a good clairvoyant. (laughter.) She also told him he was "in a secret sect."
My own
Kilner : I was rather afraid of you. instinct told me to be careful. Witness: You did not appear afraid. Kilner: I was deceived. You were so affable and looked such a gentleman.

BORN UNDER JUPITER. P.C. Oldham's evidence stated that Kilner told him he was born under the planets Jupiter and Venus. There was honour for him under the Crown, and he would take a long voyage. He might be successful as a doctor, a minister, or in the commercial world, and he was a great explorer. (Laughter.) He would he married three times and would have five children, lie, would die a natural • death—from liver or kidney complaint. He would receive a pension at 25. While he was there two ladies were admitted to the kitchen. Answering Superintendent Owen, witness said he had not recently been in danger of his life. (Laughter.) Inspector Breese said when he told prisoner he had a warrant for her arrest for pretending to. tell fortunes, she said "Yes, that is my living. I have done it for bread."

A TOTAL FINE OF La Accused made a statement on her own behalf and denied that she "read" persons' hands on the Sunday. She was in poor health and did not want to be sent to prison. If the Bench would dismiss the case she would report herself to the sergeant every day and give up fortune telling. Superintendent Owen. said Blaney had been convieted three times of fortune telling, having been before the Bench at Warrington. Her last conviction was at Manchester in 1912, when she was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour. A fine of £lO in each case, with the alternativg of two months' imprisonment, was imposed.

div.head: SWING BRIDGE TRAGEDY. A Verdict of "Found Drowned"
div.p: SWING BRIDGE TRAGEDY. A Verdict of "Found Drowned"

Returned. tin F. A. Jones held an inquest at Warrington on Wednesday on James Douglas Broughton, who lived with his uncle, Thomas Lister, at 24, Market-street, Warrington, and who was em- ployed as a bridgeman on the Stockton Heath Swing Bridge. Mr. F. Kershaw (Manchester) appeared for the Canal Company. In answer to the Coroner, Lister said his nephew's sight was good, and there was nothing ailing the lad.

BRIDGEMASTER'S STORY. Daniel Lennon, bridgemaster at Stockton Heath, 5, Greenbank-street, Warrington, said the lad came on duty at 5.30 on Monday night. At 2.15 on Tuesday morning the lad closed the read gates on the Stockton Heath side and went on to the bridge, which was being opened to allow of the passage of a vessel. Broughton walked along the bridge and passed him (Lennon) in the centre, and made some remark. He went to the other end, and when the bridge was fully opened heard a splash and missed the lad. He called assistance and obtained a life- buoy, which he threw to Broughton, who was struggling in the water. The youth touched it several times, but appeared only semi-conscious. Witness went for a boathook, and when he re- turned Broughton had disappeared. The body was recovered at 6.20 a.m. The depth of the water at the spot is 28 feet and the drop from the bridge 30 feet. It was a clear morning and he could see from end to end of the bridge. The lad could not have stumbled over anything.. The Coroner: How do you think he got in the water? •

MATTER FOR CONJECTURE. Witness: Well, it is only a matter for conjec- ture. When the lad passed me he had his hand up as if he had a cigarette in it. He went, I think to a sheltered part of the bridge, struck a match, and was so dazzled by the light that he misjudged the distance and fell in the water. Mr. Kershaw: Have there been any accidents like this before?—Not that I know of. In answer to a question by the Coroner, wit- ness said .it was ordinarily sae on the bridge without a light. The Coroner: Is there anything You can sug- gest to prevent a similar accident?—No!

div.head: 'LIGHTING OF THE BRIDGE. – _
div.p: 'LIGHTING OF THE BRIDGE. - _

Mr. James Whitley (chair—in;ii...; the Parish Council) said there had been many discussions as to the inadequacy of the lighting about the bridge. There were two good lights on the Stockton Heath side, but only one on the War- rington side, and that was hidden by a standard. They suggeitted a hanging lamp in the middle of the bridge.
The Coroner:, Do you think such a lamp would have prevented the accident? _ _
Witness: There would have been more light. Mr. Kershaw:_ I aln told that if there were a
light on the bridge it--;Waid-.1;;;;ie those on the steamers and mislead them.

Mr. Whitley said the general public had com- plained about the poor lighting of the bridge. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned," there not being sufficient evidence to show how the lad got in the water. They were of the opinion that there was insufficient light, and referred that matter to the propel authorities. _ _
Mr. Kershaw expressed the sympathy of the company with the relatives.

div.head: SMART SERVANT GIRLS
div.p: SMART SERVANT GIRLS
What They Discovered at Grappenhall

Hall. _ _ How two seryant girls outwitted three would- be intrunrs at Grappenhall Hall was told at the Stockton Heath I'olice Court on Tuesday, when James Finn and Martin Watson, both of Warrington, but with no settled address, and John Thomas O'Kelly, Manchester, were charged with being on the enclosed premises of Mr, F. Aylmer Frost, at Grappenhall Hall, Grappen- hall, on March 16th. - -

How the incident arose was narrated by Super- intendent Owen. He said the men went to the side door of the Hall and knocked. Before thc knock could be answered one stepped into the lobby. Another stood immediately behind, and the third was on the step. One of the maids, hearing the door open, rushed to it. The first prisoner tried to push past her, but was pre- vented by another maid. Eventually the men were got out of the house by the girls, who then rang the alarm bell. Two male servants came, and afterwards fol- lowed prisoners until they were apprehended. The matter was a serious one, as the house stood in its own grounds, and the men were practically forcing their way into it. Sarah Lewis and Kate Guest, the servants, gave evidence. Edward Eastham, chauffeur, and Arthur Lea, Higlifield House, Thelwall, gave evidence as to following prisoners. Finn said he went to ask for work. He had been in gaol seven days for this. (Laughter.) Watson said he had had a "drop too much" drink, and did not know what he was doing. O'Kelly said he was hawking. Watson was committed for 14 days, O'KellY, who had 35 previous convictions against him, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment, and Finn, who had four previous convictions against him, to one month. Councillor H. Roberts (the chairman) compli- mented the servant girls on their smartness.

TEMPERANCE QUEEN. A Brilliant Crowning Ceremony at Band of Hope. The last entertainment of the 18th winter session of the Hill Cliff e and Stockton Heath Band of Hope took place in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Monday evening, when the mem- bers gave a splendid performance of the cantata " Crowning the Temperance Queen," Mrs. Dodds (president of the Warrington Band of Hope Union) presided, and appealed to the parents to encourage the children to carry out the principles taught in the Band of Hope. The children formed a pleasing spectacle as they took up their positions on 'the platform, after marching in procession down the school. Miss Florrie Sandford (retiring queen) was escorted by the heralds, guards of honour, maids of honour, train-bearers, and the chief attend- ants—Love, Peace, Industry and Thrift. She, was followed by the queen-elect, Miss Elsie Whitfield, with her attendants—Faith, Hope, Pleasure and Mercy. A song and speech was given by the first herald, George Walton, and this was followed by a song and speech by the second herald, Joe Judd. Then came an appeal from Sorrow, Want and Cruelty to enter the Court, but they were told by the Doorkeeper to come when they treasured self-denial, learned from experience. Love and Peace having removed the crown from the retiring queen and placed a wreath of bay on her head, Faith and Hope placed the crown on the new queen, who vowed throughout her life to maintain jt dignity. Allegiance to her Majesty was sworn by all. The characters were: Love, Lizzie Brook; Peace, Bessie Clarke; Hope, Sarah Gamble; Faith, Eva Mather; Pleasure, Hilda Adamson; Thrift, Hilda Taylor; Industry, Eva Philps; Mercy, Emily Rustage; Doorkeeper, Reggie train- bearers, Phyllis Moss, rounds; Captain of Guard, John Shaw; train- Elsie Moss, Dora Gerrard and Bessie Gerrard.

PLEASANT ENTERTAINMENT. At interludes in the programme the action songs, "Little laundresses" and "I won't go to school any more," and a dialogue "Rival coun- sellors," were given by members of Bold-street Band of Hope. Miss Eva Tanner, contributed two songs, for which she was encored, and humorous songs were rendered by Mr. J. H. Bibby. The event of the evening proved to be the duet "I don't want to play in your yard," by Daisy and Rennie Summers.
Mr. G. A .Whitfield, who had charge of the musical arrangements, and acted as accom- panist, deserves credit for the success which attended the function.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
STOCKTON HEATH
continued.
THE PARISH MEETING. ' No Burning Questions and a Quiet Gathering.
HOUSES FOR WORKERS.
The half-yearly Parish Meeting was held in the Church Room on Thursday night. Coun- cillor J. Whitley kchairman of the Parish Council) presided over a comparatively small' meeting. _

On tile minutes of the last meeting coining up, Mr. Boyle asked what had been done in regard to public meetings in Victoria Square. *Mr. Bradshaw (the clerk) said he had received a letter from the Deputy-clerk to the County Council, in which it was stated that the police had nothing to do with granting or refusing permission for the holding of public meetings in Victoria Square. The place was not suited for public meetings, and if they were held it might mean that the police would have to interfere. •

div.head: RECREATION GROUND.
div.p: THE RECREATION GROUND.

egniaidn—stoa"rdt'hieh. iCahar letter e ;tpt.r.at-phaeajr-Jjatcal received recreation ground from Colonel Egerton War- byrton, the landowner, who died this week. His death would probably delay the matter. In regard to a playground for children, they had, approached Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., who stated that they could not give land in West-avenue or Victoria-road which had to be devoted to other purposes. They might. have a piece of land available at Lumb Brook, which they Might give on generous terms, once they knew the definite purposes .to which the land would be put. The subject then dropped. READING ROOM QUESTION. _

_ The Chairman said there was a committee appointed to go into the matter of a reading room, but only Mr. Charles Hallows turned up, and he plight have something to 'say about the. matter. As there was no quorum the committee meeting could not be held. Councillor Hallows: I was by myself and could not hold the meeting. That is all I have to say about it. WORKING-CLASS COTTAGES.

The Chairman reported that a committee was formed to go into the question of working men's dwellings, .and the matter was referred to the Parochial Committee, and they decided thatd owing to there not being any real inquiries t 6 the Council for working men's cottages, that the question be deferred for six months. Ni'. M. Boyle: May we have a word on that now? The Chairman: Yes. Mr. Boyle: I think Councillor Dukes brought :this matter forward and he has asked me to say he cannot be here to-night because he has gom. to Sheffield. You sar there have been no appli- cations. You would have plenty of applications if men would only come forward at all. From the men I work with I think you would have plenty of applications if you provided houses at a rent of 6s. 6d. per week, with a bath upstairs and not downstairs in the scullery. I live in a house that was ss. 6d., but there has been six— pence per week added on, and there is nothing extra for it. That has gone on all over the village. The idea seems to be that now we can- not get houses they put the money on, and you can either pay it or leave. 1 think that really. the Council should provide houses. In the early discussion I see in the paper that a coun- cillor came out with the remark that he was not going to be a supporter,. of any betterment of housing for the working people. I think that man odght not to be on the Council. A BREEZE._

_ Councillor Mclntyre: Name! Name! The Chairman: Was that expression used in the Council meeting? Mr. Boyle: It was in the paper. The Chairman: It was not said. Mr. Boyle : If that is the case I misunderstood it. I think there are a large number of pro- perty owners in the Council, and that might account for the matter being shelved for six months. I think you ought to go on with the matter. The Chairman : Do you mean to say the Parish Council is bound to create a supply of houses for people to come to live in the village? We have had no applications. Mr. Boyle: I Councillor Mclntyre: Such a remark as Mr. Boyle suggests was never made in the Council. , Mr. Boyle: I will try to get the report latei on. _ _

THE CHAIRMAN'S QUESTION. The Chairman: Where do these people work who require houses? Are they natives of the village? Mr. Royle : I don't know what you mean. Do you mean natives bred and born here? The Chairman: Have they been here a num- ber of years? Mr. Royle: They live in the town. The Chairman: They have been asking you for houses?

_ Mr. Royle : Not asking me. I was only saying-- The Chairman: Do you know this is a serious matter fOr the Council? In order to erect these houses they will have to take up money which will have to be paid for out of the rates, and wo shall have raised our rateable value in the village: I think the committee was unanimous in the feeling, not against houses being erected for bona-fide tenants or people likely to stay in the houses when they take them— _

BUILD FOR THEMSELVES. Mr. Royle: You mean to say You want Some- one else coming in and denianding houses. The Chairman: We have no objection to a man taking up a house if he gets the money and builds it himself. (Laughter.) Councillor Bottomley : Mr. Chairman— The Chairman : I, as overseer of this parish would object to taking up money and increasing our rates considerably for the sake of creating people to come in houses that we build. Councillor Bottomley : In the first instance this gentleman makes a statement that he has read in the paper a certain remark made at a par- ticular meeting of the Council, and he also made the remark that the particular gentleman is not fit to be on the Council. He cannot qualify that statement. lie says he will have a look at the paper again— The Chairman: Ile ought to withdraw. SHOULD WITHDRAW. Councillor Bottomley : I think it would be well for that statement to be withdrawn. I think this Council as a public body should not take into consideration the qaestion of house building until such time as they are satisfied there is an absolute dearth of houses and a necessity for them, and they have no right, until that time comes, to interfere with private enterprise and build houses. When it comes to a question of overcrowding and houses are badly needed, then is the time for the Council to deal with the question. Until that time comes it is not the duty of the Council to interfere with private enterprise. (Applause.) _

HOUSES REQUIRED. Councillor 11cDermid : In connection with this matter I think the Parochial Committee It was discussed and practically decided t UP. re was a necessity for houses, and for some more to be made. There was a sub- committee appointed, and it was referred to them to forward plans and approximate cost of houses such as were thought to be necessary in the village. That committee and the Surveyor went to considerable trouble and expense in getting out plans, &c., of the houses which they thought would be suitable for the demand. They brought their report to the Parochial Commit- present when the discus- sion mnte:otkingilaacned, I was a member of that sub- committee, with regard to the different class of houses suggested to be built, and there seemed to be a pretty unanimous opinion that as things were at the present time, whatever we might think about private and public enterprise, not only in Stockton Heath, but throughout the country, there was a considerable dearth of houses for working classes. Private enterprise seems to be stifled, and that was one of the reasons which actuated thE Parochial Committee to take up the matter. It was decided that the committee had supplied no reason, nor had it shown there was a demand for these houses. The objection I had to that was that it was not included in the powers of reference of the committee that they, should ascertain whether there was a demand. That had been decided previously. They had to bring suggestions as to the approximate cost, and that was only a convenient method of shelving the question—to put it off for six months. As a public body we are in an infinitely better position to borrow money at a better rate than private in- dividuals, and we ought to have gone further
