div.head: MARCH 28, 1914.
div.p: LAYMM.
The Overseers.—At the meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council on Thursday night, Messrs. Groves and S. Gould were re-elected overseers.

Minister's Illness.—The Rev. J. A. Penalig- gon, who has been suffering from nervous col- lapse and concussiOn as the result of a serious fall last week, is progressing as favourably as can be expected.

School Holidays.—At the meeting of the Dis- trict Council on Thursday, Mr. J. H.. Holt sug- gested to the Council's representltives that they should endeavour to alter the EITAMMar School holidays from August to July. This was being done up and down the country. Such a change would be beneficial, for the students would then have the advantage of longer days.—Mr. Smith: Quite an excellent suggestion.—The matter was left to the Head Master to decide.

Sewerage Scheme.—The report of the Sewerage Committee, which was adopted at the Ly-mm District Council meeting on Thursday, con- tained the following: Mr. Beckett attended and reported on a new scheme for sewering Lym.ro and Barr's Bank, and also produced plans and estimates. It was carried unanimously that the resolution passed with regard to the above at tho meeting of the Council, held on 19th Febru- ary last, be recommended to the Couhcil to be rescinded. - It was further decided that as a recommendation to the Council, the scheme, plans and estimates be approved. and that the Clerk be instructed to apply to the Local Gov- ernment Board for sanction to the scheme and to the borrowing of £3OO.

Council Election.—Since Tuesday, the last day fixed for withdrawal from the Urban District Council elections, there have been many ex- pressions of regret that Mr. David Daniels, one of the candidates for the Booth's Hill Ward, has, after long and careful consideration, de- cided to retire. Mr. Charles Edward Cowper, the other candidate, is therefore elected unop- posed. We may say that Mr. Daniels had pre- viously been requested to stand for Lymm Ward, but declined. In the meantime the contest be- tween Mr. Septimus Critchley and Mr. James Jolley, the rival candidates for the Bentley Ward, is proceeding merrily. A meeting in support of Mr. Jolley's candidature was held in the Farmer's Arms tearoom, Rush Green, on Wednesday night.

Late Councillor Gould.—The meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council was held on Thursday evening, when Mr. S, Davies presided. —The Chairman said that since their last meet- ing one of their members was no more. They little thought at the last meeting of the Coun- cil that that same evening Mr. Gould was going to meet such a sad death. Mr. Gould was not w a great a very frequent speaker in the Council,_ but when he did it was to the point. It as loss not only to the Council, but to the district in general.—The following resolution was carried in silence: "That this Council desires to ex- press its regret at the tragip death of the late Mr. William Gould, and its sympathy with Mrs. Gould and family in their bereavement, and to record its appreciation of his services as a mem- ber of the Council."

Sewage Farm.—At the meeting of the Lymm District Council on Thursday, Mr. T. H. War- burton asked if the Council had taken over from the contractor the new sewage farm and all the responsibility, including the machinery.—The ChairnAan : Our clerk of works has not passed it. —Mr. Warburton: Is the thing running satis- factorily? It is necessary it should be in good order before we take it over.—Mr. Mort (sur- veyor): It does not make very much difference : for the time being if the pump is working or not, for we will be able to go on without much difference for a month, but we will get the tanks very full if the pump doesn't work soon. Mr. Mort added that they would certainly only take it over if it was in perfect condition.—Mr. T. Dixon asked if they would only take over the machinery in good order ?—The Chairman: That I is so.--The matter then dropped.

Matinee Concert.—The Matinee Concert which took place in the Higher-lane Baptist School- room on Saturday was something of an innova- tion as far as Lymm is concerned, and Miss Mary Brundrett, the organiser, is to be con- gratulated on both the splendid audience at- tracted and the capital programme provided, and it is hoped the sustentation fund, in whose aid the concert was held, benefited substantially. The programme was opened with a choice ren- dering of Stainer's duet, "Love divine," by Miss Mary Brundrett and Mr. Charles Dawson. Miss M. Brundrett appeared to be in excellent form, her rich contralto voice being heard to advantage in the above duet, her solo, "Sum- mer rain," and in the duets with Madame Wil- son, "Twin stars;" and as an encore, "Night of stars." Madame Wilson's cultivated soprano singing is popular with Lymm audiences, and her songs '"The enchanted forest," "The reason," together with her encore, "A birth- day (Cowen), were given with good effect. The other vocalist, Mr. Charles Dawson, is a good bass, and his interpretations :of " The awakening," " Shipmates o' and " Song of sleep," were very acceptable, and his treat- ment of "The little Irish. girl" made ample amends for his somewhat inadequate rendering of "Young Tom o' Devon." Mr. Fred Randall's violin solos, Gavotte with variations (Rameau), and "Le Cygne " (Saint-Saens), were played with taste and skill. Miss Edith lirmson was an elocutionist of undoubted merit, and was deservedly, well applauded for the recitation, " The lady of Provence," and at a later period the humorous selection about the old maid, an encore being requested and given. Pianoforte accompaniments were artistically provided by Mrs. Slee and Mr. Hurbert Iddon, the latter contributing a fine performance of Movements ll and 111. of Beethoven's "Moonlight sonata." During the interval the Pastor, the Rev. E. E. Lovell, explained the object of the sustentation fund, namely, that of assisting the poorer Baptist Churches. He said that the fur- ther sum of £20,000 was required before the end of April, and efforts were being made to raise it by means of the manse boxes, which .had‘ not yet been opened, concerts, several bazaars, and a large meeting to be held in the Albert Hall.

div.head: PARISH MEETlNG—continued.
div.p: THE PARISH MEETlNG—continued.

in the matter. I don't wish to cast any reflec- tion, but our Chairman has said we were prac- tically unanimons in the opinion expressed. I dissented very strongly with the opinion expressed. We ough't to have ascertained what could be done in regard to meeting the demand. I know a young man who was on the point of getting married, but although he hunted the village, he could not find a suitable habitation. It is a matter which ought to be decided by.the ratepayers themselves. The Chairman said he had gOne through the district and found 19 empty houses, some of which had been weeks vacant. Mr. Farnhill : What is the class of the houses vacant? The Chairman: From 4s: 9d. a week upwards.

STREET WORKS. The Chairman reported that the re-making of streets was progressing satisfactorily and the work would soon be completed. The village was nqw well lighted. (Hear, hear.) He thought some credit was due to the Council in regard to that. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. Taylor asked if anything had been done in regard to the tip near Grappenhall-road. Councillor Pearson (chairman of the Sanitary Committee) explained that the Council were considering the adoption of a system of water- carriage in place of the present system of col- lecting the sewage. There was also under consideration the question of providing a destructor. The Council would have to borrow money, and the Clerk was endeavouring to jet a loan spread over a longer period than was usually allowed. The cost of introducing the water-carriage system would be about £7 pee house.

The Chairman: And there are 1,076 houses in the village. Councillor McDermid : The re-arrangement of. the sewers would also be an additional expense. Councillor A. Bottomley said something would have to be done, and the Council were giving careful consideration to the matter.

The Chairman said the question was whether it would be cheaper with a destructor. Mr. Moss asked if they could not get Warring- ton to take over the collection of the refuse. Councillor McDermicl We don't want them. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.
div.p: THE MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.
The Pretty Function to be Continued.
Lymm is wto have its May Queen. This was decided at a public meeting held in the Pepper- street Schools on Tuesday night. Mr. W. Jones presided over a rather disappointing attend- ance.

The Chairman thought the children of the district deserved a treat once a year, as they looked forward to it. The festival was good for Lymm, as it brought a number of people into the village, and thus helped the shopkeepers. (Hear, hear.) _

Mr. A. H. Hudson, the hon. treasurer, thought it would be a pity if the festival was given up, and an effort should be made to continue it. It was widely known and was highly praised by the Press. It was the only old festival they had, as the Rushbearing had practically gone. It had been ascertained that last year ~t 75 was spent in the village, and therefore some people must have benefited. • Mr. Hudson said several hotel keepers had promised doubled subscriptions. Councillor Gotobed thought that if the- fes- tival was to be Successful there must be re- trenchment. Then, given the help that was promised, he had little doubt it would be a suc- cess in the future.
The meeting decided unanimously to continue the festival; the committee agreed to seek addi- tional subscriptions, and a further report will be presented to another meeting.

div.head: TWO COUNCILLORS RETIRE.
div.p: TWO COUNCILLORS RETIRE.

Tributes to Messrs. AVelford and Smith. The last meeting of the Lymm District Coun- cil's year was held on Thursday, when a letter was received from Mr. G. L. Welford, in which he stated that through a chill he was unable to attend. "One," he wrote, "could not break an association of 19 years without feeling it very severely. During the last few years the work of the Council had grown to such an extent and the extra meetings had become so many, that they ,had often to be held during the daytime, and he had felt that the demand upon his time was rathey greater than he could spare, as he had less new at his disposal than before. "lie wished to express his deep sense of the loyalty shown to him and the confidence reposed in him during the 19 years by the electors of Booth's Hill Ward, and he hoped to express his thanks in person. What had impressed him about the Council had been the unselfish and disinterested services of the mohbers, none of whom had any axe to grind. He also thanked the Officials, especially the Clerk, and wished to support the vote of sympathy with Mrs. Gould."

VERY GREAT LOSS. Mr. R. li. Gotobed referred to the very great loss the Council would sustain by the resigna- tions of Mr. Welford and Mr. Smith. Mr. Wel- ford was the father of the Council, and they all knew the services he had rendered to Lymm. Those who were associated with him during thp negotiations for the purchase of the water works knew the care he devoted to the matter. In Mr. Smith they had always had a loyal col- league, and one who whenever he spoke did so with sound judgment. Messrs. W. G. Groves, T. Dixon and J. H. Holt also added their testimony. Mr. Smith, replying, said that during his twelve years' connection with the Council he had formed associations not easily broken. He felt that through Mr. We'ford's retirement,the Council had suffered a serious loss, for his legal and business knowledge was always at the dis- posal of the Council. Mr. Welford had always given of his best, and hjs hest was of the high- est quality. The speaker said that lie himself had always' tried to do his best. (Hear, hear.) A resolution was passed that the services of Messrs. Welford and Smith be placed on the minutes.

TIIAT GAS AGAIN. Alleged Obnoxious Odours. The gas of Lymm is again causing trouble, and although it has forsaken its previous danc- ing habits, it is alleged to now give off an offen- sive odour. Complaints to this effect were made at the meeting of the Lymm District Council, on Thursday, when Mr. Dixon inquired if there had been any alteration at the gas works during the previous two days, for there was an obnoxious smell aris- ing_ from the gas.

- Mr. Donaldson (the gas manager) stated that this was due to a change in purifying material, which he hoped to remedy. Mr. Dixon: Quite so. We understand that there must be a difference owing to a change of this kind, bu 4 we have had the same kind of smell during the last two or three years. The smell is very strong now, and much more objection- able. I would like to know if there is anything wrong with (he plant.
_ --Mr. W. G. Groves stated that he found a black substance when he removed the mantlE from his incandescent light. Mr. Dixon: I can only suggest that the plant is at fault. _ _
—Mr. Donaldson said there had been a slight defect in a valve for some years.
TURNED TO CANDLES.

_ Mr. Dixon said he would like to know if the valve could be put right. If it was wrong some- thing would have to be done to put it right. It was a very serious thing, and people seemed to think that they were spending money on other—
The Chairman: Fe have been spending at the gas works. Mr. Dixon: There will be no need to spend any there if the people turn to candles!

_ Dr. De Jong agreed that there was a very bad smell, and as the odour in some cases was apparent while the gas was not burning, it be- hoved them to look to their fittings. He was glad in one sense that the smell had been ob- served, because the escape of gas was dangerous to health. Mr. Donaldson said there would always be an escape into the mains of unpurified gas as long as they had the valve. The matter was left over to a future meet- ing.

div.head: LIBERAL WOMEN MAKE MERRY,
div.p: LIBERAL WOMEN MAKE MERRY,

Then They Discuss Votes for Vomen. The members of the Lymm and District Women's Liberal Association held their annual tea, meeting and concert in the Eagle-brow Schoolroom on Thursday evening. After the large number present had partaken of a choice repast, the business of the yearly meeting was transacted. Mrs. Dodds, of Penketh, presided. Miss Welford, the hon. secretary, gave her report, which was of a very encouraging nature, a considerable increase in the membership being announced.

The report of the treasurer, Miss Mclntyre, showed that the finances of the Association were in a flourishing condition, there being a good balance in hand. . Mrs. Barton, of Manchester, speaking on woman suffrage, pointed out the desirability of asking the Men's Association to select, if pos- sible, a candidate who was in favour of woman suffrage. She said that she thought the men ought to ask the assistancC of the Women's Association in the selection of their candidate.

The following resolution was proposed by Mrs. Lord, seconded by Miss Welford, and carried unanimously: "That the members of this Association, assembled in annual meeting, request the Par- liamentary Selection Committee of the Altrinc- ham Division Liberal Association to urge upon any candidate they may, select the desirability of supporting woman suffrage, and further, desires that Mrs. Dodds be added to the Parlia- mentary Selection Committee." The election of officers and committee resulted in the re-election of Mrs. Dodds (president), Miss Welford (hon. secretary), and Miss Mclntyre (hon. treasurer). The vice-presidents are: Mesdames Champ, Clark and Rawlins, and

Miss West; chairman, Mrs. Wyatt; committee, Mesdames C. I. Barnes, L. Broadey, D. Daniels, J. Edwards, R. 11. Gotobed, F. Guest, W. Mort, J. Radcliffe, and W. Seymour, and the Misses Barker, D. Barker and Rawlins.

Business completed, an enjoyable concert was provided. Miss Wright was the lady soloist, and her songs gave much pleasure. Mr. J. H. Brazendale contributed "The Young Royalist," "Four Jolly Sailormen," and "I'll sing thee songs of Araby," in his inimitable style. "Eleanore," " Melisande," and "Friend of -mine were the titles of the tenor solos of Mr. Harris. Miss Fanny Holt afforded pleasant variety with her violin solos.

Head Master's Farewell.—As most of our Lymm readers will be aware, Mr. C. H. H. S. Willson, the head master of the Lymm Gram- mar School, has been appointed to a similar position at Odiham Grammar School, Hamp- shire. In connection with his approaching re- moval a series of interesting events were enacted at the Grammar School on Saturday. In the afternoon the Old Boys played the Present Boys at football, whilst the Old Girls tried con- clusions with the P'resent• Girls in a hockey match. The old scholars were then entertained to tea by Mr. and Mrs. Willson. This was fol- lowed by a meeting of Old Boys, at which Mr. Charles Johnson, on behalf Of the Old Boys, presented Mr. Willson with a silver cigarette case and a smoker's cabinet. Mr. Willson suit- ably replied. The past and present scholars afterwards enjoyd a sing-song, the programme of which consisted of songs by Miss Catherine Parr, Mr. C. H. H. S. Willson, Mr. C. Johnson, Mr. A. Bruce, Mr. K. Hillier, Form 11., Forms IV.a and IV.b ; a musical monologue by Mr. V. Kimber ; pianoforte solos by the Misses Meakin, Whittle, and Master B. Atkinson, the Misses Whittle also contributing a pianoforte duet; violin solo by Miss F. Holt; a recitation by Miss W. de Jong; and selections on the hand bells by the Heatley B.P. Scouts. Mr. Willson, in a short speech, spoke of his happy relation- ship with the school.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

Members Present.-=Those present at the San- key Parish Council at the Commit Schools on Monday were Messrs. W. Furness (in the chair). W. Taylor, S. Fair, A. G. Pownall, R. Long, and the Clerk (Mr. J. Smith).
More Light—lt was decided_ at Monday night's

meeting of the Sankey Parish Council thai' the special sub-committee'S recommendations that more light be provided in the village should Im accepted. Mr. Po7nall stated they had agreed to erect one lamp at the corner of Liverpool- road and Hood-lane and one between the Garden Village houses and Mr. Smith's garden. It was also decided to move two other lamps to better positions in their present vicinity.

div.head: BRIDGE TROUBLES. Further Complaints at the Parish Council Meeting.
div.p: THE BRIDGE TROUBLES. Further Complaints at the Parish Council Meeting.

Bridge troubles seem rampant in the Warring- ton district, 'and Sankey is not immune—in fact, it has two! Complaints were made at the meeting of the Parish Council on Monday that the canal bridge scheme was proceeding too slowly, and a letter was read from the County Bridge Master in reply to one from the Clerk, which stated: " Our drawings have been finished a considerable time, and, in accordance with the agreement with the Railway Company, they have been submitted to them. Various modi- fications have been suggested, some of which have been withdrawn and some have been agreed to, and with regard to some, we were, until this week, awaiting 'further particulars I saw the Chief Engineer to the Railway Com- pany on Monday, and I think I have got all outstanding matters cleared up, and expect, at an early date, to receive notification of theft approval of the drawings." Mr. Pownall : We have receded. Some time ago they said tenders were to be invited, and now we have gone backward. It is certainly time that something was done. (Rear, hear.) The Chairman (Mr. Furness) intimated thai the District Council were moving in the matter.

div.head: FOOTPATII OF "SLUSH." More Strong Protests at the Parish
div.p: FOOTPATII OF "SLUSH." More Strong Protests at the Parish
Council.
The state of the footpath from Hood-lane to Buttermilk Bridge again• came in for strong comment at the meeting of the Sankey Parish Council on Monday.
Mr. Fair said that at the present time the footpath was a disgrace and that it was scanda- lous to see men, women and children "slushed" up to the ankles every morning. _ _

-The Chairman: The District Council has al- ready sent out notices to the two parties. If they don't comply the District Council will do the work and take action for the recovery of the expenses. Mr. Fair: This thing cannot go on for ever. The Clerk: As a Parish Council we cannot take a barrow or a brick over the land. Mr. Fair: Cannot we move the District Coun- cil?
The, Clerk: That is what we are doing.

The Chairman: We cannot move any quicker, for we are bound to keep to the law. I think the District Council have done all they possibly can to bring the matter to an issue. I quite agree it-is scandalous that the path should be in its present state.

div.head: • ROADS AND RATES. Lively Incidents at the Annual -Parish Meeting.
div.p: • ROADS AND RATES. Lively Incidents at the Annual -Parish Meeting.
itEITI4

TIIE BRIDGE 01110 N. i!ivmeleyetiinnegideoini t s moant dtahye. There Sankey awnenrueals"Per:rils Chief attention was bestowed upon the footpath from Buttermilk Bridge to Hood-lane, whilst the rates were mentioned. Mr. W. Furness presided and said that as no notice of any propositions had been received, it appeared that the parishioners were quite con- tent with the services of the Parish Council. They were not a very important body, and as a spending body they were less important, as they WOuld agree when he told them that during the year they had not had the privilege of spending ..E2, but if they were not an important spend- ing body, they, in their small way, did all they could to improve the district.

THE BRIDGE QUESTION. They had taken steps to improve Buttermilk' Bridge. The bridge gnestion was a very trying one, for men entered public life discussing it,and when out of public life they were doing the same, thing. That had been the case of Warrington Bridge, and they could not expect that bridges could be erected like an ordinary house. The District Council Surveyor had been in commu- nication with the Warrington Town Council, and they were agreeable, in conjunction with the District Council, to pay half the cost of in- creasing the width of Buttermilk Bridge. to eight feet. It was intended to drive a few piles down and to have creosote beams laid across, and that would improve the bridge. They had received a report from a small sub-committee, and had agreed to two additional lights in the parish, which would be welcomed.

Probably the largest butter record ever made in Australia by a young Jersey on her first calf must be placed to the credit of the Yanco dis- trict. During one. • lactation period, Yellow Aster, by Golden Lord, from Aster, according to her testing, gave 5,9111 b. of milk, producing 4101 b. of butter; another Scow by the same sire gave 5,6861 b. of milk, producing 3541 b. of butter; and a third Jersey gave 4,4471 b. of milk; produc- ing 31411). of butter.

div.head: Sterilised Milk no Good.
div.p: Sterilised Milk no Good.

It has been stated not for the first time that sterilised milk is a ruined food. The last authority to sound the alarm is Mr. Robert Mond, says " Science Siftings." He states that kittens fed wholly on sterilised cow's milk died miserably, whilst others, used as a control and fed On plain cow's milk, grew up and flourished. Dr. Edmund Owen, consulting snrgeon to the Great Ormond-street Hospital for Sick Children, endorses Mr. Mond' e views; He. has seen chil- dren ill-nourished, ricketty and scorbutic on sterilised milk, thrive and do well when the sterilised milk was stopped and untreated milk' substituted. Thus ends, we hope, the enormous boom of sterilised raj&

div.head: Cream Cheese as Cure for Ulcers.
div.p: Cream Cheese as Cure for Ulcers.

Dr. George 0. Williams, of Greene, N.Y., has found that soft curd cheese in an excellent poul- tice for varicose ulcers. He tells in the Medical Record of one case, in which he healed an old and deep ulcer two inches wide by three inches long. Giving thd liatient steel pills internally he applied to the sore poultices made from " soft, well ripened, full cream cheese, to which was added a mixture of equal parts of cream and water. The whole was worked into a soft mass. The water and cream were added to pre- vent drying." It was renewed morning, noon and night. The application was painfql for about an hour and a half; the cheese entirely disappeared within five hours, seemingly being eaten up by the ulcer. Twenty days of this treatment resulted in the healing of the ulcer, with no scab remaining. -

£lOO Per Acre From Oranges. Mr. William Barrett, who took up land about seven years ago at Dporalong, near Wyong, New has demonstrated the profitable ioduet f Wales, fruit-growing. This ,season he has marketed £470 worth of oranges and mandarins from four and a half acres. From three and a half acres £4OO was produced, one acre of late fruit returning £l6O and giving 400 cases. Man- darins did not give anything like this result, as one acre of land of a similar nature, which received the same attention, returned only £7O. Mr. Barrett is convinced that oranges pay much better than mandarins. The orchard has been planted only five years, all the trees being worked. Taking the orchard right through, the trees averaged three and a half cases, the best trees giving nine cases.

Ontario's New Cottonopolis. The town of WeHalal, Ontario, is rapidly ac- quiring a very important place in the industrial development of Canada, and if present plans are carried forward will soon rank as one of the cotton centres of the country. The latest in- dustry to decide to locate there is the Toronto Cotton Company, a company with a capital of £40,000 subscribed. The company agrees to commence the manufacture of cotton cloths in the building on or before October Ist, 1914. It is interesting to note the practical encourage- ment given by Ontario towns and cities to new industries. The agreement provides that Wel- land is to pay 90 per cent. of the cost of the Iluildings and site; and the company 10 per cent.

• English Eels for German Rivers. Stewed eels and eel pie were once esteemed dainties by English people; but nowadays they tend to disappear from the table. They have become almost as scarce as rook pie. In Ger- mau this change of 'taste has not become ap- parent. The German loves eels and cannot have too many of them. In 1909 the experiment wits tried of transferring some twenty thousand English elver ;i from the Severn to an East Prmiiian lake called the Paprotker See. These have thriven. amazingly. The lake in which the English eels were placed was thoroughly well supplied with food, and the experiment seems to show that there is a great commercial future for the business of feeding English eels in Prussian lakes to sell as articles of diet.— "Country Life."

A Colony of Celery Growers. There are few tracts of land in Canada for which a good use cannot be discovered. For a long time, what is now the fruitful irrigated land, was • given a wide berth. Then southern farmers, who had been accustomed to such soil and conditions, came along with results to them- selves and the land that were little short of phenomenal. Now amither •tract of so-called "worthless land" is about to be taken up. Four hundred Hollanders, who have been living in the Kalamazoo district of Michigan, the great celery-raising country, are migrating to the township of Dunwich, in East Elgin, Ontario, to start a similar industry there. They have secured some 2,000 acres of low and swampy lands, suitable to celery culture, and plan to start business on an extensive scale. There are millions of acres of rich: soil awaiting settle- ment, but these new colonists have selected this as most suitable to their purpose.

Music Note. As one who loves his Mendelssohn, I was glad of the reminder that the older masters in music are coining to their own again. I remember one critic comparing '7 It is enough" to a " snuffling whine," while another wrote of "If with all your hearts" that it is pretty enough, but "smacks of the Sunday school!" One more of these superior persons condescendingly said: "Much of 'Elijah' is certainly attractive if not hearirtoo frequently, and it would pot be necessary to use 'disparaging words about it if a great majority of the puldic would only leave it in its proper place and not seek to establish its composer on the same pedestal with the grrtest masters of the divine art." Of bite years it has been the fashion to deride Men- delssohn, or to "damn with faint praise," but assuredly the reputation of the master may safely be left with such representative organisa- tions as the Warrington Musical Society, who have this week given BO excellent an account of him.

Trial of the Seddons. Edited by Filson Young. Edinburgh: Published by William Hodge and Co. ss. net.

This book is one of a series of "Notable Eng- lish Trials," published by Messrs. Hodge, the chief aim of which—as expressed in the pre- face to the present volume—is to supply the public wilh the means of studying, at leisure, in carefully prepared records, the working of the important machinery of our Criminal Courts, to which people's lives and liberties are entrusted; and we think the Claim which is made is fully established—namely, that the reader's patient perusal of the entire proceed- ings of a trial to the end "will not only engage his curiosity aml afford a very considerable mental exercise, but will inspire some sober re- flections on the present-day administration of the criminal law."

The tendency of the ordinary citizen is to arrive at a too h4ty judgment, after reading portions of evidence given in condensed reports, and quite early in a ease to make up his mind, and say, "I atii sure he did itr or "I am sure he is innocent." Ey such persons the verdict brought in by the jury—arrived at after care- ful consideration of every detail of the evidence, and having also the means of judging, approx- imately, at any rate, from the manner and bear- ing of each witness, the relative proportions of truth or falsehood in the statements made—is very rarely received with satisfaction, unless it happens to accord with their peconceived notion, or too hastily-formed judgment. The great importance of this trial lies in the fact that it focusses in itself a number of changes which have gradually been developing in the administration of the criminal law; and it is likely to be epoqh-marking for this and various other reasons.

It stands, for instance, as a classical example of the working of the Prisoners' Evidence Act in capital cases. There is hardly any doubt that the Crown:would have failed to prove a case sufficient to secure 4 verdict of wilful mur- der had, Seddon not gone into the witness-box. Reading his evidence-in-chief and the cross-ex- amination which followed it, we feel it borne in upon us that in his cool and clever attempts to account for any and every suspicious feature in the chain of circumstances, he himself fur- nishes‘the most convincing evidence of a guilty knowledge. The whole of the evidence was cir- cumstantial, and it has been stated that the old maxim that "the accused. is presumed innocent until he is proved guilty" was, to all intents, reversed by the judgment in this case, large numbers of people expressing the opinion that it was by a presumption of guilt alone that Seddon was condemned, the necessity for the Crown to establish an indubitable chain of proof, by testimony, being ignored.

There cannot be a better exercise for fill who took a casual view of the trial than to read the entire case cal* and dispassionately—to con- centrate their minds on the evidence and its significance, sentence by sentence, and thus at- tempt to reach a cool and unbiased judgment. To the expert legal mind this trial has a pro- found and far-reaching significance, which makes it worthy Of the study and consideration of all who are in any capacity engaged in the practice of the law. It is also rich in the human interest which makes an appeal to every citizen who is intelli- gent enough to care for exact knowledge of the social conditions which surround him.
The book itself is monumental in its reflection of the procedure of our criminal courts. Every detail is reproduced with what may be described as photographic accuracy.

The introduction by -Mr. Filson Young is most helpful to a clear understanding of the case as presented; 'and the get-up of the volume— clear in type, on good paper, embellished with numerous photographs, and neatly and substan- tially bound—makes it creditable alike to editor and publishers.
Studies in the Evolution of Industrial Society. By Richard T. Ely; Ph.D. LL.D. (The Stan- dard Library). London: Maculakm and Co., Ltd. '.2s. net. Pp. 497.
This volume is a new aml cheaper impression of Dr. Ely's book, the first edition being pub- lished in 1903.

It is the best book, dealing within a reasonable compass with those great social and industrial problems, which are affecting most civilised countries, that we have met with for some time. The sanity, the breadth of mind of the author. and his wide acquaintance with the 'best thoughts on the various topics discussed, make it a book which no student of social problems should neglect to read. It is eminently suited to that increasing body of students associated with our Adult Schools, Study and Reading Circles, and the Workers' Educational Associa- tion. As an introduction to an extended course of reading on economics, sociology and practical politics, we do not know of any other book that will serve so well. And as it deals, necessarily, with American conditions in greater detail than those of other countries, the reader has the ad- vantage of seeing familiar political and indus- trial problems considered from other points of view.

The book is divided into two parts, the first of which is a general survey of the evolution of society in its economic aspect from the very earliest ages to the present time; the second part being a series of studies of specific 'problems of industrial evolution, most of which have been previously published as separate articles. Dr. Ely is thoroughly in accord with the view that conscious social co-operation will be one of the chief determining factors in industrial and social life in the future, but be does not think that the result will be a socialistic state. Indeed, he is thoroughly opposed to Socialism, although he gives the arguments, generally adduced in its favour, very impartially. His main objec- tions to Socialism rest on the same ground as his objections to monopoly, viz.., that where com- petition is eliminated the general welfare of a community suffers. His analyses of compe- tition and monopoly are very keen and search- ing. Dr. Ely is a firm believer in the doctrine of natural selection, but he tempers it with the admission that we have now reached a stage in evolution when conscious selection mist re- place the "natural " methods of the past. The " fit " will still survive, but society itself must determine the "fitness." Competition, in Dr. Ely's view, is the chief selective process in modern economic society, and he believes that "competition increasingly comes to mean worthy struggle, and true progress implies that success will be secured hereafter by conformity to higher and ever higher, nobler and ever nobler ideals." But while maintaining that the competitive order of society is essential to future social progress, Dr. Ely is in favour of applying the principle of public ownership (either State or municipal, as the case may be) as far as it will go, and the distinction lie draws between the industries adapted to public ownership and those in which the maximum of efficiency is achieved by private enterprise and initiative, though not, perhaps, meeting the objections of the Socialist to the latter's satisfaction, is, we think, eminently reasonable, and worthy of full consideration. But with an extension of public ownership a further development of civilisation

A LITTLE FRENCH TRAIN.

Announced by an optimistic French time-table to leave at 1.55 precisely, the little train pushed its way through a smoky haze from the rackety derricks of big tramp steamers moored at the quays saw trouble ahead, shrieked with despair and stopped. Two miniature trucks of a long string drawn by a goods engine had rebelled, jumped the metals exactly opposite the station, and were now being heaved and shoved back by the driver, the stoker, the stationmaster, the ticket-clipper, a gendarme, and the unofficial public in general, assisted by advice from a nondescript seated at a table of a cafe close by. After some wonderful escapes from death on the part of inquisitive children and dogs the trucks were placed on the lines and hauled to a siding, whereupon, with a prodigious assump- tion of dignity, the little train gave its well- known imitation of the Flying Scotsman. It hissed and puffed and fumed into the station as though four hundred dusty miles lay behind it stopped in the roadway outside .a wooden shed. —or, to be sadly accurate and commonplace, it Its rows of garden seats were soon comfortably filled; certain aristocrats of the company climbed into stuffy boxes, having for some mys- terious reason purchased first-class tickets— whichonl should ticket-clipper, without any fuss, became a guard, Y don on a wet day; the e and paper-sellers trotted up, calling their wares. With hoarse whistles, in order that sundry fruit lorries. horses, and traps, nurse-maids with go-c4rts, and other heavy traffic might not col- lide with it—in which case the little train would in'evitably have turned over—the start was made and time smother of the noisy wharves was left behind.

A leafy country lane, Ang which most incon- gruous rails had been laid, engulfed our rattling affairs for a minute or two, then the narrow track swerved to follow the course of the Ouistreliam Canal, and on the footpath by the edge of the water a boy on a bicycle made the pace. With much forbearance he checked the speed of his machine for a time to keep abreast of its; but probably his errand was urgent, for presently he pedalled on ahead with an encour- aging wave of the hand, and was Soon lost to sight. Steadily, without hurry and without delay, we passed the tranquil, shimmering waters, until a blue board, nailed to a post, indicated a station—or rather a stopping-place under the trees—known on maps and time- tables as Wrouville. Two hatless, garrulous ladies with big baskets and umbrellas alighted, one man, half farmer, half brigand, ascended, the guard blew a squeak from the tiny trumpet slung at his belt, and off we went once more.— From Our Little Train," by Wilfrid L. Randell, in the Vllobe."

div.head: BIG VOICE.
div.p: A BIG VOICE.

"The reverberating voice of Constable A. Richards, of Windsor-street Station, Montreal, is now hushed in illness." For thirty years he has been train caller at the station, and now that he is ill, no human throat can be found to replace his stentorian voice. Many novices have tried to do justice to his big megaphone and lusty tones. Practice gained by announc- ing train departures since the building of the first C.P.R. station in Montreal had enabled him to gauge his voice exactly to the acoustic pro- perties of the waiting rooms and lobbies. But when his successors failed repeatedly to "put over" the stentorian reverberations, those in charge of the building decided that the big volume of his voice could never be filled, and the first musolophone was installed.. The musolophone is nothing more than a telephone instrument, with electrical properties of multi- plying the tone waves several hundred times. A horn, about the size of a photograph attach- ment, is located 300 feet away from the mouth- piece of the musolophone, and, when the speaker picks up the transmitter from the hook and talks in an ordinary voice, he may hear his utterances thundered back in most oratorical manner within less than a second. The whole is operated by it low-voiced individual in the stationmaster's office, who mildly asserts that the passengers will do well to get aboard their train. Then some hundreds of innocent travellers jump with surprise at the emphatic mandate coming from the ceiling. German, French and Austrian are given equal opportun- ities for dissemination with English, for it is understood the C.P.R. interpreter, who is of too retiring a disposition to proclaim the departures of trains through a blatant megaphone, will now suggest them meekly hid within the shelter of an office.—" The Canadian Mail."

is necessary, and we think that the following passage applies equally, in this connection, to ourselves, as it does to the Americans. "The civic conscience," says Dr. Ely, "with us is slow of development. The satisfactory performance of Public duties implies, in some Particulars, a nt higher civilisation than we have reached. It requires some development of the imagination to see the harm and suffering brought to lesscount- science than that now generally found among us, to reach that state in which there is a con- nobi eys a lapseshigher in civic virtue. Fur- thermore,hiindividuals s developme of con- scious desire to abstain from all acts which may hurt people who are not seen. Many a man will give to a poor widow, whom he sees, money to relieve her distress, but at the same time will not hesitate to increase the burdens of poor widows whom he does not see, by fraudulent evasion of taxation." We cannot doubt, how- ever, that the social conscience, as distinct from the individual conscience, will emerge as the development of mankind proceeds: Already in some quarters we see indications of its presence. But the rapidity with which it will come gener- ally depends largely upon mankind itself. Each man and woman who cultivates the social sense hastens the day when humanity will have lost the individualism that often mars the present in that larger indWidualisin which is possible only witß the fullest development of the feeling of the solidarity of mankind, when the " con- sciousness of kind," to use Prof. (lidding's ex- pressive phrase, shall extend to the whole human race. There are many questions in Dr. Ely's book on which we should have liked to say something, such as "Social Progress and Race Improvement," "Concentration of Wealth," " The Inheritance ,of Property," "Industrial Liberty," &c., but considerations of space for- bid. We can only record our admiration of the masterly manner in which the author discusses these weighty problems. Dr. Ely is no pessi- mist. He faces the future secure in the confi- dence that the social forces in the world are working in the direction of great improvements in social and industrial conditions. With Utopian viii he will not be beguiled. The work of social betterment must proceed step by step, each one contributing his full part "to make this world of ours an increasingly good world—a better and better world for the chil- dren of men during their sojourn here." We unhesitatingly recommend Dr. Ely's book to the attention of s all interested in social and industrial problems as a broad-minded and illu- minating contribution to political and social thought.

SEND IN TO-DAY.
My Dear Children, , How many of 'you have entered for our competition? As I am writing this early in the week, I have not received so many essays as I expected, but doubtless they will come in later.

The competition closes today, but any letters which bear the post-mark of to-day, or are found in our letter-box this evening, will still be ill time, so I hope to receive many. The com- petition asks you to write a short essay on what you would like to do during the Easter Holidays, and state your reason why. I have received a number of letters, but, of course, these will not be opened until after the oompetition closes. A niece has sent me the following poem, which I regret I could not find the space to Publish until now. Doris Owen is thanked for her contribution :
Mother's Little Woman. • •I'm mother's little woman, As you can plainly see, And when I start to help her, I'm busy as can be.
I dust and sweep and polish The tables and the chairs, I love to take the big broom And brush all down the stairs.
There never is a dust speck,. Or cobweb to be seen, ' So mother always tells me Where busy I have been.
I wash the cups and saucers, The glasses shining make, And never, never break one, Because such care I take.
She says I am her treasure, What that is I don't know; I only know I do it, Because I love her so.
Now, then, those who are competing do not forget that your essay Must be sent in without Your loving UNCLE JACK.

div.head: SCHOOLBOYS' REMARKABLE TOUR.
div.p: SCHOOLBOYS' REMARKABLE TOUR.

A plucky walking pilgrimage was undertaken just before Christmas by a party of twelve native schoolboys from a very remote district in the North of New Zealand—Te Kao (to which the directory assigns an adult population of 10 souls) to Auckland, a distance of 323 miles, with the final object of visiting the Exhibition now in progress in that capital. The boys were from 10 to 16 years of age, and the tour, planned by their schoolmaster, was made at the rate of 11 to 23 miles a day.

This was the 'lads' first excursion, and it was mapped out, not only to visit the Exhibition, but to utilise the opportunities allorded by the journey for an observation and study of the farming methods practised in the districts which they traversed. For many months beforehand the boys rehearsed native songs and other items, so that they might be qualified to give entertain- ments stead' settlement visited, and also at the Exhibition, to meet the expenses of their travels.
BE CHEERFUL—SOMETIMES. Dick Marshall is a youthful Scout—
A jolly good one, too— tle tries his best to .keep the laws —That's more than some chaps do!
His honour you may safely trust, He always is polite. He has a shilling in the bank, And tries to do the right.
And when it'rains on Saturday, Ile doesn't frown and swear; He smiles and whistles -cheerfully, As if he didn't care.
But once, at school, at dinfier-hour, Dick found a wondrous pool— lie fished for newts—and quite forgot That he was due at schoal.
When memory at length returned, lie ran_ to school in haste, Into his classroom boldly walked— For "troubles must be faced."
"You're late, Dick Marshall !" sternly cried The master—cane in hand. "Of all offences this is one
. I really wnA, NOT stand !" And sO* this youthful Scout gut tuned_
I tell you, it was sore! - He firmly vowed in his own mind He would be late no more.
Then—oh, it was unfortunate, For all things have their place— Dick to his master sweetly smiled, And WHISTLED IS HIS FACE!
"Boy," cried the master,, full of wrath, " I don't know how you dare To stand and grin from ear to ear, As if you didn't care !"
Please, sir," the trembling boy replied, "The law I must obey, To smile in trouble and in pain, To whistle, come what may.
I'm sorry I've been rude to you, Sir, I apologise!' To tell the truth, despite the smile, The tears were in Dick's eyes.
"You've kept the LETTER of the law, To bravely bear, the pain, But, IN TEIE SPIRIT, it demands • You should not NEED the cane!" •
CRABS . THAT STEAL EGGS.

Some interesting facts respecting -t-1-1-e—destruc- tiveness of certain species of crabs in Grand Cayman, an island in the British West Indies. appear in a bulletin just issued from the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. They are great bur- rowers, and cannibals, too. In places where they abound nothing is safe from them. They will take into their holes things for which they cannot conceivably find a use—a knife, for in- stance, or a pocket compass. They will eat the eggs from under a sitting hen, if not the hen herself, as readily as the leaves of seedling cocoanut trees, and of these from six to ten per cent. have to be replaced if they are planted in newly-cleared ground before the crabs have been thoroughly thinned out. They are responsible for frequent patches of bare soil in the "bush," which get covered with vegetation when the crabs are gone. During the drier months of the early part of the year they go underground to change their shells, and add to their destructive- ness by barricading the mouths of their holes: with masses of sticks and rubbish like jackdaivs nests, nipping off or rooting up saplings as much as three-quarters of an inch in diameter for the purpose.

div.head: WONDERS OF ANIMAL INGENUITY.
div.p: WONDERS OF ANIMAL INGENUITY.

From our earliest days we hear of the mar- vellous works performed by ants, bees, wasps, and °titer common e..euttires. We get ,so familiar with their singular powcrs that we almost cease to'wonder at them and to take them As a Matter of course. In this short article w..? propose tocall attention to a few other creatures that eihibit :extraordinary in- g,enuity and that are not quite so wellicnown ! as our friends, or foes, ot the field add the , garden. THE TRAP-POOR SPIDER. .•:

First of these is a member of the, family of spiders, the trap-door spider. She, for the male takes no part in the building of the structure we are about to describe, first digs a little tunnel into some soft earth. Once in shelter she spins a- tube that lines the cavity and projects beyond it sonic inches into the open. Over the end of the tube, a door is made of silk strengthened with. earth and working on a hinge so placed that it closes of its own accord. The entrance is hidden by the planting of moss or lichen in a very in- genious manner, for the spider is liable to attack from•many enemies. When the door is completed the internal excavation is con- tinued, and each tiny•pellet of earth removed, has to be carried out through the front door and deposited at some distance from the en- trance. To prevent the .roof and sides of the tunnel from falling in ..she lines them with silk and constructs supports that the most skilful of, engineers might envy. Some varieties of trap-door spider build a door that resembles a cork in the way in which it fits into the aperture, while others have a projection like a spur which acts as a lever aucl allows the door to be easily opened from the outside. When attacked, the spider, if at home, fastens its legs and claws into the door and the walls, and holds en with such force that one naturalist has left it on record that the blade of his steel pen- knife bent in the. attempt to force the door open. Other creatures besides spiders dig 'holes, such as the mole and the badger and many birds. A sand martin will dig a hole in a sand bank three inches wide and over a yard , in depth, and excavate a cavity at the end of that for the nest, all in about two days, and then, if dissatisfied with the situation, set to work and di.' out another equally spacious. Tortoises dig holes in which to deposit their eggs. They°first make a hole with the tail • and afterwards enlarge it with their feet. The feet at such-a time are used exactly as we should use our hands, and the earth that is removed is placed in a circle round the hole. When the hole is as deep as the tor- toise can dig it places the eggs, in, one by one, and then carefully covers them with the earth again, a 'handful' at ii time, in an al- most ludicrously human fashion. Darwin tells us of a race of crabs that make burrows at the roots of trees, climb the neigh- bouring palms in search of cocoa nuts, and actually succeed in opening the nuts by ham- mering on them with their, huge pincers. THE HOME OF THE GOLDEN EAGLE. Coming above ground we may turn our at- tention to the wondertul homes built on or above the surface of the earth by birds and other animals. Take for instance, the Golden Eagle which inhabits high mountains, and places his home on practically inaccessible cliffs. This home is a mass of sticks, and some idea of the strength and perseverance of the creature may be obtained from the fact that old nests have been found which contain- ed as much as two cart loads of wood. -Sticks a, inch in thickness cannot be wpven to- getherbutany and the, are merelypikd one on top of the other. l'he interior isliAi, d mustthat.un c eoxlmeief4oril b 2 fu ce experience at atat the outset as t the ilaoffeutu gambboaiutredtisi as sl itionhgaebttihitieeaur,ttsree.iiiste. most 'unlucky of eesasrettelhisisies rialle pulls t(ifehinbirpianntezhee one with another and in due timeagehtesi,ahreelids ground. Once or twice a day the parents -come to examine the nest and it it be too hot they scrape away a part of the mound; if too cold they pile on fi 0 more fuel. They possess a power of esti- mating the temperature of the incubator al- most as accurate as that of a thermometer. A WONDERFUL BUILDER.

The male bower-bird of the same continent is also a wonderful builder. He has no fine feathers and no brilliant song with which to attract his lady love and has to exert his per- suasive powers in another way. In some out of the way part of the scrub he builds a bower about three feet in length. This is of twigs and is lined inside with tall grasses.— The side walls slant together forlning a ridge where they meet. 'rhe floor is daintily covered with small pebttles arranged in an artificial but well designed fashion. From the door there diverge two rows of pebbles, shells, feathers, scraps of rag or any other oddments that the bird can discover. 'These show the way to the bower and are stated to he quite as efficacious in attracting his lady love as the brilliant plumage or song of some A his apparently more fortunate neighbours. 'Animals often show just as great ingenuity in attacking their fees as in efending them- selves. In the Far East there is a fish tbat rests placidly under the surface of the water near to branches where, as it knows from ex- perience, insects that are pleasing to its pal- ate, are apt to congregate. When a particu- larly dainty morsel is within reach it pops up its head and shoots. Its aim is sure; its am- munition, drops of water ejected with such force as to knock the insect off its perch and bring it within reach of the marksman. The Chinese often keep these creatures as pets in jars. They place insects on the edge of the jars and amuse themselves by watching. the fish knock them off into the water. Another fish, the sea-angler dangles from the front of his body a long filament with a silvery tuft. Some unsuspecting creature takes the 'tuft for a morsel of food, darts to- wards it and finds itself constituting, refresh- ment for someone snore wily than itself.

AN INGENIOLS WEEVIL. Whenever an animal provides us with an. 'example of almost reasoned effort we may take it that it is usually for the purpose of -rearing or feeding the oifspring or of storing food. The end is always utilitarian. Ani- mals seem never to waste their time in mere amusement. ani what they can accomplish for their own ends is iitteu little short of the marvellous. Take, for instance, the tiny weevil that lives on the poplar trees. The poplar leaf forms suitable nourishment for the larva, if it can be placed so as to be with- in reach at the moment when it is needed. and if the larvip at the same time call be protected from attacks on the part of those who have an appetite for undeveloped weevils.

The weevil bores a hole in the stalk and so stops the supply of sap from the trunk. 'When the leaf is &weeid the insect begins at (rue end, digs its feet into it and begins to roll it up like a cigar leaf. It works backwards and torwards from end to end of the leaf like a ploughman ploughing a field, and it takes good care never tit let go with more than one foot at a time till the whole has been rolled. in each fold a few lar- vae are deposited and when the insect gets to the end of its task it braises the glands on the edge of the leaf, frees a sticky substance there secreted, presses the edges of the roll together, and holds on like grim death till the cement has done its work. Here the young can develop, out of sight of foes and with a - sul)l2lv of food within reach of their mouths as soun as that useful organ nas come into existence. Our last example shall be the ant-lion. It digs in the sand; not an easy matter when , one considers the nature of sand, and it lies there till some insect falls into the pit. It at once makes an attempt to seise and devour its prey. If the frightened creature manages to escape and crawls up the sides a the trap, , the ant-lion throws sand at it and knocks it back into the bole again. When the soft parts of the prey have been c.onsumed, the hard pails are ejected from the tvp so that the inside is always free from. refuse.

" Na, na !" he said. "A bargain's aye a bargain, and ye canna get your money back. The best I can dae for ye is to swop the cup ye sent for the one I lent ye." "Look here, Meldrum— " Hirsch began and Harris, with surprise, corrected him. "Not Meldruni," he remarked. "Sir Gil- bert_Quair..".. • ..

" exclaimed the partners simultaneously, and he grinned at them, with his stout old breast across the door-way like a cliff. " The greed of English thieves brought them here mar- auding for good six hundred years. and it seems ye're no' done yet ! "That is worse," replied Sir Gilbert, mak- ing: for his door. "We Scots are still at feud wi' the Jews for what they did out yonder in Jerusalem."

THE TUDOR CUP.
NEIL MUNRO.

When the Tudor Cup was sold at Sotheby's in the year 18— for the sum of £7,000, the fall of the auctioneer's hammer echoed round the world, at all events round the world of men who gather bibelots. There were only three such treasures in existence—the one now destined for America, which was under- stood to have come from Holland, another in the national collection in Paris, and a third in Scotland, the property of Sir Gilbert Quair whose ancestor had acquired it one hundred- and-fifty years before by winning a game of cards in a London coffee-house. Among those people who were profoundly moved by this record price for a quite unim- pressivo-looking battered silver tankard was the firm of Harris and Hirsch the Bond Street art-dealers, and two days after the sale in London, Mr. Harris hastened up to Scotland; quartered himself at an inn 'in Peebles, and pushed some discreet inquiries. Sir Gilbert Quair, he discovered, was in a state lapproachiAg penury, living an almost hermit life in the House of Quair be- side the Tweed, with a deaf old house-keeper, a half-daft maid who never, came out of doors, and an equally recluse man whose duty it was to act as guide to the: numerous tour- ists who flocked to the house for the sake of its place in Ballad Minstrelsy and its anti- quarian collection. If the gossips of Peebles could be trusted, the baronet lived upon the shilling fees his guide exacted from the , visi- tors, dodging, himself, from room to room of his mansion for fear of encountering Ameri- cans and English, whom he hated, resenting, their intrusion on his privacy, but counting their numbers eagerly as from his window he watched them coming up the long yew av- enue.

Harris, the Bond Street dealer, modestly bent on hiding his own importance in the commercial world of art, for the nonce a sim- ple English gentleman with a taste for minia- tures, called next day at the House of Quair whose crenelated tower looked arrogantly over ancient woods and fields where lambs were bleating piteously, and men were walk- inF along the furrows scattering seed, rhe avenue of yews, which led from the highway into Peebles through neglected and dishevelled grounds, brought the Bond Street dealer to the forlorn façade of the mansion and the great main door. He rapped upon the iron knocker; the sound reverberated as through a vault, with hollow echoes such as come from vacant chambers. Far back in the dwelling's core there was a clatter of something fallen, but no one answered to the summons of the visitor, and having rapped in vain again, he ventured round the west-ward wing to find himself confronted by a door on the side of which was hung the evidence that this was properly his entrance. It was a painted board with the legend QUAIR COLLECTION.
Open to the Public Tuesdays. and Thursdays
Admission One Shilling.

Now this was neither a Tuesday nor a Thursday, and Harris swore softly. He was just on the point of making his retreat when a footstep sounded on the gravel of a little walk that led to a bower upon the terrace, and turning he found himself face to face with Sir Gilbert Quair. "The collection is not on view to-day, sir," said the baronet, an elderly, thick-set gentle. man wearing a shabby suit of tweed. Mr. Harris took off his hat, not to the wearer of the shabby tweed suit but to the owner of the Tudor Cup. "I am most unfor- tunate," lie stammered. "I was not aware that the collection was only on view on cer- tain days, and unhappily I must return to England this evening. It happens that I am something of an amateur in miniatures, for- tunate in the possession of a few choice ex- amples, and being in this neighbourhood I could not resist the temptation to see the celebrated collection of Sir Gilbert Quair which is rich in miniatures." -

He passed the baronet his card to which the name of a well-known London club con- tributed the proper degree of uncommercial importance. Sir Gilbert turned it over in his fingers with a little hesitation: shot a shy glance of the keenest scrutiny from under his bushy eye-brows at the visitor. "In the circumstances—" he began, and taking a key from his pocket unlocked the door which led to the collection, but before he let his visitor through he held out to him a little wooden box with a slit in the lid of it. "In the absence of the usual guide," said he, " I'll collect your shilling for him, Mr. Harris."

bert's miniatures, Five minutes later Harris was manifesting the most rapturous appreciation of _Sir Gil- thing wonderful, but at every opportunity, when unobserved by his host. Iris eyes went which in truth were no- ranging in search of the Tudor Cup. It was his host who finally called attention to it un- der glass in a corner cupboard. "If you had been interested in old English silver, Mr. Harris, this piece might have liid some attraction," said Sir Gilbert, drench- ing his flaring nostrils with a pinch of snuff from a tiny ivory spoon. "I'm no great judge, myself, but my father highly prized It." The Bond Street dealer with a thudding heart peered through the glass at the very counterpart of that tarnished goblet which had fetched £7,000 in Sotheby's. He was wondering if the dry old shabby gentleman looking over his shoulder and odorous with maccoboy was aware that this was a Tudor Cup, or if he had read the newspapers care- fully, and knew what Tudor Cups were worth in Sotheby's. **** * *

" But Himmel ! did you not make him an offer ?" demanded Hirsch next day in the Bond Street shop—they called it gallery—to which his partner had returned from Tweed- side with the profound depression a man might have who had -for a ..fleeting moment seen the only woman he could ever love and then had lost her in a panic. " Offer. Joel !" he replied in accents of des- pair. "I offered him five thousand, and he only chuckled. He would not even take it from the cupboard. ' No, no, Mr. Harris,' he said with his head to the side, flicking'llP his abominable snuff, 'lt is an heir-loom old- er than any here, and I am not selling.' And the galling thing is that he doesn't even know he has a Tudor Cup, nor what a Tudor Cup can fetch in Sotheby's." , ' Ah, you should have had the money with you. Harris," said his partner. " Always show the money, I say; it talks for you through a speaking-trumpet. By heavens I will go myself to Scotland and have that Tud- or Cup if I have to steal it !" A spirit of romance and a solemn homily on mutability were in the scene when Hirsch walked into the grounds of Quair, though he was not the man to understand. Six hund- red years of history cried from the old bastion; still in its shelter men sowed oats and their shabby dwellings clustered, no way changed, to look" at, since the Borderland was vexed with wars, and Ouair was lord and warden; but vessels no more, save to that grim seigneur Commerce, who took from them triple-tithes and children instead of the I service of the sword which was all the old lords claimed. A valley of peace.l and nights untroubled, and the old bold fighting Quairs in their resting graves, and their troopers dust at the roots of English pastures; surely at eve in the woods of Quair, or riding spirit horses through the pusses of the hills, a thou- sand ghosts went seeking lost passions, old delights. It was Thursday afternoon. Hirsch stepped in at the door which led to the Quair collec- tion, to find the man in charge of it had all the customary cicerone's dull loquacity. He dribbled dates and gushed details of family history as if he were a gargoyle who had never got refreshment from the currents pouring through him. Thick-set, short, and room atomo-canlosei oshtiallvionnt hraesplielodkeudpotnhet lh,eerychcign from f figure of the empty suits of mail that flanked the entrance to the gallery, and even to the shop- man's eye of Hirsch he had an air of trucu- lence that somehow seemed to accord with the situation. ")ou do not appear to.bave, many. visitors

to-day,/' said the picture-dealer, having looked perfunctorily at dingy tapestry and pictures, and now with eyes, in ivhich the fires of covetousness were with difficulty re- strained, upon the tarnished Tudor Cup in its corner cupboard. " Ye're the first this week," said the guide with acerbity, as if the shilling fees were a more personal matter than the gossilla of the country-side believed, and Hirsch the dealer, rubbing his hook-nose to conceal the tremulous avidity of his mouth, saw that dis- appointed avarice yvas in this creature's eyes. " I should like, a little later on, to see Sir Gilbert," said the dealer who had five th(iu- sand pounds in his pocket, and a Jew's con- viction that an impecunious Scot could never resist the delicious crackle of English notes. "Ye canna; he's from home, explained the guide. "He's awa' to Edinburgh for a month." A thought came there and then to the deal- er which made him pale. Avarice and cun- ning were in the old man's face; his shillings plainly meant a lot to him; his clothing was in poor accord with the guardianship of trea- sure. "Look here," said Hirsch in a confidential whisper. "If your master is to be away for a month, there is no reason why the matter I meant to arrange with him should not. be ar- ranged with you and put a handsome sum of money in your pocket. I have taken a fancy to this silver jug, and though I know Sir Gil- bert will not part with it, I thought he might at least agree to let me have it copied. It's a thing that is often done, Mr.— " Meldrum," said the guide with a promis- ing air of equanimity. "In two or three weeks I could have my copy made in Paris, and this cur) returned to you in safety, and no one else except ourselves need be a bit the wiser, Mr. Meldrum." The guide gave a laugh that was half a sneer, and checkedv it suddenly with a hand upon his mouth. "It's a maist singular pro_ i position," he remarked reflectiyely. the four-and-twenty years I have lieen show- in' folk the Quair Collection I havena heard the like of it. And it comes from a total stranger !" "I represent one of the most reputable firms in London," Hirsch hastened to ex- plain, with the simultaneous production of his business card. Meldrum looked at it with interest. "Har- ris and Hirsch. I take it that you are Mr. Hirsch ? There was a Mr. Harris calling ea Sir Gilbert, I was tell't, some days ago.' , " Exactly.," answered Hirsch. my part- ner. He had almost completed negotiations for the loan of the cup for the purpose I have mentioned. But really there seems no ' need for us to be* troubling Sir Gilbert. The cup will be back before 'his return from Edin- burgh and____" Just that !" said Meldrum dryly. " And what about my security ?" Delighted with such apparent pliability, Hirsch produced his English notes whie,h brought a very passion of greed to Meldrum s eyes. "Let us not be calling it security: Mr. Meldrum," he remarked insidiously. `lf a hundred pounds—" Again the guide ironically chuckled. "If I could trust ye ;or a hundred pounds, Mr. Hirsch, I could trust ye mair for ten time that," he said. "I take your word for't that we needna ca't security, if I'm to risk my job and my reputation, the cost of three weeks lean o that siller tankard is exaeltlY a thou- sand pounds !" * * * * * * *

Three weeks later, the Quair Can and its duplicate came back from Tregastel of Paris, 60 much alike that Hirsch wolild have been beat to see 'a difference had it not been that he found en one a private microscopic mark he had put on it himself. But it was not the cup so marked that he returned to the accommodating Meldrum. Two months more. and the curio world was shaken once again by the intimation of an- other Tudor Cup for sale at; Sotheby's. Amongst the host of possible bidders who ex- ainined the precious piece of tarnished metal taken out impressively from Sotheby's strongest safe some days before the sale, was Barraclough; the expert who had bought its fellow earlier in the season for his client in America. "A brilliant forgery," lie exclaimed on careful scrutiny. "'One of Jules Tregastel's charming reproductions," and departed. Harris and Hirsch were sent- for by the auctioneer. " Nonsense !" they protested, and Hirsch satisfied himself a,,„ffain that the microscopic mark of the veritable cup from Quair was there. " Trcgastel never had a tool on it."

"Hadn't you 'better ask ? " said the ann. tioneer. and they asked by telegram, with astounding consequences. "The cup you sent was a copy made a year age by myself for another client. I thought you knew," replied Tregastel. " Mein Gott !" cried Harris, appalled. "Tregastel has made so cunning a job of it he has even copied your private mark, and you have sent the original back to Quair." "I will not believe it ! I will not believe it !" said his partner, almost weeping with chagrin. That night the two of them went to Scot- land. and in the morning Harris went out from Peebles to the House of Quair to see Sir Gilbert. "Might I have another look at the cup ?" he asked without periphrasis, and the baronet snuffed and chuckled. "It seems to have wonderfully taken your fancy, Mr. Harris," he remarked with an ironic cough. " Again you. are unfortunate in the day you call, for this is Wednesday. And in any case I thought I made it clear that the cun was bound to stay here in spite of your most temptine. offers." "I know," replied the dealer, " but I should like to see it; that is all." "Ah ! you mad collectors !" said Sir Gil- bert humorously. "Ye can be as crazy over a bashed old siller cup as I might have been myser at one time over . a bonnie lassie !. Well, come your wave in and you shall see it. It is aye another shilliW ! " Harris not only saw the cup but this time got it into his hands. In a fever of appre- hension he turned it up 51151 down Ind "1"11r€ for a microscopic mark like that which Hirsch bnd pointed out -upon the other—it was not there ! At the sight of the blank look on his fare Sir Gilbert chuckled and took snuff. " I see you have discovered, Mr. Harris," he re- marked with his eye-brows twitching. "You connoisseurs are not to be deceived so easi- ly !" Tbec—then You know it is a forgery !" cried Harris with amazement, " I would not use that word for it exactly, Mr. Harris," said the baronet with a gesture of distaste. " A copy—and a wonderful copy too. by Tregastel of paris. The truth is I sold the original some months ago in Lon- don, haying first had this one made. You see my if of a Tudor Cup is notorious and if it got about that the uair Collection wae being in any way depleted. where won:el our shillin's come from. Mr. Harris ?" and he 10c.:66Y poked his visitor in the ribs. Harris flew back to the inn at Peebles, an object • of unutterable despair. " Mein Gott ! the.se Scotch !" cried Hirsch wringing his hands. " But I will have my money back from that Meldrum man if • I have to take him to the courts."

" Harris an wouict cut a runny fig- ure in the courts in the circunistances, Joel," said hie partner. "it is better that we go out together to-morrow, when your Mel. drum's place is open and compromise." The entrance to the Quair Collection had been hardly opened on the morrow when the dealers tried to push their way within. Har- ris was perturbed when he saw who checked them on the threshold—Sir Gilbert Quair himself, who greeted him with a crafty smile, only a little shabbier in dress than when he had seen him hitherto, and with the box for the adinission shillings hanging round his neck.

div.head: CRUELTY TO A SWAN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CRUELTY TO A SWAN AT RUNCORN.

The killing of a swan led to Gilbert Ains- worth, Frodsham Bridge, being charged at Run- corn on Monday with cruelty to the bird. The evidence showed that defendant, on the 12th inst., in company with two companions, went along the side of the river Weaver on to Weston Marsh. When they reached what is known as the " Soapery " four swans were seen to fly over, having come from the direction of the river Mersey.
- Ainsworth, who had a gun, fired at the birds, and one was seen to fall, flapping its wings. The defendan't ran towards the injured swan, and he was seen to strike at the bird with a stick.

Inspector Dee, of the R.S.P.C.A., said that he received information from Supt. Owen, and saw the Wall at the Runcorn Police Station on the 13th +inst. It iwas very badly knocked about. Its beak was broken, the left wing was splin- tered, the right eye was knocked out, and the skull was broken. It was covered with blood. The chairman referred to the killing of the swan as an act of, the grossest .cruelty, and in- flicted a fine of 40s. and 15s. 6d. costs, with the alternative of One month's imprisonment. Ainsworth was afterwards charged with using a gun without having a licence, and for this offence he was fined ss. and 4s. fid. 'costs.

div.head: ST. HELENS WOMAN'S ADVENTURE.
div.p: ST. HELENS WOMAN'S ADVENTURE.

The story of a St. Helens woman named Mary Wilson, who walked i4lto the Marine Lake at Southport with the intention of drowning her- self, but who changed her/ mind and came out again, was told at the Southport Police Court on Saturday.

_ Appleton said he'found the woman in a shelter-house in the King's Gardens, near the Marine Lake. Her clothes were dripping wet, and she was sitting in pools of water. She said she had been attempting to commit suicide because she was desperate, having left her hus- band in London. He (her husband) was a had man. She had tried to get work but failed to do so, and said she considered she was better dead than alive under these circumstances. She told the Bench she had a drop of drink and did not know exactly what she was doing. She had been getting it living by selling flowers. The Police Court Missionary said the woman told him that she left her husband in St. Helens, and went away from him because he ill-used her. She asked him not to try to com- municate with her husband. The Bench discharged her,'ihe Clerk remark- ing that it was on condition that she did not act in that silly way again.
