BREAKFAST. PARTIES.

Breakfast parties, that were such a feature of the mid-Victorian era, are to become fashion- able again. The term was applied formerly to garden parties. His late Majesty King Edward favoured this form of entertainment, and often gave breakfast parties during the summer months, more especially when on the Continent. During the last fortnight of Lent there is always a cessation of gaiety, and this year it should prove welcome, since the season began un- usually early. Only a few years ago the first of May was the earliest date at Which fashion- able people arrived in London, but this Mardi has been almost as gay as June, indeed ever since Parliament met there has been a con- tinual round of dinners and dances. Self-Contained Houses.

King Edward remarked on the lack of cup- boards, when, on one occasion, inspecting a block of new workmen's dwellings, and suggested that more accommodation of that kind would be an advantage. Whether or not architects took the hint, they are introducing into the up-to-date house 'much more built-in furniture than formerly. It has always been the custom in modern times to provide the kitchen apart- ments with dressers, cupboards, shelves, plate- racks, and sinks, with hot and cold water, and there is no ,logical reason why the rest of the house should not be similarly self-contained, Hence houses are being built with fixed hat stands, sitting-rooms have fitted bookcases let into the walls, together with fixed sideboards, carving, serving and writing tables; whilst bed- rooms are Provided with wardrobes, tiers of drawers, and self-closing hot and cold water washstands. It is all very convenient, and saves not only a lot of space, but also a good deal of household labour. This new style of house will appeal to the housewife burdened with a lot of superfluous furniture, which has to be kept spick and span, and it also offers attractions by way of saving trouble and expense to young people setting up a home. • A Consumers' Union.

The Housewives' Union is a new organisation which is being formed in London to regulate in some measure the prices of all necessaries— food, clothing, and fuel. It was the women who broke the milksellers' " ring" in London to put up the price to sd. a quart. At Edmonton and elsewhere they refused to pay more than 4d.,. and either used condensed milk or did without milk altogether, until the lower price was re- stored. This campaign did much to open the eyes of consumers to the possibilities of collec- tive bargaining, and it is possible that this new movement may go far in regulating relation.- ships between tradespeople and the public. In some towns co-operators are supplying milk at seven pints for a shilling, and pay a dividend of 2s. in the X.

New Evening Gowns. Tulle is the material par excellence for even- ing gowns. This being so, it is satisfactory to learn that in buying it one is helping a home industry. In fact, the greater part of the tulle used in this country and on the Continent is manufactured .in Devonshire. This charming material, which is particularly suitable to the young, in white and pale shades, is equally be- coming to older women in black, or in darker colours. It also lends itself to the three or four tiered skirt, and to the tunic, the edges of both being finished with a pretty picot stitch. The range of variety that evening dress has assumed is nothing short of amazing. Draperies are wonderfully graceful, or aggressively_pannier- like, and some quite full skirts are drawn in by means of trails of roses in spiral fashion round the figure. Tunics could scarcely be more varied, or more übiquitous. They are single, double, and treble; long, short, full or fiat, ac- cording to taste, and their reign promises to be a long one.

Evening Collars and Corsages. Wired lace collars of the medici type that do not go all round the neck, are exceedingly smart and becoming. They are also, dignified and graceful, standing out as they do in points from shoulder to shoulder. The modified Eliza- bethan collar was seen on many of the Court gowns, and in each case proved a success. Even- ing corsages 'ire generally of tulle, even when the skirts with which they are worn are of bro- cade or ,silk. Sometimes they are made with points at the back and front. The material that composes evening bodices this season must be transparent and as fragile as possible in ap- pearance. Tulle is often made up on a lining of chiffon, a tiny sleeveless coatee of silver tissue reaching the decolletage—which is always low—in ,front and at the back, and giving a touch of solidity to the fairy confection. Sleeves to evening corsages are sometimes dispensed with altogether, and When in evidence are of the most limited proportions imaginable. Ribbon Hats.

White hats are to be very much worn this summer and the new imitation Tagal will doubtless have a vogue. It is in two qualities, is soft and makes an ideal sports or seaside hat. Ribbon plays an important ;art in the new mil- linery, and some of the latest models are com- posed of narrow ottoman silk ribbon threaded . in and out to form squares. Wide ribbons form the ruchings and ruffles that give the re- quired height to all hat trimmings. Many crowns are swathed with ribbons that are drawn up into bows towering aloft. Fancy ribbons are in endless variety, and those with velvet effects are largely used. Innumerable novelties may be noted in these, one of which deserves special mention on account of its attractive- ness and beauty, viz., the ribbon that is an exact imitation of Dresden china. The most natural clusters of tiny flowers and posies with foliage seem to grow on a delicate groundwork that throws them up, as in the porcelain. Trimming for Hats.

„ Artificial flowers are equally beautiful, and many novelties have appeared in this depart- ment, also notably the .most natural-looking roses in gold beaters' skin, dyed in every beauti- ful shade. Trails of tiny flowers surround the flat crowns of double brimmed hats, whilst those . of the Dolly Varden and other quaint, turned- op types, are filled ill at the sides with bunches of roses or other flowers, always in bright colours, such as Purple, tango, lemon, or cerise. Upright floral mounts are used in many in- stances to give the required height, and have a miniature Maypole effect. Feather mounts are ' equally curious. Ostrich feathers are turned, and twisted in the weirdest of fashions, and are

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

.STOCKTON HEATH v. CHORLTON. " Stockton Heath were the visitors to Chorlton on Saturday, and after a moderate game won by four goals against two. At Warrington the home team won by three goals against one. •The ground, after the recent heavy rains, was in a wretched condition, the ball often sticking in the mud. The home team quickly adapted themselves to the conditions and were one up in the first few minutes, McKenzie opening the scoring from a corner. Chorlton continued to have most of the play. A• fine clearance by Partridge brought relief, Bainbridge equalising after 15 minutes. The visitors were now adapt- ing themselves better to the condition of the ground, and play was fairly even. Towards the interval Stockton Heath played up strongly, Richardson giving them the lead after the goal- keeper had saved two hot shots in rapid suc- cession. Half-time: Stockton Heath, two goals; Chorlton,9ne goal. _ _ .

From the bully Chorlton got away and at- tacked strongly, 'Dunne equalising in the first five minutes. Play was mostly confined to mid- field until about ten minutes from time, when the .visitors attacked strongly, the goalkeeper _ _ _

having a warm five minute:, iticharason even- tually scoring from a corner. The home side strove hard to equalise, but found the defence too strong, the backs playing a strong, steady game and keeping th4m out of the circle. In the last minute Bainbridge, getting possession near the half-way line, ran through and scored a fourth goal for Stockton Heath. Result: Stockton Heath, four goals; Chorlton, two goals. . Stockton Heath complete their fixtures for this season to-day, when they visit Bebington on the Spittal ground.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING. Local Men in the International Race.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING. Local Men in the International Race.

To-day at Chesham, Bucks, the selected of England, Ireland, France, Scotland and Wales meet, and an interesting race should result. Warrington has a special interest owing to two members of the local club being included in the side representing England. Frank Antrobus resides at Moore, where he first saw the light 23 years ago; he is a natural runner, who trains very little, and his friends have every reason for holding the view that by closer application his many meritorious per- . - -

formance; of the past five years would be-ex- celled. This is his second appearance for Eng- land. and recent attention suggests that he will render a good account of himself. William Bolton, resident and born at War- rington 27 years ago. At 20 he started with the defunct Bewsey Wesleyans, then Sankey Har- riers found him a very reliable team unit; he has represented Warrington A.C. in the last four nationals (27th, 16th, 6th, Bth), and this season has won the five miles fiat and ten miles cross-country championships of his club. On the track he has recorded many successes; a little deficient in speed, but generally has enough at the finish to make the opposition wonder where he gets his running from. Mak- ing his second appearance for England.

div.head: BOWLING. PREPARE YOUR WOODS! The Season Is Fast Approaching.
div.p: BOWLING. PREPARE YOUR WOODS! The Season Is Fast Approaching.

Out of what preserving concoction you may have, just bring your woods and prepare, for the bowling season is now near at hand. Good prospects are reported from the majority of the clubs,. and, with a decent spell of weather, the greens should be in fine condition for the open- ing of the season. We have received the fol- lowing notification from Mr. Patrick, honorary secretary Warrington Works Association, 71, Legh-street :—The Inter-works Cup Competition will again be held for teams of 12 a-side. Entrance 6s. per team. All entries must be in writing and will he received by me up to eight o'clock on Saturday evening, April 4th. Handi- capping of teams and draw will take place dur- ing the following week at headquarters. The first round to commence on Saturday, April 18th. Entries—along with entrance fee—can be seht to me either at the above address, or to the Horse and ,Jockey, not later than Saturday, April 4th. All players to be registered at the same time of entering teams, and any works having more than one team entered, the players for each team must be registered separately to the Secretary. Eighteen names only can be registered for each team. You will assist the ' General Council when entering a team if you will state what you consider a fair start to any ! player, who did not take part in our coropeti- tions last season. When entering teams please notify Secretary of any date or dates your team cannot play, otherwise they will have to play on the date arranged at Council meeting."

div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT
ASSOCIATION.

The annual general meeting of the above Association Will be held in the Pelican Hotel on Tuesday. Amongst the business to be trans- acted appears the following: "To decide whether it would be advisable to run the Cham- pionship and Consolation Competitions on the system of eight players to comprise a team of home and away." "To revise the entrance fee to the Association, so that the Championship and Consolation winners may have better value and furthermore if the above motion is carried, the Association will have to find more prize money on account of more players participating in the Competitions." The statement of accounts shows that there is a balance in hand of Bs. 3d. The total income was .255 Sc. id.

NEW -WARRINGTON PLAYERS'.
Three Promising Youngsters.

The Warrington Committee have signed on three new and promising players. Two come from Pemberton, and they signed the Warring- ton form on Saturday. They are James Taberner and John Nicholls. They are smart wing players, and with a little bringing out should make smart men. Both men are about,22 years of age, and for- merly have been sought after by several other League clubs, so Warrington seem to have done a smart bit of business in signing on the lads. The committee have also signed on a local lad of promise, George Shepheard, a forward, who has played with the Butchers' team. He is 23 years of age and turns the scale at over 14 stone.

First Division.
Rylands' Recs. V. Flixton.

At Flixton. Rylands' were short of Warren, Laws, Stretford, Mason and Gallop, the first four being on the injured list. Flixton winning the toss, Morris kicked off for Rylands'. Good play by A. Hill took the game right into their opponents' territory. From a mark A. Burgess failed at goal. There was a strong wind blow- ing from goal to goal,. and Flixton taking ad- vantage of this began to force matters, but the defence of the " Wiremen " held good, half-time arriving with a clean sheet. Flixton commenced the second half against the wind, and Rylands' began to press. The game at this point started to get rough, and! Floyd, of Rylands' and Hough, of Flixton, were sent off for fighting. Riley scored for Rylands'. Morris failed at goal. From a pass by Riley, liorrocks went over the line, but in trying to get under the posts was tackled, the referee award- ing w dead ball. Whittaker, of Rylands', was sent oft, a rough game ending in favour of Rylands' by one try (three points) to Flixton, nil. Teams for To-day.

div.head: LIVELY DOINGS IN WIDNES.
div.p: LIVELY DOINGS IN WIDNES.

Three brothers, Thomas, William and John Roach, residing in Cromwell-street, Widnes, were charged on Monday with being drunk and disorderly, and assaulting Sergeant Watersou and Police-c6nstal)les Chester and If aydon. All pleaded not guilty.—lt was stated that a ser- geant requested the three to go home, and then found it necessary to arrest Thomas; The othei two then attacked the sergeant and Constable Haydon. A melee took place; the street lamps were turned out, and the officers were handi- capped by the increasing crowd.—Thomas Roach was fined 40s. or a month, William and John 20s. or one month each.
It was announced on Saturday that the dis- pute in the silk trade at Brighouse, which has been in progress over six months and which a few weeks ago took. a very critical turn, had been settled.

FRIENDLY MATCHES. Emmanuel Old Boys V. Seedley. Played at Liverpool, on the Aigburth Vale enclosure. The visitors lost the toss and Mil- lington started the game before a large crowd. Good combination between Rowe and Allen re- sulted in the latter hitting the cross-bar with a strong shot, but Wilkinson cleared from the rebound, and broughton, gaining possession, drew the defence and placed to Donaghy, who opened the scoring from short range, Smerdon immediately afterwards adding another with a fast grounder, which curled into the net off the post. The Old Boys now asserted themselves, and Thompson was repeatedly called upon to clear his charge. Rowe eventually beating him with a beauty. The Seedley defence had many anxious, moments, the visitors doing everything but score. Miflington made a great effort, but be was brought down, and Wainwright dashing up netted, only to be ruled off-side. Thompson just before the interval made several fine saves, and he ialone prevented the Old Boys from draw- ing level. Interval: Seedley, two goals; Em- manuel Old Boys, one goal. The play on resuming was very fast, both sides playing good football. Broughton, receiv- ing from Donaghy, had a fine chance, but shot outside, while at the other end the Old Boys. made many fine attempts to equalise, but the homesters' defence was very sound. Allen broke away and finished with a fine centre, Mil- lington heading through. Encouraged by their success, the Old Boys came again, and Wain- wright gave them the lead, beating Thompson easily. Seedley livened up, and play was very exciting, Donaghy eventually equalising the scores. This finished the scoring, and a good game ended in a draw of three goals each.

div.head: CURIOUS INCIDENT.
div.p: A CURIOUS INCIDENT.

The Stockton Heath Club should have played their return fixture with Weston, but only eight die.eatlhiesejdoutre: Y, and, on their arrival had left their outfit at home. The Weston officials, anxious to have a game for their players, secured the loan of a set aptlawyeerssto rana, of shirts, but the visitors refused to play with- out a full outfit. Crosfield's Reserve played their return fixture with the Weaver Refiners at Acton Bridge, and after a match in which there was plenty of scoring abilities shown they won by five goals against three. In the Warrington Medal Competition St. Barnabas' defeated Fairfield in their postponed tie. The match between Bank Quay Recs. and Wilderspool could not be finished owing to the bursting of the ball at the interval. The home club were not in the position to supply another, and the gathe had to be abandoned. The Latchford Works Competition matches are in full swing, and some interesting and keenly. fought games have been witnessed during the week. The support at these matches has been very satisfactory-, and there is a prospect of the club's funds being recuperated from the result of the competition.

NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. First Division. Crosfield's v. Lymm. - On the Thelwall-lane ground. Crosfield's were without the services of Poster and Worra.ll, and the visitors were short of Hind and Clare. Crosfield's, getting into theft( stride, became aggressive, and after ,several fruitless efforts Clemo opened the score. This success put Crosfield's on good terms with themselves and they continued to confine the play in the Lymin quatters and were awarded a Penalty, from which Clemo registered a second goal. The visitors tried hard to reduce the arrears, but failed to get past the home defence. Whitfield scored again and Crosfield's were leading at the, interval by three goals to none. On resuming, Lymm now had more of the game and they made a few attacks on Crosfield's citadel, Watson scoring for Lymm with a good shot. Crosfield's now played, hard to retain their lead, and the game was very interesting. The defence on both sides showed up very well, and towards the close Crosfield's began to gain the upper hand. The Lymm defenders had a very busy time. Whitfield Scored the fourth goal for Crosfield's, and later the same player was successful in registering a .fifth goal, thus completing the "hat trick." Time was shortly afterwards called with the result: Crosfield's, five goals; Lymm, one goal. Mobberley Amateurs v. Latchford. The Latchford team should have made the journey to Mobberley to meet the Amateurs, but received a letter cancelling the engagement and a statement to the effect that the .Amateurs had withdrawn from the League owing to their in- ability to raise a team.

DELIVERY OF BOTTLED STOUT.

div.head: Prosecution of Warrington Brewers.
div.p: Prosecution of Warrington Brewers.

The Widnes magistrates on Thursday dis- missed a case on payment of costs, brought by the police against Matthew Cunningham, of Cunningham Brothers, bottlers, Warrington. The charge was of unlawfully selling beer on March 12 at 17, Eleanor-street, Widnes, not being quthorised by licence. Mr. Knowles prosecuted, and Mr. Madden de- fended. Defendaat pleaded not guilty. For the prosecution it was stated that on March 11 a traveller called at 17. Eleanor-street, which was in the occupation of P.C. Wilson and his wife. He said he called from Cunningham's, and Wilson asked what was the usual order. Henegan replied, "Half a dozen bottles of stout," whereupon Wilson handed him 2s. On the 12th Sergt. Moseley was secreted in the parlour, when the stout was delivered. The stout bottles had no labels or descriptive marks, and they were taken out of a box containing two dozen and placed in a smaller box before being handed in at the door. Inspector Bannister, who was close at hand, drew the carter's attention to the bottles hav- ing no labels, and asked him how he knew the bottles delivered were for Mr. Wilson. The carter thereupon, said the sergeant, produced some labels which were lying about. Continuing, the prosecution said that the de- fendant, if proved guilty, was liable to a fine of XSO. -

—,„.. P.C. Wilson gave evidence of the order and payment of 2s. In answer to Mr. Madden he denied all knowledge that his wife had sent a postcard for a 'standing order with Cunning- ham's for half a dozen stout to be delivered each week since November, 1912. Mr. Madden: Did you tell your superintend- ent about this order? Witness: N0,.1 did not. For the defence, Mr. Madden said in such a business as Cunningham's the law was that the orders must be accepted at the brewery as licensed premises, and that the goods must be previously appropriated. In this case the post- card constituted a valid order, and the stout in question was really appropriated and purchased sixteen months ago. Cross-examined by Mr. Knowles, defendant said that he held a licence for Frogball-lane, Warrington. The stout sent to Widnes was --ken from Owen-street, for which he had no
licence. The Bench agreed that a technical offence had been committed and dismissed the case on payment of costs.

div.head: DIS rRicT NEWS. PADGATE.
div.p: DIS rRicT NEWS. PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—On Thursday evening Mr. and Mrs. Gipsy Evens, of Liverpool, paid their an- , nual visit. There was a large attendance, and Dr. Ferguson presided. Mrs. Gipsy Evens sang the solo "For whom Christ died," and Mr. Gipsy Evens, in his excellent address entitled "Luminaries of a darkened city," gave some humorous and pathetic incidents of their work in the Liverpool Mission. At the close a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Gipsy Evens and Dr. Ferguson was proposed by Mr. Lunt and sec- onded by Mrs. J. Dakin.

div.head: LATE REV. G. W. DICKINSON. Impressive Scenes at the Funeral Service.
div.p: THE LATE REV. G. W. DICKINSON. Impressive Scenes at the Funeral Service.

One of the most impressive funerals ever wit- nessed at Padgate took place on Saturday, when the Rev. .G. W. Dickinson, the vicar, was laid to rest in the Parish Churchyard. The service was attended by the Bishop of Liverpool and about 30 other clergymen, who were friends of the dead Vicar. A stately pro- cession was headed by girls from the Sunday Schoel and members of the Young Women's Class, who carried wreaths and other floral tri- butes. Then came the choir, the clergy, and members of the church and its organisations. Canon Morley Stevenson read the prayers and Archdeacon Spooner read the lessons. The Bishop of Liverpool gave a short, touching address

The five years the Vicar had been in Padgate, said the Bishop, had been marked with acts of many kindnesses. I have heard of not a few, continued his Lordship. His name, his income his strength were devoted to the furtherance of the work which he loved. You can think now of words that he spoke, of kind acts that he did for you; you can remember, above all, the fra- grance of his life.

Just as when the western sky after sunset blazes with a hundred lights, the after-glow IS often more beautiful than the light of noon, so the memory of some good man who has lived and moved amongst us becomes more beautiful and potent when he has gone than his ministry was While, be lived.

If you wish to show that you loved your late minister, reznerober—and remember in the best Carrying vtlt the .."ret,erts be taught FM completedo tk and living the life he set before yeth by As the cortege was filing out of • the Aura Mr. F. 131ackwell, the organist, played the Dead March ,4 „ a from rm Saul." ..ie titßheisio graveside the ser- vice

MEMORIAL TRIBUTES._ Canon Morley Stevenson, preaching in the Warrington Parish Church on Sunday morn- ing, Paid it warm tribute to the late Vicar. Mr, Dickinson's bright, genial disposition made him friends wherever be worked. At the evening service the Dead March was played by the organist, Mr. F. Darby, and the chop: sang a special anthem. Special memorial services were held a the Padgate Church on Sunday. The choir sang appropriate hymns- and the Dead March was ' played. - The Rev. Canon Willis, preaching in the morning, said Mr. Dickinson had three noted qualities. The first was affection. It was im- pulsive and energetic. He had a genuine love for his people and for children. He was also courageous. He was never afraid to let men know what his convictions were. The third point was his unfeigned piety. The Rev. J. M. Bnckmaster, who preached in the evening, also paid -a tribute to the late Vicar's work and life: GUARDIANS' .CONDOLENCE, At the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of . Guardians, held on Wednesday, Mi. E. L. Bent presidinc, a vote of 'condolence was Passed with the family of the late Rev. U. W. Dickinson, who was the Chaplain at the Cottage Homes.
Mr. Bent said they all lamented his death, for he was an able minister and highly esteemed by all the Guardians, and particularly the members of the Cottage Homes Committee.

EDDIS BURY. Liberal Meeting.—Speaking at a meeting 'in support of Dr. Hayward, the prospective Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury Division at Tarpor- ley on Saturday, Mr. C. W. Tomkinsori, of WU- lington Hall, said the Home Rule question over- shadowed politics at present, but he thought that the seriousness of the situation in Ulster was being a good deal exaggerated. 'After all, they must remember that newspaper owners were like other tradesmen—they had got to do the best they could for the goods they had to sell. Some of the newspapers at the present time were findin,g that the Ulster question was making their papers sell very well, to they were doing their best to make it as exciting as they possibly could. Dr. Hayward said that 411 the bother about Ulster was not made by Ulstermen, nor for Ulster; it was made by other people for the purpose of frustrating the Parliament Act. That Was why Ulster had been stirred up and strife fomented. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: MASTER SMITHS
div.p: THE MASTER SMITHS
First Annual Dinner of the Newly- Formed Association.
BOROUGH SEWAGE SCHEME.
Business troubles vanished into smoke, and anvils and hammers were forsaken, when, at the Royal Oak Hotel on Wednesday night, the newly-formed Master Smiths' Association held its first annual dinner.

There were no signs of competition, except it was to rival one another in the art of merry- making, and the unanimous verdict of the com- pany was that the foundations of their associa- tion had been well and truly laid. Mr. J. Robson Chorley presided over the genial gather- ing. THE ASSOCIATION'S BENEFIT. The CHAIRMAN, in proposing the toast of thk "Warrington Master Sirkiths Association," saiu it gave him pleasure to be present at their first annual dinner. The association had been al- ready of great benefit to them all and had pro- moted a good feeling amongst the members, and now they all regarded one another as friends, instead of enemies, as used to be the case. Ili, trusted it would continue to prosper.

• PRACTICAL UNANIMITY. Mr. GEORGE ALLEN, responding, said they as an association were only infants, for they ' only amalgamated on September 26th last year, but, nevertheless, they already had between 30 and 40 members. Their work up to the present had been very good, and, taking the town in general, they were practically unanimous, and those who had not thrown in their lot would do so at an early date.

They had a lot of hard work in preparing a schedule of prices, but that they had drawn up would not drive the trade away, but keep it in the town. They were not banding for the policy of grab all, but were trying a • little more friendly competition than in the past. (Hear, hear.) Their meetings had been an education to all, for they had been educating one an- (Apowise)

TOWN ANti tfiAbE 6.0 WARRINGTON. Councillor J. BROADHURST, in proposing tll6 toast, said that he had travelled long distances, and he was quite justified in saying that they had a town of which they had no need to be ashamed. They might not be able to boast of beautiful buildings, but from his experience he thought that their sanitary arrangements wem second to none in Britain. That was saying a great deal, but he (lid feel justified in saying that, they could not learn much from other municipalities.

..... Altbough they were the master smiths, every member round the tables were as much working men as any employe in the town. They were closely connected with the iron and steel trade, and that trade was an object lesson to the whole of Great Britain. In these times of crises and strife in reference to trade union matters, there were no disputes amongst the employer and employe of the iron trade, there was no cessation of work, and no downing tools, for both worked amicably through their Conciliation and Arbi- tration Board. He was only sorry the trade unions in the town could not form their unions on the same principle to settle all the little grievances which arose. It would be in the interests of the employer and employed to adopt some similar system by which there would be no cessation of work. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

"TOO PROGRESSIVE." Councillor G. ARCHER, replying, said that if the suggestion by Councillor Broadhurst could take effect it would, bring about a much better state of things. There was no doubt that the town had made rapid progress during the last 20 years. However, there was a tendency at the present time, and he thought many ratepayers would agree, to be a little too progressive. When they considered that the tradesmen were burdened with high rates he thought it was high time that those in authority should bring about a pulling-up process. (Hear, hear.) Posterity ought to take a little of the burden. (Hear, hear.)

With regard to the extension of the Town he•said that the time was not ripe for an expenditure of ,t 30,000 or ,t 40,000. Warrington at present had sufficient burdens on its shoul- ders for many years to come. ,(Hear, hear.) Councillor Broadhurst was under the impression that Warrington was up-to-date from a sanitary and sewaging point of view., He, however, thought that the plant that was sufficient foi 25,000 people was not sufficient for 73,000, and it behoved the present generation to realise the fact that the seweraging of the town was not up, to the requirements. It was a mighty pro- blem and one that would have to be faced. He suggested that a nucleus fund be formed and money set aside every year, so that when the time came for tackling the question the burden would not be too great. (Hear, hear.) The nucleus would grow and grow, and they would be able to meet the difficulty without rushing the town into a sudden expenditure of a quarter of a million sterling. (Hear, hear.)

OTHER TOASTS. Mr. S. PICKTON proposed the toast of "The Visitors,' Mr. PAIN responding; whilst the toast of "The Artistes" was honoured on the propo- sition of Mr. WILSON, Mr. A. E. Mow respond- ing, _

• Mr. P. MATHER proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mr. W. ALLEN seconding. A pleasing entertainment was sustained by Mr. W. Moores, Conncillor,-Archer, and Coun- cillor Broadhurst, Mr. A. E. Trow accompany- ing.

CHAPLAIN'S STIPEND.
Warrington Guardians Discuss the Living Wage Question.

div.head: AN AMUSING DIZOUSSION.
div.p: AN AMUSING DIZOUSSION.

The question of paying a living wage to a chaplain was raised at the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday. The matter arose over appointing a successor to the late Rev. G. W. Dickinson as chaplain at the Cottage Homes. Mr. BRooEs said that the I)..st way would he to appoint whoever was given the living. (Hear. hear.) Mr. MATHER : That is right, and I have no doubt that the Rector of Warrington, who is the patron of the living, will see that the in- struction to the children at the Homes is not neglected. (Hear, hear.) The CLERIC: Will you leave the matter for the present, pending the appointment of a -succes- sor?

This course was agreed to. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL said that if the sti- pend of the chaplain were. increased it would give him more interest in the social and spiri- tual work he was called upon to do. Mr. GARNETT : If that is so, it ,onght to be the rule all round. Mr. Bracecamp only gets 4;75 for his attendance here twice in the week time, on Sundays, and special calls. It is little enough for .1;1 is. per day on Sundays.

div.head: LOVE OF THE WORK.
div.p: LOVE OF THE WORK.

Mrs. SIMPSON : If the love of souls is in the heart of the chaplains they will not do their work for pay. If a man is devoted to God's work he will be willing to do a little voluntary work and make some sacrifice, not seeking to be paid for trying to win souls for heaven. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GARNETT : If you ,will only put it on a ttade union basis and pay what is a fair wage for a fair day's work, you will agree £lO for visiting the Homes is little enough, and the .175 for Mr. Bracecamp and £5O for the Roman Catholic instructor are inadequate amounts. Mr. DALE: What about the Nonconformists? D 2 their 1114.1erers r:rothinq for the inmates v ? Mr. DALE i ROW much do they get? The CIIAIRMAN : Nothing.

div.head: SOMETHING SUBSTANTIAL.
div.p: SOMETHING SUBSTANTIAL.

The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Mrs. Simpson has said something which I appreciate very much, but at the same time what was said does not help to pay your grocer's bill or pay your tailor. We require— Mr. MATHER, : Something substantial. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: A living wage. Something ought to be done to increase the sti- pend of the chaplain of the Cottage Homes. If it is desirable .to give notice of motion I do so.
The CHAIRMAN: I don't think it is necessary at this point. Leave it till the appointment is made.
1,110 Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Right. Mr. DALE: How are the Nonconformists covered?
_ . The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: By the English chaplains.
Mr. DALE : Is there a Nonconformist service held?
Mr. GARNETT: Here or at Padgate? Mr. DALE: Here?
The CHAIRMAN: Yes, on Wednesday 'evenings. Mrs. SIMPSON : They give their services.

div.head: WORKHOUSE NAMES./
div.p: WORKHOUSE NAMES./
Mr. W. FLANAGHAN said there was a tendency to give workhouses another name instead of workhouse.

Mr. Mather laughed loudly. Mr. FLANAMIAN : You may laugh as long as you like, but we find by reading the papers that at various place they have altered the name and called them institutions or some other names, and. I think we ought to fall in line. ,I suggest that in future this institution shall be given the name of t 4 "Guardian-street' Hospital," or " The Winmarleigh Hospital." The CLERK explained that the matter would be considered by the sub-committee appointed to go into the New Order. They had met on three or four occasions, and they would consider that matter at a future meeting. The matter was referred to the sub-committee.

div.head: PRESENTATION.
div.p: A PRESENTATION.

It was decided to ask the Chairman, Mr. Rent, to present, on behalf of the Guardians, officers and staff of • both institutions, as well as the outdoor officers, a diamond ring to Miss Biggin, the late superintendent nurse. Reference was made to. the excellent work done by Miss Biggin by various Guardians.

UNPLEASANT TERMINATION. In moving the confirmation of the minutes, Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said that what was reported about Mr. Brown was a somewhat unpleasant termination to his services. Various Ways of Saying "Howdy D 4." • "How do you 'do?" That's Tlglish and American. "How do you find yourself?", That's French. "How do you stand?" That's Italian. "How do you find yourself?" That's German. How do you fare?" That's Dutch. ." How can you?" That's Swedish. "How do you perspire?" Egyptian. "How is your stomach? Have you eaten your rice?" That's Chinese. ' "How do you have yourself?" That's Polish. "How do you live on?" That's Russian. "May thy shadow never be less." That's Persian. And all mean much the same thing.

COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY PALATINE OF CHES- TER will be held at the COURT-HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on IMONDAI, the 6th day of APRIL NEXT, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Altrincham, Buck- low, Dnkinfield, Middlewich, Sandbach, Congle- ton, Northwieh; Pilestbury, and Stockport, form- ing tile linutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Divisions will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the COURT-HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 6th day of APRIL NEXT, at ' 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the CASTLE OF CHESTER on WEDNESDAY, the Bth day of APRIL NEXT, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The haring of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Broxton, Chester Castle. Daresbury, Eddisbury. Nantwich, Run- corn, Winsford, and Wirral, forming the Ches- ter District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from the last-mentioned Divisions will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the CASTLE OF CHESTER at ,the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the Bth day of APRIL NEXT, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County Palatine of Chester. Chester, 19th March, 1914.

LORD NEWTON AND KNUTSFORD TORIES. No Civil War to Take Place in Ulster. Lord Newton, addressing the Knutsford Divi- sion Conservative and Unionist Assodation on Saturday, expressed the view that there would be no civil war in Ireland. In the first place, he did not consider the Government possessed the ability to wage civil war or war of any kind. The Government had been waging war on Mrs. Pankhurst for a number of years and had not succeeded in defeating her. But in the case of Ulster, they had 110,000 grimly determined men, and the Government had at last given up the idea that they were impostors. It seemed improbable that 110,000 men could successfully defy the whole force of the British Government, but he was told on high authority that the utmost military force which the Gov- ernment could put into the field to coerce Ulster only amounted to 4,500 men. That sounded grotesque, but it was perfectly obvious that if there was civil war it would not be confined to Ulster, and troops would be required to stop the disturbances which were sure to break out up and down the country. The Rev. David Barnett, pastor of the Black- ford Bridge Congregational Church, Bury, inti- mated to his congregation on Sunday night that he had decided to accept the " call" to the pas- torate of the Clayton Congregational Church, Manchester. The local authorities whose areas adjoin the boundaries of Birkenheail are intimating theii intention to oppose the Bill by which the Cor- poration seek powers to run motor 'buses in the outside areas. , ;10,, •

Novelty Which Prevents Thieving. A novel burglar alarm has been placed on the market in Germany, composed of a small metal disc, circular in shape, which may easily be car- ried in the vest pocket. It is so arranged that a detonating cap may be inserted and, so loaded, it becomes a terror to sneak thieves. Suppose a traveller is staying in a strange hotel and finds that he cannot lock his door. lie places a chair against the door, and slips the disc under one of its legs. Should anyone attempt to enter the room the chair is forced out of position, the disc flies open and the cap explodes, awakening the sleeper. The disc may be used under bag- gage, in purses, under bicycle or automobile tyres, and in many other ways.
